title: Make report_internal_error report the correct pickleable exception type
body:
## Description

`report_internal_error()` makes sure `exc` is pickleable, but doen't do the same for its type. So if `_type` returned by sys.exc_info() is unpickleable, it causes an error during serialization.

This PR normalizes both the exception instance and its type before constructing ExceptionInfo.

title: Bump version: 5.7.0rc1 → 5.7.0
Make beat's pidbox stop test tolerate slow runners
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html) & [Anti AI spamming Guidelines] (https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/10932). Before opening an AI based PR make sure you asked
in the discussion forum or in the related open issues first.


## Description

Fixes #11023

`test_stop_interrupts_a_connect_that_is_backing_off` failed in the `Unit (pypy3.11)` job on `main` ([run 41840761477](https://github.com/celery/celery/actions/runs/41840761477/job/126611417157)) and passed when the job was re-run on the same commit. The test gave `stop()` 0.3 s to join the consumer thread, which is too little on a slow runner, even though `stop()` did interrupt the backoff.

Only the test changes:

- It waits on an event set by the fake backoff instead of `sleep(0.1)`, so `stop()` always comes during the backoff the test is about.
- `pb.join_timeout` is 5 s instead of 0.3 s. The fake backoff now runs until the test ends it, instead of for 2 s. A `stop()` that can't interrupt the backoff still times out and fails, and the `finally` ends the backoff so the thread doesn't outlive the test.

A passing run still takes about 0.01 s.

### Tests

- The CI failure is timing-dependent, and I couldn't trigger it on demand: 100 runs on CPython 3.14 with all 10 cores busy, and 12 runs each in a PyPy 3.11 container (8.0.1) with `coverage run` and one CPU shared with 3 busy loops, all passed on `main`. To simulate a slow runner, I added `time.sleep(0.5)` to the `except BaseException` path in `BeatPidbox._connect()`:

  | Test | With the delay |
  | --- | --- |
  | on `main` | fails with `assert <Thread(BeatPidbox, ...)> is None`, as in CI |
  | this PR | passes in 0.67 s |

- Mutations of `celery/beat.py`, against this PR's test:

  | Change | Result |
  | --- | --- |
  | `_connect()` doesn't pass `callback=self._abort_if_stopping` | fails after 5 s |
  | `_abort_if_stopping()` never raises | fails after 5 s |

- `pytest t/unit/app/test_beat.py`: 167 passed, 2 skipped. pre-commit passes on the file.

title: Drop the unreachable get() and assert in test_soft_time_limit_exceeding_time_limit
body:
`test_soft_time_limit_exceeding_time_limit` wrapped three statements in its `pytest.raises` block:

```python
result = soft_time_limit_must_exceed_time_limit.apply_async()
result.get(timeout=5)

assert result.status == 'FAILURE'
```

`apply_async()` is what raises. The check is the first statement in `Task.apply_async()`, at `celery/app/task.py` line 710, before anything connects to the broker. So `result` is never assigned, and neither the `get()` nor the `assert` can run. This drops all three for the bare call, and drops `@flaky` with them, since the test makes no network call. It needs no broker and passes in 0.06s.

What the test does and does not catch, mutating that guard:

| mutation | caught |
| --- | --- |
| check removed | yes |
| `>` to `<` | yes |
| `>` to `>=` | no |
| `time_limit` guard dropped | no |
| `soft_time_limit` guard dropped | no |

The two it catches were caught before this change as well, but took 41s and 6s, because `get()` sat waiting on a timeout that cannot arrive. The three misses are what ChristianMurphy's suggested unit test covers. I ran that test against all five mutations and it caught each one, so I am happy to open it as a follow-up replacing `test_soft_time_limit_failure`.

title: Don't store RETRY for an ignored result when retrying after a lost worker
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html) & [Anti AI spamming Guidelines] (https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/10932). Before opening an AI based PR make sure you asked
in the discussion forum or in the related open issues first.


## Description

Fixes #11008

With `task_retry_on_worker_lost`, `Request._retry_worker_lost()` wrote `RETRY` to the result backend even when the request's result is ignored. That happens when the task has `ignore_result=True`, or when only the call sets `apply_async(ignore_result=True)`, which the retry keeps since #10958. The retried run of an ignored result stores nothing, so the task stayed at `RETRY` for good. `Task.retry()` doesn't write `RETRY` in that case (`TraceInfo.handle_retry()` checks `store_errors`).

The fix checks `self.store_errors` before `mark_as_retry()`, as the other failure paths in `Request` already do. With `store_errors_even_if_ignored`, `RETRY` is still stored. The retry message, the ack, the `task-retried` event, `on_retry` and the `task_retry` signal are unchanged.

### Tests

- `test_on_failure_WorkerLostError_retry_on_worker_lost_ignore_result`, for an ignored result set on the task and on the call. Both cases fail on `main` with `Expected 'mark_as_retry' to not have been called. Called 1 times.` and pass here.
- `test_on_failure_WorkerLostError_retry_on_worker_lost_store_errors_even_if_ignored` keeps `RETRY` stored with that option. It passes on `main` too, and fails if the new condition is inverted. Removing the condition makes the first test fail.
- `t/unit/worker` and `t/unit/tasks`: 2102 passed, 3 skipped, 1 xfailed. flake8 and isort are clean on the changed files.
- The reproduction from #11008, with a prefork worker whose pool process is killed: on `main` the result stays `RETRY` after the retry succeeds, and with this change it stays `PENDING`, the same as a retry through `Task.retry()`.

Not run: integration and smoke tests. I don't have Docker here, and killing a pool process needs a smoke test. I haven't added one, and can if you want it.

### CI

`Unit (3.14, windows-latest)` fails with two DST tests that this change doesn't touch. `main` fails the same way on every run since tzdata 2026.6 was released, e.g. [98b7ba94a](https://github.com/celery/celery/actions/runs/41591733086/job/125769775695). That's #11010, fixed by #11011.

title: Run the mock assertions that sit inside pytest.raises
body:
Three mock assertions sit inside `with pytest.raises(...)`, below the call that raises, so none of them has ever run.

Two of them also patch the wrong module, which is why moving them out is not enough on its own.

## `test_get_timeout` and `test_get_timeout_longer`

Both patch `celery.result.time`, but the polling sleep is `time.sleep(nap)` in `celery/backends/base.py`. `celery/result.py` only uses `time.monotonic`. So `_time.sleep` could never have been called.

Moving the assertion out unchanged fails:

```
E           Expected: sleep(0.001)
E             Actual: not called.
```

Repointing the patch at `celery.backends.base.time` makes both pass. They now guard the calculation that the surrounding comment exists for:

```python
nap = interval if timeout is None else min(interval, timeout - time_elapsed)
time.sleep(nap)
```

`test_get_timeout` asserts `sleep(0.001)` for `timeout=0.001, interval=0.001`, and `test_get_timeout_longer` asserts `sleep(1)` for `timeout=1, interval=1`, so between them they cover the `min()` both ways.

## `test_on_blocking`

This one needed only the assertion moved out. `_on_blocking` calls `inspect.getframeinfo(frame)` to build its message before raising, so the assertion holds once it runs.

## Verification

`t/unit/tasks/test_result.py` and `t/unit/utils/test_debug.py`: 149 passed, 1 skipped.

Each assertion was also checked individually in three states: as written it passes vacuously, moved out unchanged it fails, and moved out with the correct patch target it passes.

There is a fourth instance of the same shape at `t/integration/test_tasks.py:650` in `test_soft_time_limit_exceeding_time_limit`, left out of this PR because it needs a live broker to verify.

title: Fix#10997 - redis chord claim cleanup ownership
body:
## Description

Fixes #10997.

Concurrent deliveries of the final Redis chord header task could both observe a completed chord and publish its callback, sometimes with missing results after one worker cleaned up the chord.

## Implementation

- `CHORD_PART_RETURN_LUA` atomically deduplicates each header task completion, records the result, detects readiness, and acquires a dispatch claim with `SET NX EX` and a unique token.
- Only the worker that acquired the claim restores and joins the header results and publishes the callback.
- Immediately before publishing, a token-checked Lua script extends the claim TTL. It does not replace a different token or recreate an expired claim. The lease estimates Kombu's nested reconnect/retry budget using the callback's effective `retry` and `retry_policy` options (including signature overrides), retry intervals, and `broker_connection_timeout`. If retry count or connection timeout is unbounded, the bounded fallback is twice the initial claim TTL. This estimates connection retry time, not the full publish duration: transport writes or waiting for publisher confirmation can outlast the lease. Time spent restoring/joining also occurs before the extension.
- Cleanup uses Lua to verify token ownership, delete `.j`, `.t`, `.s`, and `.d`, and replace the claim with a `done` marker. Late duplicate completions are ignored. Initializing a chord size deletes an earlier `.c` key so applying a frozen chord again with the same group ID starts a new run.

## Failure semantics

The claim prevents concurrent workers from dispatching the same chord body while the owner retains a valid lease. A worker crash after acquiring the claim but before successfully publishing the callback can lose the callback until the claim expires and a later header delivery retries. When `result_chord_join_timeout` is `None`, the initial claim still has a bounded 10-second lifetime; an unusually long restore or join can outlast it before the publishing extension starts. Unbounded publish retries or connection timeouts cannot be covered by a finite extension, so those configurations get an extension twice the initial claim TTL. A callback publish or confirmation wait that runs longer than its lease can still permit another worker to acquire a claim. The extension reduces duplicate dispatch during a slow publish within the estimated reconnect/retry budget, but cannot eliminate every duplicate or loss window. This is not an exactly-once callback delivery guarantee.

## Tests and validation

- `python -m pytest t/unit/backends/test_redis.py -q`: 201 passed. Includes Python mock-client tests and Lua execution with fakeredis/lupa.
- `python -m pytest t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py -q`: 406 passed, 1 xfailed, 31 subtests passed.
- `python -m pytest t/unit/backends/test_base.py -q`: 198 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files celery/backends/redis.py t/unit/backends/test_redis.py t/integration/test_canvas.py`: all hooks passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Added a retry-budget test for three retries, a four-second broker connection timeout, and default retry intervals; it asserts a 41-second reconnect/retry estimate and checks the bounded fallback.
- Added `test_reapplying_frozen_chord_dispatches_body_again` to `t/integration/test_canvas.py`. The attempted run, `python -m pytest t/integration/test_canvas.py -k reapplying_frozen_chord -q`, could not start its worker because the configured AMQP broker at `127.0.0.1:5672` refused the connection. No real Redis integration result is claimed.

body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 2.3.1 to 2.4.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Mypy 2.4

We've just uploaded mypy 2.4.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Python 3.15 Support

Mypy 2.4 supports running on Python 3.15 and type checking most Python 3.15 features. This includes the new builtin sentinel type for sentinel values (PEP 661), which mypy now supports (see below for details). Lazy imports (PEP 810) and unpacking in comprehensions (PEP 798) are also supported. Closed TypedDicts (PEP 728) have been supported since mypy 2.2, but the extra_items TypedDict argument, also introduced in PEP 728, is still unsupported. Support for extra_items will be added in a future mypy release.

Native Parser Enabled by Default

Mypy now uses the new native parser by default. It's based on the Ruff parser, and it's significantly faster than the legacy parser, which uses the stdlib ast module. The native parser also has other benefits:

  • You can target newer Python versions and use recent Python syntax even when running mypy on an older Python version. For example, you can use --python-version 3.15 when running mypy on Python 3.14.
  • Stub files can use syntax that is newer than the target Python version. For example, stubs can use the PEP 695 generic class syntax (class Box[T]: ...) when running on or targeting Python 3.10.
  • Parallel type checking requires the native parser.

The legacy parser is still available through --no-native-parser, or native_parser = False in the config file (native_parser = false under [tool.mypy] in pyproject.toml). We are planning to remove the legacy parser in early 2027. If you run into a problem with the native parser, please report it on the issue tracker.

Unlike the legacy parser, the native parser doesn't support type comments for variables defined by for and with statements. These type comments are silently ignored, and the types of the variables are

title: Wait between retries when the broker refuses a callback publish
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html) & [Anti AI spamming Guidelines](https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/10932). Before opening an AI based PR make sure you asked
in the discussion forum or in the related open issues first.

## Description

Fixes #10725. Related integration contract: #10726.

When the broker briefly refuses a link, chain step or chord body, wait between publish attempts using the callback's merged retry policy. Retry each message separately so links already accepted by the broker are not sent again, and preserve `retry=False` and custom `retry_errors`.

The parent body runs once. Exhausted callback retries use normal failure and errback handling. A backend `OperationalError` after successful dispatch keeps the existing internal-error handling. Worker-side `max_retries=None` uses the application's finite limit, falling back to three retries if necessary. Backoff occupies the worker slot until publication succeeds or the limit is reached.

The worker tests use RabbitMQ publisher confirms and a full `reject-publish` queue, with Redis results. They observe actual broker refusals rather than counting publish signals. Custom worker/queue coverage lives in the smoke suite, including early/late acknowledgements, solo/threads/prefork, quorum queues, chain failure propagation, and two links where only the second is refused.

Validation:

- 42 smoke cases passed without reruns at `4683f6c43` against RabbitMQ 4.2.5 and Redis 7.4.10. The later warning and result-write follow-ups were checked with unit regressions; that smoke matrix was not rerun for them.
- Current follow-up: 737 focused AMQP, tracer, chord and backend unit tests passed. New tests cover callback/chain result-write errors and bounded retry policies. All three targeted mutation checks fail their regression assertions. The earlier seven code-removal checks passed at `c42cf667a`.
- Regression controls reproduce the lost callback on main and duplicate accepted links with the earlier group-level retry implementation.
- Configured file hooks, including mypy, and whitespace checks passed.

The full platform matrix remains for CI. Local API/configuration documentation checks report the same existing errors on unchanged main and this branch.

title: fix: prevent worker hang in WorkerLostError when result_backend_always_retry=True
body:
## Description

Fixes #10957.

As noted by @MehrazRumman in the review of #10752, the `_success_was_stored` check uses `backend.get_state()` which goes through `get_task_meta() -> _ensure_retryable()`. If the result backend is down and `result_backend_always_retry` is enabled (with the default `inf` max retries), this call will retry indefinitely. Since `on_failure` runs in the worker's main process, this blocks the entire worker.

## Changes

- **Explicit bounded retry:** `_success_was_stored()` calls `backend._ensure_retryable(..., max_retries=min(backend.max_retries, 3))`. This caps retries for that call only while respecting a lower user-configured `result_backend_max_retries`. It does not mutate `backend.max_retries` (which is shared across threads when `result_backend_thread_safe=True`, and could otherwise cut short unrelated operations on the same backend object). Also fixed the retry log message in `_ensure_retryable` to report the per-call limit (`limit - retries`) instead of `self.max_retries - retries`.
- **Reverted broader changes:** Reverted the modifications in `_fail_chain` and `trace_task` per review, as they introduced regressions and didn't prevent the write hang.
- **Tests:** Added `test_repro_10957_requeue_with_failing_backend` (requeue path) and `test_repro_10957_does_not_hang_on_inf_retries` (uses `max_retries=inf` with a `_sleep` counter that raises after 10 calls; asserts `sleep_calls <= 3`, so it fails on `main`). Renamed `test_repro_10957_event_block_retries_on_backend_down` to `test_repro_10957_event_block_does_not_retry_on_backend_down` since the assertion is that no retries happen. Removed the obsolete `test_deduplicate_successful_tasks_uses_get_task_meta_for` (since `trace.py` was reverted). Restored deleted comments.

## Trade-off

As noted by @ChristianMurphy, a 3-retry limit handles short outages (~0.07s), but a longer pause (e.g., 2s) might exhaust the retries and incorrectly record a failure. The broader architectural fix for `mark_as_failure()` and a time-based retry budget are tracked in #10969.

The retry cap counts retries, not time. A hanging backend will wait for `redis_socket_timeout` per try (up to ~8 minutes with the default 120s), which is still bounded and prevents the infinite hang, unlike `main`.

title: Preserve ignore_result overrides across task retries
body:
## Description

I found this while working on #10953. I'm keeping this separate because I think it's worth its own PR.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Define a task that ignores results by default and retries once:
   ```python
   @app.task(bind=True, ignore_result=True)
   def retry_once(self):
       if not self.request.retries:
           raise self.retry(countdown=0)
       return 1
   ```
2. Explicitly request a stored result:
   ```python
   result = retry_once.apply_async(ignore_result=False)
   ```
3. The first attempt retries and records `RETRY`.

4. The retry loses the caller's override and uses the task's `ignore_result=True`. It succeeds, but does not record `SUCCESS`.

**Expected:** `SUCCESS`, with result `1`.  
**Actual:** The result remains stuck in `RETRY`.

This PR preserves `ignore_result` across retries.

title: fix(backends): track every AsyncResult waiting on a task id (GH-4925)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #4925.

`GroupResult.get()` and `AsyncResult.get()` hang forever on the redis and rpc result backends when a second `AsyncResult` exists for an id that is already pending, even though every task is in `SUCCESS`. Two deterministic triggers, both reproduced on `main` with a prefork worker:

```python
g = group(slow_add.s(1, 2, 1.0), slow_add.s(3, 4, 1.0))()
AsyncResult(g.results[0].id).state      # e.g. a progress poll
g.get(timeout=8)                        # TimeoutError, both members SUCCESS
```

```python
g = group(slow_add.s(1, 2, 1.0), slow_add.s(3, 4, 1.0))()
AsyncResult(g.results[0].id).get(timeout=8)   # TimeoutError, state SUCCESS
```

The second `AsyncResult` does not have to come from user code. Celery creates duplicates for the same id internally too (`freeze()`, `children`, `parent`), and whether the hang happens depends on when the garbage collector frees one, which is why it was reported as a random hang.

This is also why two integration tests had been marked `xfail(reason="Task is timeout")` since 2022: `test_group_results_in_chain` and `test_nested_chain_group_lone` both put a group in a chain, which freezes the members and applies them, creating exactly these duplicates. Both pass now, so their markers are removed.

## Root cause

`AsyncBackendMixin` kept one result object per task id in `_pending_results`:

- `remove_pending_result()` popped the entry **by id** and called `on_result_fulfilled()` (which cancels the redis subscription) without checking which object asked. `AsyncResult.__del__` calls it, so garbage collecting a throwaway `AsyncResult(member_id)` removed the group member's own entry and unsubscribed its channel. The member's result then arrived with nobody registered for it, was buffered, and `join_native()` waited for it forever.
- `_add_pending_result()` skipped any object whose id was already registered, so a second waiter for the same id was never tracked, and `on_state_change()` only ever filled the first one's cache.

## Changes

- `celery/backends/asynchronous.py`: `_pending_results` now holds the waiters for each id keyed by object identity. `on_state_change()` resolves every waiter, `_remove_pending_result()` removes only the object that asked, and `remove_pending_result()` only cancels the subscription once the last waiter for the id is gone. Weak waiters stay weak through a per-id `WeakValueDictionary`, and an empty one is dropped even when the cycle collector cleared the weak reference before `__del__` ran.
- `celery/backends/base.py`: initialise both mappings as plain dicts (the weak semantics moved one level down).
- `t/unit/backends/test_asynchronous.py`: tests for both triggers on the redis and rpc backends, for cancelling only after the last waiter, for the cycle collector path, for adding the same result object twice (weak or not), and for a native join where a duplicate waiter exists for a member.
- `t/integration/test_canvas.py`: drop the strict xfail markers on `test_group_results_in_chain` and `test_nested_chain_group_lone`, which the fix makes pass.

## Test plan

- [x] 6 new unit tests; 5 fail on `main` and pass with this change, the cycle collector one guards the new structure against leaking an empty entry per id
- [x] Every changed line and branch in `celery/backends/asynchronous.py` is covered (branch coverage over the full unit suite); the same-object and duplicate-waiter tests fail when the early return is removed or only the first waiter is resolved
- [x] Full unit suite: 5171 passed on macOS; Linux (3.14, unprivileged user, 4 CPUs like the CI runners) 119 passed in `t/unit/concurrency` and 5203 in the rest
- [x] Reproduced and verified against real brokers in Docker (RabbitMQ 4.4, Redis 7.4) with a prefork worker, for amqp + redis, redis + redis, and amqp + rpc: both triggers hang on `main` and return in about 1s with this change; 0 hangs in 300 two-task groups, 60 ten-task groups and 50 groups whose members were polled by id before `get()`
- [x] Smoke tests touching `_pending_results`: `test_pending_tasks_released_on_forget` (rabbitmq and redis brokers) and `test_redis_backend_reentrant` (threads and gevent), 4 passed
- [x] Integration suite in a Linux container mirroring the CI jobs (python 3.12, tox `3.12-integration-{redis,rabbitmq,rabbitmq_redis}`, brokers on localhost like the CI services): every `t/integration` module passes on all three envs
- [x] `test_canvas.py` compared against `main` on all three envs: the only outcome changes are the two "Task is timeout" tests going from xfail (timeout) to pass; `test_redis_subscribed_channels_leak` and the non strict rpc xfails are unchanged
- [x] pre-commit (flake8, isort, mypy, pyupgrade, codespell)

## Backwards compatibility

No public API changes. With a single `AsyncResult` per id the behaviour is the same as before. `_pending_results` is private, but its values are now per-id dicts of waiters instead of result objects, so third party code that reads it directly would need updating; nothing in celery or its tests does besides `len()` on the mappings, which still counts pending ids.

Because every waiter is now tracked, an `AsyncResult(id).get(timeout=...)` that times out keeps that object alive until the task is ready or `forget()` is called. As @ChristianMurphy measured, 50 timed-out `get()` calls on new `AsyncResult` objects for an unfinished task keep 50 objects, all freed once the task finishes. `main` kept none, but only because dropping any one of them also dropped the tracked entry, which is the bug fixed here. Code that keeps polling a task that never finishes with a new `AsyncResult` each time will see memory grow; reusing one `AsyncResult` keeps it to a single tracked object. A comment in `_add_pending_result()` says the same.

title: Fix send_task() overriding ignore_result defaults
body:
## Description

`send_task()` treats an omitted `ignore_result` as an explicit `False`. The worker honors that override and stores the result, even when the task has `ignore_result=True`.

This PR uses `None` for an omitted option so the worker follows the task’s `ignore_result` setting. Callers still override that setting by explicitly passing `True` or `False`.

title: fix(saferepr): restore closing bracket when last element is truncated
body:
## What

`saferepr()` drops the closing bracket when the last element of a container is the one that exhausts `maxlen`.

Fixes #10760.

## Root cause

`_saferepr` processes tokens from `reprstream` one at a time. At the start of each iteration it checks `if maxlen <= 0` to detect exhaustion. At that point the current `token` was already consumed from the iterator, it is not in `it` any more.

If `token` happens to be a closing bracket (e.g. `LIT_LIST_END = _literal(']', False, -1)`), the code discards it, pushes `it` back onto the stack for the dangling-paren pass, and breaks. The dangling-paren pass scans `it` from its current position and emits any non-truncatable literals it finds, but the closing bracket was already consumed, so it is never re-emitted.

```python
# before fix:
saferepr(['v' * 100], 30)       # "['vvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvv..., ..."  missing ]
saferepr(['v' * 100, 1, 2], 30) # "['vvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvv..., ...]"  correct (] is after v*100 in the iterator)
```

## Fix

When entering the truncation branch, check whether the just-consumed `token` is a closing bracket (`isinstance(token, _literal) and token.direction < 0`). If so, prepend it to the stack so the dangling-paren pass emits it before continuing with the rest of `it`:

```python
if isinstance(token, _literal) and token.direction < 0:
    stack.appendleft(iter([token]))
stack.append(it)
break
```

## Tests

Added three failing → passing test cases to `t/unit/utils/test_saferepr.py`:

- `test_truncated_last_element_keeps_closing_bracket`, list
- `test_truncated_last_element_keeps_closing_bracket_tuple`, tuple
- `test_truncated_last_element_keeps_closing_bracket_dict`, nested dict/list

title: Keep the first SUCCESS in the Cassandra backend
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Refs #10929 (Cassandra only). The MongoDB portion is handled in #10944.

Skip state writes when the newest stored Cassandra row is already `SUCCESS`, so a redelivered task does not replace it with `STARTED`, `FAILURE`, or a different successful result. Inspect the stored status directly without decoding the old result, traceback, or children. Initialize the write connection before reading, including when an earlier reader opened the session, so the result table exists.

Implement `forget()` by deleting the task's entire partition at `cassandra_write_consistency`. A task id can then be reused without waiting for `cassandra_entry_ttl`: storing `SUCCESS 'monday'`, calling `AsyncResult.forget()`, then storing `STARTED` and `SUCCESS 'tuesday'` returns the new result. Forgetting an unknown task is harmless.

Regression tests cover preservation across backend instances, updates before success, undecodable payloads, table initialization, and the public forget/reuse flow. The forget tests also check cache clearing, isolation from other task ids, repeated deletion, custom table names, bound task-id parameters, write consistency, and reuse of an earlier read session. Add a changelog entry and a 5.7 `versionchanged` note under `cassandra_read_consistency`.

## Validation

- Python 3.13: `pytest -q t/unit/backends t/unit/tasks/test_result.py` — 1,204 passed, 11 skipped.
- Cassandra unit tests — 41 passed; 100% statement and branch coverage for `celery/backends/cassandra.py`.
- The 3 new forget regression cases fail with `NotImplementedError` on the previous PR head and pass with this change.
- All repository pre-commit hooks pass.
- Bandit passes for `celery/backends/cassandra.py`.
- `apicheck`, `configcheck`, and repository-wide Bandit report the same failures on the unchanged PR base `6ef562b` and this branch: 4 undocumented modules, 28 undocumented settings, and 49 Bandit findings, respectively. Sphinx successfully parses the new version-change note.

Each attempted store adds a read using `cassandra_read_consistency`, so writes depend on that read succeeding. Weaker reads can miss a successful row on another replica. The read and insert remain separate operations; concurrent writers can still race. A live Cassandra server was not available for local validation.

AI assistance: prepared with Codex.

title: mongodb backend: keep the first SUCCESS instead of overwriting it
body:
Refs #10929

The MongoDB backend stored every result with an unconditional `replace_one`, so when a task ran a second time (redelivery after the worker was killed past the visibility timeout, as in the report) the second run overwrote the first run's SUCCESS, and later updates could replace it too.

`BaseKeyValueStoreBackend` already ignores any write once a SUCCESS is stored, and #10920 applies the same rule to the database backend. This does the same for MongoDB: `_store_result` puts the status check in the `replace_one` filter (`status` is not SUCCESS), so the check and the write happen in one step. When the stored document is already a SUCCESS the filter does not match and the upsert raises `DuplicateKeyError`, which is ignored, with one retry for a document inserted by a concurrent run.

Cassandra has the same bug, but this PR does not cover it: its write path goes through the session/table-creation lifecycle in `_get_connection`, and a pre-read there needs more care than a straight port of this change.

Tests: `test_store_result_after_success_is_ignored`, `test_store_result_retries_duplicate_key` and `test_store_result_keeps_first_success` cover the filter, the retry and keeping the first SUCCESS. They fail on the old read-then-write logic and pass with this change. The mongodb unit test file shows no new failures against the unmodified tree. A `Changelog.rst` entry under Unreleased notes that writes after a SUCCESS are now ignored.

title: Give entries copied by LimitedSet.update() this set's sequence numbers
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Follow-up to #10758, for the issue @GangEunzzang found while reviewing it (https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10758#issuecomment-6164805687).

`LimitedSet.update()` with another `LimitedSet` copied that set's `(insertion time, sequence number, item)` entries as they were. The sequence numbers come from the other set's counter, so they can be the same as numbers this set has already given out. Two entries with the same insertion time and the same sequence number make the heap (and `__iter__`, which sorts the entries) compare the items themselves. For items that can't be ordered against each other, that raises `TypeError`.

On main:

```python
a = LimitedSet(); a.add('x', now=5.0)

b = LimitedSet(); b.update(a)
b.add(1, now=5.0)          # TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'

b = LimitedSet(); b.add(1, now=5.0)
b.update(a)                # TypeError, raised in update() itself

b = LimitedSet(data=a)     # same path
b.add(1, now=5.0)          # TypeError
```

This change numbers the copied entries from this set's counter, in the other set's order (insertion time, then its sequence number). For items with the same insertion time, the ones copied in count as added after this set's own, and among themselves they keep the order they had in the other set. Insertion times are kept as before, and so is what happens when an item is in both sets (the other set's entry wins, as `dict.update()` did).

The worker isn't affected: it only passes lists of ids to `revoked.update()`, so this only affects code that merges one `LimitedSet` into another, or builds one with `data=` another set.

## Tests

New tests in `t/unit/utils/test_collections.py`:

- `test_add_after_update_from_limited_set`
- `test_update_from_limited_set_into_non_empty_set`
- `test_init_from_limited_set`
- `test_update_from_limited_set_keeps_its_order`, which checks that items with the same insertion time keep the other set's order and that the source set isn't changed

The first three fail on main with the `TypeError` above. The fourth passes on both and guards the order.

- `t/unit/utils/` (except `test_annotations.py`, which needs pydantic), plus `t/unit/worker/test_state.py`, `test_control.py` and `test_consumer.py`: 961 passed.
- 3000 random sequences of `add`, `discard`, `update` (from the other of two sets), `pop` and iteration, with items of mixed types, compared with a simple model: 2772 diverge or raise on main, 0 with this change.
- flake8 and isort pass on the changed files.

title: Log connection retry traceback at debug level
body:
## Description

Fixes #9236.

`on_connection_error_after_connected()` logged the broker retry warning with `exc_info=True`, so every reconnect warning carried a full traceback. When Celery logs are forwarded to an application logger, that traceback is captured there too.

Keep the warning free of the traceback, but include the exception repr so default-level logs still identify what failed. The traceback itself moves to debug level. The debug record uses the exception passed to the handler instead of relying on the ambient exception state, so it also works when the handler is called outside an `except` block. Operators who need the traceback can enable DEBUG logging for `celery.worker.consumer.consumer`.

## Test

Added `test_connection_error_traceback_is_logged_at_debug_level` in `t/unit/worker/test_consumer.py`. It asserts the retry warning keeps the exception repr but has no `exc_info`, and the debug record carries the original exception.

On the previous code the test fails at the warning-message assertion; with this change it passes.

```bash
pytest t/unit/worker/test_consumer.py -q
# 134 passed, 2 skipped
pytest t/unit/worker -q
# 774 passed, 10 skipped
```

title: Fix MultiParser to honor its configured Node class
body:
## Description

Instantiate parsed worker nodes through `self.Node` so `MultiParser` subclasses can provide their own `Node` implementation. The default node class and the arguments passed to its constructor remain unchanged.

Add a regression test using a real `Node` subclass and a parser subclass that selects it. The test checks that both parsed workers use the custom class and retain their expected names. It fails on the original code because the parser always instantiates the module-level `Node`.

Fixes #4697.

title: Keep the first SUCCESS in the MongoDB result backend
body:
### The bug

`MongoBackend._store_result()` replaces the document for a task id unconditionally:

```python
meta['_id'] = task_id
self.collection.replace_one({'_id': task_id}, meta, upsert=True)
```

A task whose worker is lost before it can ack gets redelivered and re-run, so a second run overwrites the result the first run already stored, and `AsyncResult.get()` reports the re-run's failure instead of the success that really happened:

```
after first run  -> ('SUCCESS', 42)
after second run -> ('FAILURE', KeyError('second run blew up'))   # before
after second run -> ('SUCCESS', 42)                               # after
```

`BaseKeyValueStoreBackend._store_result` (celery/backends/base.py) refuses to write over a stored SUCCESS, with a comment naming exactly this scenario:

```python
# Retrieve metadata from the backend, if the status
# is a success then we ignore any following update to the state.
# This solves a task deduplication issue because of network
# partitioning or lost workers. This issue involved a race condition
# making a lost task overwrite the last successful result in the
# result backend.
current_meta = self._get_task_meta_for(task_id)
if current_meta['status'] == states.SUCCESS:
    return result
```

and the database backend gained the same guard recently (#10920). MongoDB was the remaining backend without it. This is issue #10929.

### Fix

```python
query = {'_id': task_id}
if state != states.SUCCESS:
    query['status'] = {'$ne': states.SUCCESS}

self.collection.replace_one(query, meta, upsert=True)
```

The decision is made **by the server as part of the write**, rather than by reading first and writing second the way the base backend does. That matters here: the guard exists because of a race, and a read-then-write in this backend would open a fresh window in which a concurrent re-run could still land between the two round trips. A write whose state is itself SUCCESS keeps the plain `{'\_id': task_id}` filter, so a later success still wins - the same contract as the database backend.

### Testing

`t/unit/backends/test_mongodb.py` gains four parametrized cases (a re-run in `STARTED` and in `FAILURE` must be ignored; a later `SUCCESS` must still win; a first `SUCCESS` must be stored):

- on the untouched base (`451381d52`, with only the test file copied in and `celery.__file__` verified from that worktree): **2 failed, 2 passed** - the two failures are the `STARTED` and `FAILURE` re-runs, and the two that pass are the intentional controls
- with the fix: **4 passed**
- `t/unit/backends/test_mongodb.py`: 136 passed / 3 skipped on base, 138 passed / 3 skipped with the fix
- `t/unit/` in full: `2 failed, 4887 passed` on base vs `2 failed, 4891 passed` with the fix - the 2 failures are `t/unit/app/test_beat.py::test_Scheduler::{test_pending_tick,test_ticks}`, which **already fail on untouched base** and are unrelated
- `flake8` 7.4.1 and `isort` 9.0.2 (both pinned in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`) exit 0 with no output; black is not configured in this repository

### Limitations I want to be explicit about

1. **These tests run against the module's existing fake in-memory collection, not a live MongoDB.** They exercise the backend's real BSON round trip and the filter semantics the fix adds (the fake honours `$ne` and `_id` uniqueness), but they cannot demonstrate server-side behaviour.
2. **Consequently I have not verified how a real MongoDB handles this particular upsert**, and I could not: there is no MongoDB binary or server available anywhere on this machine and the download is unreachable through the proxy here. The shape to check is `replace_one({'_id': k, 'status': {'$ne': 'SUCCESS'}}, doc, upsert=True)` against a document that **does** have `status == 'SUCCESS'`. My reading is that the upsert is suppressed because the filter reaches the document through the `_id` equality, which is the normal reason to write the guard this way; but if your supported MongoDB versions raise a duplicate-key error there instead, the guard needs to move to `update_one` with the same filter, and I would rather you tell me that than have me assert it.
3. **The sibling Cassandra backend has the same defect and I deliberately did not fix it** in this PR. It needs a SELECT before each INSERT and I could not make that atomic, so a fix there would either add a round trip to every write or reintroduce the race. It deserves its own change.

AI assistance: this change was produced with AI assistance (an autonomous coding agent); the analysis, the reproduction, the before/after test runs and the lint runs were executed locally, and a human reviewed the result before submission.

title: Allow `ResultSet.add()` after the set's results are ready
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`ResultSet.add()` raises `ValueError: Cannot add promise to full barrier` once every result in the set has been seen as ready, for example after polling `rs.ready()` until it returns `True`. It appends the result before it raises, so the set has grown anyway. On the rpc backend, `rs.get()` also triggers it, and a later `rs.get()` returns `None` for the added result.

The set waits for its results with a vine `barrier`:
https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/451381d5229627058c9a647fe54c34d7292e3dce/celery/result.py#L593-L609

When all of them are ready, the barrier fires, and after that it raises if you add to it:
https://github.com/celery/vine/blob/8c08b391a9f8976153a3a1972c66296e01f60c66/vine/synchronization.py#L68-L93

`finalize()` can also fire the barrier, and then it doesn't set `ready`. That happens when `iter_native()` starts on a set that started empty (#10407) and whose results were all ready already. `add()` doesn't raise in that case, but the barrier won't fire again, so on the rpc backend `rs.get()` returns `None` for the added result.

With this change, when the barrier has already fired, `add()` waits for the new result with a new barrier and a new `on_ready` promise. It calls `finalize()` after adding the result, so a result that is ready already fulfills the new barrier at once. `then()` callbacks added after `add()` wait for the new result, and callbacks that already ran don't run again. I left `remove()`, `discard()`, `update()` and `clear()` alone; they don't use the barrier.

Reproducer (in-memory broker, in-process solo worker), run as `python repro.py <backend>`:

```python
import sys
import time

from celery import Celery
from celery.contrib.testing.worker import start_worker

app = Celery('repro', broker='memory://', backend=sys.argv[1])


@app.task
def add(x, y):
    return x + y


with start_worker(app, pool='solo', perform_ping_check=False):
    rs = app.ResultSet([add.delay(2, 2), add.delay(5, 5)])
    while not rs.ready():
        time.sleep(0.1)
    try:
        rs.add(add.delay(7, 7))
    except ValueError as exc:
        print('add() raised:', repr(exc))
    print(len(rs), rs.get(timeout=10))
```

| Backend | main (451381d) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `cache+memory://` | `add() raised: ValueError('Cannot add promise to full barrier')`, then `3 [4, 10, 14]` | `3 [4, 10, 14]` |
| `rpc://` | `add() raised: ValueError('Cannot add promise to full barrier')`, then `3 [4, 10, None]` | `3 [4, 10, 14]` |
| `rpc://`, set started empty and filled with `add()`, polled, then `get()` before `add()` | no error, then `3 [4, 10, None]` | `3 [4, 10, 14]` |

Testing on Python 3.12:

- The new `test_add_after_ready` and `test_then_waits_for_result_added_after_ready` in `t/unit/tasks/test_result.py` fail on main with the `ValueError` and pass with this change. The second test checks that `then()` callbacks wait for an added result that is still pending, and that adding a result that is ready already keeps the set ready.
- `pytest t/unit/tasks`: 1194 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed.
- `pre-commit run --files celery/result.py t/unit/tasks/test_result.py t/integration/test_canvas.py`: all hooks passed.
- The new integration test `test_result_set::test_result_set_add_after_ready` in `t/integration/test_canvas.py` collects the set's results with `get()`, adds a result and calls `get()` again. It fails on main with `ValueError: Cannot add promise to full barrier` and passes with this change, both with RabbitMQ and the rpc backend (5 passed, 2 skipped for the class) and with Redis (7 passed). It doesn't poll `ready()`: with RabbitMQ and the rpc backend, `rs.ready()` never returned true in that loop, in CI or locally.

I found this by reading and testing the code.

I made this PR and directed its development, with AI assistance from Claude and GPT-6 Astra.

title: Run a replaced task's callbacks once when it is replaced with a chain
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

If a task that has a link callback replaces itself with a chain, the callback runs twice on the worker.

`Task.replace()` links the request's callbacks to the replacement chain and then copies the chain's `link` option onto the chain's last task, but leaves it on the chain as well ([task.py#L1094-L1099](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/55e23e8b52af9cf75334668b07a304c92dc1bdeb/celery/app/task.py#L1094-L1099)). When the chain is sent, `_chain.run()` adds the chain's `link` to the last task again ([canvas.py#L1270-L1272](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/55e23e8b52af9cf75334668b07a304c92dc1bdeb/celery/canvas.py#L1270-L1272)), so the last task carries the callback twice. When the replaced task is itself part of a chain, `sig |= ...` rebuilds the chain without its options, which is why that case links the callback once. Since #6770 the copy happens for every chain replacement, not only that one.

This change pops the chain's `link` while moving it to the last task, so the callback is linked once. Replacing with a single task or a group, and replacing inside an outer chain, behave as before. A `link` set on the replacement chain itself, as in `self.replace(chain(...).set(link=...))`, was also linked twice on main even when the replaced task had no callbacks, and this fixes it too (thanks @MehrazRumman for pointing it out).

Reproducer (in-memory broker, cache backend, in-process worker):

```python
import time

from celery import Celery, chain, group
from celery.contrib.testing.worker import start_worker

app = Celery('repro', broker='memory://', backend='cache+memory://')
calls = []


@app.task
def add(x, y):
    return x + y


@app.task
def notify(value):
    calls.append(value)


@app.task(bind=True)
def replaced_by_chain(self, x):
    return self.replace(chain(add.s(x, 1), add.s(10)))


with start_worker(app, pool='solo', perform_ping_check=False):
    for sig in (
        replaced_by_chain.s(1).set(link=notify.s()),
        group(replaced_by_chain.s(1).set(link=notify.s()), add.s(5, 5)),
    ):
        calls.clear()
        result = sig.apply_async().get(timeout=10)
        time.sleep(1)  # let the callback run
        print(result, calls)
```

| Canvas | main (55e23e8) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `replaced_by_chain.s(1).set(link=notify.s())` | `12`, `notify` called with `[12, 12]` | `12`, `[12]` |
| `group(replaced_by_chain.s(1).set(link=notify.s()), add.s(5, 5))` | `[12, 10]`, `[12, 12]` | `[12, 10]`, `[12]` |
| `chain(replaced_by_chain.s(1).set(link=notify.s()), add.s(100))` | `112`, `[12]` | `112`, `[12]` |
| task replaced with `add.s(x, 1)`, `link=notify.s()` | `2`, `[2]` | `2`, `[2]` |

Testing on Python 3.12:

- The new `test_replace_chain_links_callback_once` in `t/unit/tasks/test_tasks.py` checks that the published chain links the callback to its last task once. It fails on main, where the callback is listed twice, and passes with this change.
- `test_replace_chain_with_own_link_links_it_once` does the same for a `link` set on the replacement chain itself, with no callbacks on the replaced task. It also fails on main and passes with this change.
- The new Redis integration tests `test_task_with_callback_replaced_with_chain` and `test_group_child_with_callback_replaced_with_chain` in `t/integration/test_canvas.py` fail on main with the callback counted twice and pass with this change.
- `pytest t/unit/tasks/test_tasks.py`: 142 passed.
- `pytest t/unit/tasks`: 1193 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed.
- `pre-commit run --files celery/app/task.py t/unit/tasks/test_tasks.py`: all hooks passed.

This does not change eager mode. There, `apply()` of a replaced task still runs its callback twice, even when it is replaced with a single task, because the replaced task's own result triggers it too.

I found this by reading and testing the code.

I made this PR and directed its development, with AI assistance from Claude and GPT-6 Astra.

title: Docs: note the quorum queue delivery limit
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10914

Since RabbitMQ 4.0, quorum queues drop a message (or dead-letter it) after 20 redeliveries by default. With `task_acks_late` and `task_reject_on_worker_lost`, a task that keeps killing its worker gets requeued on every crash and then just disappears, stays PENDING, and nothing shows up in the worker log.

This adds:

- a "Delivery Limit" section to the quorum queue part of the RabbitMQ broker page. It explains the limit, how to change it (`x-delivery-limit` or a `delivery-limit` policy), using a dead letter exchange to keep dropped tasks, and `task_retry_on_worker_lost` as a way to cap reruns. It links to RabbitMQ's poison message handling docs.
- a short note under `task_reject_on_worker_lost` that points to that section.

Docs only. I built the docs locally with sphinx and checked that the new section renders and the cross references resolve. codespell passes on both files.

title: test: assert exact task replacement nesting levels
body:
## Description

Fixes #6968.

The existing replacement integration tests only assert upper bounds for `replaced_task_nesting`, so they can pass if every replacement incorrectly reports zero.

Add a bound integration task that records its request's nesting level before replacing itself. Parameterize the test over zero, one, and three replacements and assert the complete sequence, including `[0, 1, 2, 3]` for nested replacements. This exercises publishing, protocol headers, worker requests, and task context propagation through the shared integration worker.

The helper preserves the caller's `reply_to` so the final sequence also reaches the RPC result consumer.

This implements the exact-sequence coverage proposed in [the issue discussion](https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/6968#issuecomment-5870995081) and accepted by the maintainer.

## Validation

- `pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure` passed.
- [Linux prefork validation](https://github.com/ZedingZhang/celery/actions/runs/39717835916) passed on Python 3.11 and 3.13 with Redis/Redis, RabbitMQ/RPC, and RabbitMQ/Redis broker/backend combinations.
- In all six configurations, temporarily resetting the published nesting header to zero made both nested cases fail with incorrect sequences while the zero-replacement case still passed.

body:

guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

In `celery/app/base.py`, `_ensure_after_fork()` checks `if not self._after_fork_registered:`. The unit tests only sometimes call it twice on one app, when a test happens to rebuild `app.pool`. title: Don't mark a task REVOKED while another worker runs it
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10913.

Since #9869, each worker that gets a revoke stores REVOKED. It skips a task that it runs itself (#10564) or that already has a final state (#10679). But with two or more workers, a worker that doesn't run the task still stores REVOKED. A revoke without `terminate` doesn't stop the task, so it then stores SUCCESS. The client that called `revoke()` reads REVOKED first, and `get()` raises `TaskRevokedError` for a task that succeeded.

This writes REVOKED only while the stored state shows that no worker has started the task: PENDING, RECEIVED, RETRY or REJECTED. A running task shows STARTED, or a custom state it set with `update_state()`, and its state is left to the worker that runs it. With `terminate`, that worker stores REVOKED when it stops the task.

Without `task_track_started`, a running task shows PENDING until it sets a state of its own. In that case the other workers still store REVOKED for it, and the revoke docs now say so.

I ran the script from #10913 with two workers. It prints STARTED, SUCCESS and `done`, as 5.6.1 did. Revoking a task that hasn't started yet still stores REVOKED right away, and `terminate=True` still ends with REVOKED.

This changes one case from main: the worker that started the task was lost, such as one killed with early acks. A revoke used to store REVOKED there. Now the state is left as it is, and `get()` waits, as it did on 5.6.1. I didn't find a way to tell that case apart from a task that is still running without asking the other workers. I'm happy to change this if you see one.

The unit and integration tests check that a STARTED or PROGRESS task isn't marked REVOKED, while a task with no state is. A smoke test runs two workers: a running task revoked without `terminate` ends as SUCCESS, and `get()` returns its result. On main, those checks fail.

title: Use the documented retry defaults in the database backend
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10911.

#10130 documents that `DatabaseBackend` turns on `result_backend_always_retry` and sets `result_backend_max_retries` to 3, unless you set them. It read them with `conf.get(key, default)`. Both keys always exist in `celery/app/defaults.py`, which means the fallback never ran. So by default, the backend didn't retry.

This uses the defaults when `conf.value_set_for()` says the user didn't set the option, or when it's set to `None`. The docs now say what `None` does.

`value_set_for()` missed a setting given with a prefix, such as Django's `CELERY_` one, or by its old name. It also returned False before the settings were loaded. It now checks the prefix and the old names, and loads the settings first, as `table()` does. Nothing else in Celery calls it.

Compared with the `@retry` decorator this backend had in 5.6:

- After the last retry, `store_result` and `get_task_meta` raise `BackendStoreError` and `BackendGetMetaError`, with the SQLAlchemy error as the cause.
- `max_retries = 3` means 4 attempts, with a growing wait and a new connection pool before each retry. The old decorator made 3 attempts in a row. Should the default be 2 to match 5.6, or are 3 retries what #10130 meant?

The new tests check the defaults, `None`, and settings given directly or by their old names. A test of `value_set_for()` also covers a namespace, an old name, and settings that haven't loaded yet.

title: Keep the first SUCCESS in the database backend
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10912.

The key-value backends ignore any write once a task has a SUCCESS. The database backend had no such check. So when a task runs again under `acks_late`, because its worker was killed after saving the result and before the ack, the second run writes over the stored SUCCESS.

This returns early in `DatabaseBackend._store_result` when the stored state is SUCCESS.

It also always writes the `status` column. SQLAlchemy only writes columns whose values changed since it read the row. If another run saved a SUCCESS after that read, a STARTED write used to update the result and skip the status. The row then held SUCCESS with the STARTED result. The new check would then ignore every later write to that row, including that run's own SUCCESS.

When the row exists, it's read again with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before the check. When a task runs twice at once, the second run waits for the first and then sees its SUCCESS. A missing row isn't locked. On MySQL, that takes a gap lock, and concurrent first writes for new tasks then deadlock. With 16 processes writing new tasks, locking every read gave 8 to 20 deadlocks per 3,200 writes on MySQL 8.4, and this version gave none. SQLite has no row locks, and the status column is still always written for it.

Other effects, all as on the key-value backends:

- Any later write is ignored. This includes a FAILURE that the same run stores when `on_success` raises, and `AbortableAsyncResult.abort()` on a task that already succeeded.
- Database rows don't expire like Redis keys. A task id that you reuse on purpose keeps its first SUCCESS until `AsyncResult.forget()` or the daily `celery.backend_cleanup` task deletes the row. That task only runs with Celery beat. The FAQ says reusing an id is undefined.

`worker_deduplicate_successful_tasks` can skip a copy that runs again, but it is off by default. The MongoDB and Cassandra backends have the same gap, in #10929.

The new tests check that STARTED, FAILURE and SUCCESS writes after a SUCCESS are ignored, and that the extended columns stay the same. They also check that a row can still go from STARTED to SUCCESS. When another run saves SUCCESS during a write, that SUCCESS is kept, and without row locks the row isn't left mixed. The crash script in #10912 now keeps the first SUCCESS.

title: Count each chord header task only once in the Redis backend
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10910.

With `acks_late`, a chord header task can run twice. The Redis backend adds each run to the chord's count. In the default ordered mode, a second run with the same result merges with the first. But a run with a new result counts again, and so does any second run in unordered mode. The body can then run before the other header tasks finish, with two results for one header and none for another.

This saves each part with a small Lua script. In one step, it records the result only if this task id and header index aren't recorded yet, and then reads the count.

What changes:

- The body is still sent each time the count is complete, as on main. So if a worker saves the last part and is lost before it sends the body, the copy that runs next still sends it.
- That also means a copy that arrives after the last part, but before the chord's keys are deleted, sends the body a second time. If the chord failed, it fails it a second time. On main, the copy pushed the count past the size, unless the chord was ordered and the result was the same. For a simple header, this window is short. For a header with nested groups, it lasts while the results are joined.
- When a chord fails, its `.s` key is now deleted, so a copy that arrives later can't fail it again. The saved results stay, as before.
- Older workers still write the same `.j` key, so chords with parts from old and new workers still finish. Parts from older workers aren't checked for copies.
- This is the first Lua script in Celery. A Redis user with an ACL that lists its commands now needs four more: `EVALSHA`, `SCRIPT LOAD`, and the `SISMEMBER` and `SADD` calls inside the script. If the user lacks them, header tasks get a Redis permission error as they store their results, so neither the body nor the error callbacks will run. I added a note about this to the Redis docs.

Tests cover a repeated header (new value, `None`, failure), a part from an older worker, a reused frozen signature, a rerun of the last part, and a copy after the chord failed. An integration test runs the script against Redis in both modes. The crash script in #10910 gives the body one result per header on this branch.

title: Pass values to backend hooks by position again
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10909.

Keeps the retry behavior from https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10130 (https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/6540)

Since #10130, `BaseBackend` calls `_store_result`, `_get_task_meta_for`, `_forget`, `_save_group`, `_restore_group` and `_delete_group` with keyword arguments. `django-celery-results` names two of these parameters differently (`status`, `group_result`), so on 5.7.0rc1 every result write and group save raises `TypeError`.

This passes the values by position again, as 5.6 did. `BackendStoreError` still gets the task id and state, and `BackendGetMetaError` the task id, now through a `partial` passed as `fallback_exc`. `_ensure_retryable` is unchanged.

Tests:

- A new test uses a backend whose hooks have other parameter names, as in `django-celery-results`. It fails on main.
- The max-retries tests now check that the raised error still has the task id (and the state, for `BackendStoreError`).

I also ran the `django-celery-results` unit tests (`91fbb17`, Postgres 17.11):

| Celery | Failed | Passed |
|---|---|---|
| 5.6.3 | 0 | 56 |
| 5.7.0rc1 | 27 | 29 |
| this branch | 0 | 56 |

All 27 failures on 5.7.0rc1 are this `TypeError`.

title: fix(database): honor result backend retry defaults (fixes #10911)
body:
Fixes #10911.

`DatabaseBackend.__init__` reads the retry settings with `conf.get('result_backend_always_retry', True)` and `conf.get('result_backend_max_retries', 3)`, but both options are declared in `celery/app/defaults.py` with no default, so they exist in the config as None. `conf.get(key, default)` then returns None instead of the intended fallback, and the documented pre-5.7 behavior (always retry, max 3 attempts) is silently replaced with unlimited retries.

Read the user's explicit value only when it was actually set (`conf.value_set_for`), and keep the backward-compatible defaults otherwise. #10130 added these options and #10334 assumed the defaults were on; this restores that assumption.

Tests: new cases in t/unit/backends/test_database.py pin both directions - a fresh backend gets always_retry=True and max_retries=3, and an explicit `result_backend_always_retry = False` / `result_backend_max_retries = 0` is honored. The first fails without the fix; t/unit/backends/test_database.py passes 107 tests with it.

title: Fix solar schedule timing across DST changes
body:
## Description

`solar.remaining_estimate()` subtracts datetimes that share the same timezone using wall time. This can delay tasks by an hour during spring-forward or dispatch them repeatedly before the event during fall-back.

For example, in America/New_York on 2026-11-01, an event at 01:40-05:00 is still 55 minutes away when the clock reads 01:45-04:00. Wall-time subtraction returns −5 minutes, so Beat treats the future event as due.

related https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10813

title: Fix chord errbacks given as a single signature
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10906 

`link_error` may hold a single signature or a list, and every other reader wraps it with `maybe_list()`. `Backend.chord_error_from_stack()` and `Backend._handle_group_chord_error()` iterated the option directly. A chord body with one errback, such as `tsum.s().set(link_error=eb.s())`, therefore had the signature's keys iterated. The errback never ran, and one bogus task per key (`'task'`, `'args'`, `'kwargs'`, ...) was published, showing up on the worker as "Received unregistered task of type 'task'". For a group body this happened once per body task.

Changes:
- `celery/backends/base.py`: both sites now pass `maybe_list(<callback>.options.get("link_error")) or []`, the same idiom used in `canvas.py` and `app/task.py`.
- `t/unit/backends/test_base.py`: `test_chord_error_from_stack_accepts_a_single_errback` and `test_handle_group_chord_error_accepts_a_single_errback`, each parametrized over a single signature and a list. The single-signature cases fail on `main` and pass with this change.

Testing:
- `pytest t/unit/backends t/unit/tasks`: 1953 passed, 49 skipped, 1 xfailed.
- flake8, isort, codespell, pyupgrade and yesqa, at the versions in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, are clean on the changed files.
- The reproduction script from the issue, run on a real worker:

```
# main
single link_error -> chord state FAILURE, errback called 0 time(s)
list   link_error -> chord state FAILURE, errback called 1 time(s)

# this branch
single link_error -> chord state FAILURE, errback called 1 time(s)
list   link_error -> chord state FAILURE, errback called 1 time(s)
```

No unregistered-task errors are logged on this branch.

title: Cancel only per-connection timer entries on broker reconnect instead of clearing the worker timer (#10888)
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10888. Supersedes #10890. Related: #10218, #10892.

### Problem
#10218 made `asynloop` call `hub.timer.clear()` when the event loop exits on a connection error, to drop stale periodic entries such as the transport's `maybe_restore_messages`. `hub.timer` is the worker-wide timer, though. Clearing it also removes the soft/hard time limits of tasks that keep running across the reconnect. Nothing registers those again, so a hung task is never killed after a broker connection drop. This affects 5.6.3 and the 5.7 pre-releases.

### Fix
Cancel only the timer entries that belong to the connection that failed, and keep everything else on the timer.

- `Consumer.start()` records the timer entries that exist before each connection attempt (`timer_entries_before_start`).
- `asynloop` takes the entries added between that point and the start of the loop: the transport's periodic timers registered in `Consumer.connect()`, AMQP and event heartbeats, and the `register_with_event_loop` callbacks (including the pool's and autoscaler's, which `asynloop` registers again on every call). On a connection error it cancels only those, with `timer.cancel()`, instead of clearing the timer.
- Entries added after the loop starts are kept. The same goes for entries that existed before the connection attempt. This covers time limits of running tasks, ETA and rate-limit entries, and timers registered once at worker start.
- If `asynloop` is called without that record, it falls back to a snapshot taken when it starts.
- `AsynPool._create_timelimit_handlers` now keeps its existing `_tref_for_id` mapping when the pool registers with the event loop again. A task that was running across the reconnect can then still cancel its time-limit entry when it finishes.
- Graceful shutdown, `WorkerShutdown` and `WorkerTerminate` behave as before: nothing is cancelled.

### Differences from #10890 / #10892
- #10890 keeps entries by matching handler names and rebuilds kombu's private `Timer._queue` heap. Its `obj.pool._tref_for_id` lookup always comes back empty in a real worker, because `obj.pool` is the `TaskPool` and not the `AsynPool`. This PR doesn't depend on handler names or the heap's layout.
- #10892 takes its snapshot inside `asynloop`. That misses the entries the transport registers in `Consumer.connect()`, which runs before `asynloop`.

### Tests
- `asynloop` timer tests now use a real `kombu.asynchronous.timer.Timer` and cover:
  - per-connection entries are cancelled
  - entries don't pile up across reconnects
  - entries registered while connecting are cancelled
  - entries that existed before, or were added while running, survive
  - nothing is cancelled on graceful, worker or terminate shutdown
  - the original error is still raised when cleanup fails
- Consumer: the timer entries are recorded before `blueprint.start()`.
- AsynPool: time-limit trefs survive registering with the event loop again.
- The reproduction script from #10888 now fires the hard time limit after the reconnect.

title: Keep celery beat running when a schedule entry fails, and reject impossible crontab dates
body:
## Description
Fixes #10893.

Currently, a single periodic task whose next run can't be calculated stops `celery beat`, and every other periodic task with it. This PR makes two changes:

### 1. beat: an entry that fails in `is_due()` no longer stops beat

`Scheduler.populate_heap()` and `Scheduler.tick()` called `is_due()` for each entry without error handling, and `Service.start()` only catches `KeyboardInterrupt`/`SystemExit`. Any exception from one entry, such as the `solar` `TypeError` reported in #10893, therefore made beat exit.

Now beat catches the error, logs it with the entry's name and the traceback, and tries that entry again after `max_interval`. The other entries keep running.

```
[...: ERROR/MainProcess] beat: Cannot calculate the next run of 'bad-entry', trying again in 5.00 minutes.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
```

Tested with a real `celery beat` process, using the `solar('dawn_astronomical', -62.2, -58.9)` entry from the issue next to a healthy 2s entry:

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| beat process | exits at startup (exit code 1) | keeps running |
| healthy entry | never sent | sent every 2s |
| bad entry | n/a | error logged, retried after `max_interval` |

### 2. crontab: impossible dates are rejected when the crontab is created

`crontab(day_of_month=30, month_of_year=2)` (or the 31st of April/June/September/November) was accepted, because each field is validated on its own. It then failed at runtime in `roll_over()` with `RuntimeError: unable to rollover, time specification is probably invalid`, which also made beat exit.

The constructor now raises `ValueError` if no day in `day_of_month` occurs in any month in `month_of_year`, in the same way it already rejects e.g. `crontab(minute=61)`. February counts as 29 days, so `day_of_month=29, month_of_year=2` is still accepted.

```python
>>> crontab(day_of_month=30, month_of_year=2)
ValueError: Invalid crontab: day_of_month 30 never occurs in month_of_year 2.
```

**Behaviour change:** schedules that contain such a crontab now fail when the config is loaded, instead of when beat calculates the next run. These specs could never run, and they made beat exit, so failing early seemed better. I've documented it with a `versionchanged` note in the periodic tasks guide.

### 3. solar: an event that doesn't happen on a given day no longer stops beat

When the sun doesn't reach the event's horizon on a given day, ephem raises `CircumpolarError`. The handler for it was broken: it added a `timedelta` to an `ephem.Date` (a float), which raised `TypeError` and stopped beat. The branch had `# pragma: no cover`, so no test ran it.

This doesn't only happen near the poles. Around the summer solstice, astronomical/nautical twilight lasts all night for weeks at roughly 49–60° latitude (London, Paris, Berlin, Amsterdam, Stockholm, …). So a `dawn_astronomical` entry stopped beat every summer in much of Europe.

Changing the line to `ephem.Date(... + ephem.minute)` isn't enough. That returns "1 minute after the next antitransit", which isn't an occurrence of the event. Because the schedule searches from `last_run_at`, the entry then becomes due every night. For example, a London `dawn_astronomical` entry would run on 15 and 16 June, when there is no astronomical dawn.

Now, on `CircumpolarError`, `solar` moves on to the next antitransit (one day later) and tries again. It returns the first real occurrence of the event. The search goes up to `max_search_days` (366) ahead. If nothing is found, it returns the time where the search stopped, so beat checks again then instead of running at a made-up time. The `# pragma: no cover` is removed.

| entry | last run | before | this PR: next run |
|---|---|---|---|
| `solar('dawn_astronomical', 51.5074, -0.1278)` (London) | 2026-06-15 | `TypeError`, beat exits | 2026-07-22 00:30 UTC |
| `solar('dawn_nautical', 59.3293, 18.0686)` (Stockhol, beat exits | 2026-07-29 23:14 UTC |
| `solar('sunrise', 69.6492, 18.9553)` (Tromsø, polar night) | 2026-12-15 | `TypeError`, beat exits | 2027-01-15 10:34 UTC |

I checked the expected times against ephem directly. I also added a short note to the solar section of the periodic tasks guide.

### 4. beat: the schedule DB is reset if a stored crontab is now invalid                                                             
Because of change 2, a schedule DB written by an older version can hold a crontab that the constructor now rejects, e.g. the 30th of February. `crontab.__reduce__` calls the constructor aled, so loading `self._store['entries']` raises`ValueError`, and beat would exit at startup after upgrading.

`PersistentScheduler._create_schedule()` now treats this `ValueError` as it already treats a corrupt or old DB (`KeyError`, `UnpicklingError`, …). It resets the stored entries, aeat_schedule`. As with the other reset cases, thestored `last_run_at` of all entries is lost.

Add these bullets to the existing Tests section:

- `test_schedules.py` (solar):
  - London/June (`dawn_astronomical`), Stockholm/June December (`sunrise`) return the first real occurrenceof the event, not an error or a made-up time;
  - a London `dawn_astronomical` entry last run on 15 e one-line fix would make it due every night);
  - if the event isn't found within `max_search_days`, the search stops and returns a "check again" time instead of raising.
- `test_beat.py`: a stored entry containing a crontab e schedule DB instead of raising.

### Tests

- `test_beat.py`:
  - a failing entry during `populate_heap()`: beat keeps going, the healthy entry is sent, and the failing entry is rescheduled after `max_interval`;
  - a failing entry in `tick()`: beat returns `max_interval` instead of raising.
- `test_schedules.py`:
  - impossible day/month combinations, and empty `day_of_month`/`month_of_year`, raise `ValueError`;
  - possible combinations (Feb 29, `'30,31'` in `'2,3'`, …) are accepted.
- `test_invalid_specification` now expects the `ValueError`. Its infinite-loop guard for `roll_over()` is kept in a new `test_rollover_gives_up_on_invalid_date`, which bypasses the constructor check.
