title: Fix retry argument conflicts when switching calling conventions
body:
## Description

Fixes #6494.

### Problem

`Task.retry()` inherits positional and keyword arguments from the original task request when they are not explicitly provided.

When a task is initially called with keyword arguments and retried with positional arguments (or vice versa), the inherited arguments may conflict with the new ones. This can result in a `TypeError` and prevent the retry from being scheduled.

### Solution

Update retry argument handling to reconcile explicitly provided arguments with those inherited from the original request.

The change:

- Supports switching between positional and keyword arguments when retrying a task.
- Prevents duplicate values for the same parameter.
- Preserves inherited arguments that do not conflict with explicitly supplied values.
- Maintains existing behavior when retry arguments are not overridden.
- Adds five regression tests covering argument overrides and different calling conventions.

### Testing

Verified locally using Python 3.12.

**Unit tests:**

```text
python -m pytest -q t/unit/tasks/test_tasks.py
144 passed, 1 warning
```

**Retry-specific tests:**

```text
python -m pytest -q t/unit/tasks/test_tasks.py -k "retry"
63 passed, 81 deselected
```

**Code quality:**

- All applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including flake8, isort, mypy, pyupgrade, and codespell.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Added contributor attribution to `CONTRIBUTORS.txt`.

title: Use the signature's own options in map/starmap apply_async
body:
## Description

`task.map()` and `task.starmap()` ignore the options stored on the signature. `_basemap.apply_async()` only passes the options given to the call itself to `celery.map` / `celery.starmap`, and never merges `self.options` the way `Signature.apply_async()` does. As a result `.set(queue=..., countdown=...)`, `.link()` callbacks and the task id from `freeze()` were all dropped.

This merges the signature's options with the call's options (call options win, `None` values are dismissed), so a map/starmap signature behaves like other signatures.

Checked with the repro from the issue (in-memory broker, solo worker): the callback now receives `[3, 7]`, the frozen result resolves to `[11]`, and `.set(countdown=3)` delays the task by about 3 seconds. Added unit tests for the stored options, for call options overriding them, and for the frozen task id; they fail without the change. `t/unit/tasks`, `t/unit/app` and `t/unit/worker` pass (one unrelated failure in `test_backend_by_url`, a missing optional module in my environment), and flake8 is clean.

Fixes #10782

title: Keep pool time limits when asynloop exits on connection error
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

#10218 made `asynloop` call `hub.timer.clear()` when the event loop exits on a connection error. The goal was to drop stale periodic entries (such as the transport's `maybe_restore_messages`) that would otherwise fire against the broken connection and crash the loop again during reconnect.

The hub timer is shared with the rest of the worker, though. Clearing it also removes the **soft/hard time limit timers of tasks still running in the pool**. Those tasks keep running across the reconnect, but their time limits are never registered again. A task that should have been killed by `time_limit` / `soft_time_limit` can then run forever after a broker connection drop.

### Fix

- Take a snapshot of the timer's entries before `asynloop` registers its own (AMQP heartbeats, event dispatcher heartbeats, `register_with_event_loop` callbacks).
- On a connection error, cancel only the entries this loop added, instead of clearing the whole timer. The next `asynloop` call registers them again after reconnect.
- Entries owned by other parts of the worker, such as pool time limits, stay in place.
- Graceful shutdown (`WorkerShutdown` / `WorkerTerminate`) behaves as before: nothing is cancelled.
- Cancelling still has its own `try/except`, so the original connection error is always re-raised.

### Tests

The `asynloop` timer tests now use a real `kombu.asynchronous.timer.Timer` instead of mocking `clear()`, and cover:

- the loop's entries are cancelled on a connection error
- entries don't build up across repeated reconnects
- entries that existed before the loop, or were added while it ran (e.g. time limits), survive a connection error
- nothing is cancelled on graceful shutdown, worker shutdown or terminate
- the original error is still raised if `cancel()` or `hub.reset()` fails

Related: #10218

title: Release Preparation for v5.7.0rc1 Release Candidate
Fix LimitedSet re-added items keeping their old expiry slot
body:
Fixes #10757.

`LimitedSet.add()` documents "add a new item, or reset the expiry time of an existing item", but re-adding didn't protect the item: `discard()` removes it from `_data` while its old heap entry stays, and neither `purge()` nor `pop()` checks whether a heap entry is still the item's current one. As a result a re-added item was:

- expired by `purge()` using its **old** timestamp,
- evicted first under `maxlen` pressure as if it were the oldest item,
- returned first by `pop()`.

The stale entries are only cleared when the heap grows more than `max_heap_percent_overload` (15%) beyond `_data`, so in any realistically sized set a few re-added items always misbehave. This matters for revocation state, which `LimitedSet` backs: a renewed revocation could silently expire early.

Fix: a heap entry is stale unless it **is** the item's current `_data` entry.

- `pop()`: skip entries where `self._data.get(item) is not entry` instead of removing the live item.
- `purge()`: discard stale heap heads the same way before reading the oldest timestamp (dropping them from the heap only, never touching live `_data` entries).

Tests in `t/unit/utils/test_collections.py` use 8-9 item sets on purpose: with fewer items a single stale entry already exceeds the 15% refresh threshold and the bug hides itself.

- `test_readded_item_expires_from_new_timestamp`
- `test_readded_item_is_not_evicted_as_oldest` (the true oldest live item is evicted instead)
- `test_pop_returns_true_oldest_after_readd`

All three fail on current `main` and pass with the fix; the full `test_collections.py` suite passes (92 tests) and flake8 is clean on both files.

title: Fix stamped header revocation
body:
## Description

Fix stamped-header revocation incorrectly stopping after the first stamped header that does not match.

When multiple stamped headers are present, `Request.revoked()` previously broke out of the revocation check after processing the first header found in `revoked_stamps`, even when its value did not match. This caused a task to remain unrevoked when a later stamped header should have matched.

This changes the loop to stop only after a matching stamped header is found, allowing subsequent stamped headers to be checked correctly.

Additional regression tests cover:

* Revocation when a later stamped header matches.
* No revocation when none of the stamped headers match.
* Later list-valued stamped headers.
* Revocation when only one of multiple stamped headers is flagged.
* Cleanup of the shared `revoked_stamps` state between tests.

Fixes #10883.

title: Fix task execution after ETA conversion failure
body:
## Description

Fixes #10875

When ETA timestamp conversion raises `OverflowError` or `ValueError`, the worker rejects the task with `requeue=False`. Previously, execution continued after the rejection and entered the normal task execution path, allowing the rejected task to be reserved and executed immediately.

This change returns immediately after rejecting the message, ensuring that a task with an invalid ETA is not executed after rejection.

### Changes

* Return immediately after `req.reject(requeue=False)` when ETA conversion fails.
* Add regression coverage for both `OverflowError` and `ValueError`.
* Verify that the message is rejected and neither reserved nor executed.

### Testing

* `pytest -q t/unit/worker/test_strategy.py -k eta_conversion_error`

  * **8 passed, 77 deselected**
* Full `t/unit/worker/test_strategy.py` suite

  * **85 passed**
* Worker test suite

  * **745 passed, 7 skipped**

title: Fix exponential message growth in chains of groups
body:
## Description

A chain of groups can exhaust producer memory while publishing JSON messages: each pending chord repeats its body in every frozen header task. With three tasks per group, the first task body grows from 2,082 bytes at three groups to 148,526 bytes at six groups.

Remove these redundant callbacks from execution copies. When the pending chord runs, it attaches its body before publishing the header. Copy mutable header lists so preparing an execution cannot replace the callbacks in the caller's frozen signature, while keeping generator headers lazy. The six-group body is now 5,394 bytes.

Refs #9475. The reproduction-only #9817 is related; this covers group-only nesting left after #10743 and #10824.

Validation on macOS arm64, Python 3.13:

- Six new regression cases fail on unchanged main; the size and frozen-signature isolation cases pass with the fix.
- Full unit suite: 4,975 passed, 67 skipped and 2 xfailed. The two callback-cleanup helpers have full local line and branch coverage, including nested chords and frozen chords without a body.
- 21 Redis worker cases passed, including protocols 1/2, JSON round trips, task errbacks and a 10x25 pipeline. All 250 stage tasks ran once, and each first-stage JSON body stayed below 128 KiB.

The complete canvas integration run passes 231 tests, with 5 existing xfails and 5 non-strict xpasses. Four filesystem-result-backend cases also pass using the fallback chord unlock task. Pre-commit hooks and mypy pass.

The end-to-end group pipelines use a final reducer. Existing group-only result-waiting and chain-level error propagation failures also reproduce on unchanged main; the patch does not address those separately observed behaviors.


Full pre-commit checks pass. `apicheck` and `configcheck` report existing undocumented modules/settings and documentation warnings; these also reproduce on unchanged main. The configured Bandit baseline is invalid JSON, and scanning both versions produces the same 49 findings.

title: Fix worker expiration checks during DST fall back
body:
## Description

`Request.maybe_expire()` gets now using self.expires.tzinfo. Both datetimes then share the same timezone object, so 
`now > self.expires` compares local times and ignores fold.

For example, in New York on November 1, 2026, 01:45 EDT (05:45 UTC) compares greater than 01:30 EST (06:30 UTC), revoking the task 45 minutes early.

This PR fixes worker expiration checks during DST fall back by reading the current time in UTC.

title: Fire chain link once on the last task in eager chains
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Eager `_chain.apply` merged the chain's own options, including `link`, into every task's apply call, so a chain level link callback fired once per task and saw intermediate results. The worker path (`_chain.run`) extends the link onto the last task only, a semantic pinned by `test_apply_options`.

This pops `link` out of the per task options in `_chain.apply` and extends it onto the clone of the last executed task instead, mirroring `_chain.run`. When the last task is a chord, the link is put on the cloned chord body's options, since `_chord.apply` only applies the body. (Routing it via `chord.link()` would append to the body's first task and mutate the caller's canvas when the body is a group.) `link_error` stays per task, as on the worker, and links set on individual tasks are untouched, so a task's own link and the chain link both fire on the last task.

Verification: added four regression tests covering `apply_async(link=...)`, `.set(link=...)`, a chord as the last chain task, and canvas mutation across reruns. The first three failed before the fix (callback fired with `[8, 16]`, `[]` for the chord case); the fourth fails if the link leaks into the caller's canvas. All pass now. Full `t/unit/tasks/` suite passes: 1171 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed.

title: Skip exited children in AsynPool._help_stuff_finish
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10858

`billiard.Pool._terminate_pool` is registered as a `Finalize`, so it still runs at interpreter exit after a warm shutdown has closed and joined the pool. It calls `AsynPool._help_stuff_finish`, which reads the inqueue of every child in the pool, including children that have already exited.

A child killed between reading the 4-byte length and the body of its `None` sentinel leaves only the pickle body in its inqueue. This happens on platforms that send SIGTERM to every process in the container. `recv()` reads that body as a negative length, so the worker printed `EOFError: Ran out of input` from the finalizer on shutdown.

Nothing will read an exited child's inqueue again, so `_help_stuff_finish` now skips children whose `exitcode` is set. Live children are drained as before. This is the `exitcode` check recommended in #10858. It was preferred over cancelling the pool's finalizer in `TaskPool.on_stop` because that would also skip the rest of `_terminate_pool`.

## Tests

Added to `t/unit/concurrency/test_prefork.py` (`test_AsynPool`):

- `test_help_stuff_finish_skips_exited_processes`, the test @GangEunzzang posted in #10858. It gives an exited child an inqueue holding only a pickled `None` body, and a live child an inqueue holding a complete message. It checks that the live child's inqueue is drained. It fails on `main` with `EOFError: Ran out of input` and passes with this change.

`t/unit/concurrency` and `t/unit/worker` pass (853 passed, 3 skipped) on Python 3.14.8 with billiard 4.3.1, and flake8 and isort are clean. With this change, the reproduction from #10858 printed no traceback in 10 of 10 runs, and the worker exited 0 every time.

title: Keep a nested group from taking its parent group's id
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10856

`group._freeze_group_tasks()` used the `group_id` it was given as the group's
own id. But `group_id` names the group a signature belongs to, so a group that
ends a chain inside another group, e.g.
`group(a, chain(b, group(c, d)))`, got the outer group's id, and
`as_tuple()` listed that id twice. Since 5.6.0, a group used as a chord body
gets the header's id the same way.

What changed (`celery/canvas.py`, 2 lines changed, 1 added):

- `group._freeze_group_tasks()` gives the group a fresh id when it has none,
  instead of `group_id or uuid()`. This is the behaviour before 4.4.0rc5.
- `chord.run()` was the only caller relying on the old behaviour, to give the
  header the chord's group id. It now sets `header.options['task_id']`
  explicitly before freezing the header.

Chord counting is unchanged: the tasks inside the nested group still get the
outer group's id as their `group_id`. On a worker (in-memory broker, threads
pool, protocol 1 and 2), for `group(a, chain(b, group(c, d)))`,
`c` and `d` see `request.group == <outer id>` before and after this change,
and `chord(group(a, chain(b, group(c, d))), body.s())` runs its body with
`['a', ['c', 'd']]` both before and after.

Tests:

- `test_group::test_group_ending_a_chain_in_a_group_gets_its_own_id` (protocol
  1 and 2) and `test_chord::test_group_body_does_not_take_the_header_id`: all
  3 fail on main and pass with this change.
- `t/unit/tasks`: 1148 passed on b69c634, 1151 with this change; merged into
  current main, 1162 passed.
- flake8 and isort are clean.

Possible breakage: code outside Celery that calls
`group.freeze(group_id=X)` and expects the result's id to be `X` will now get
a fresh id. Inside Celery, only `chord.run()` relied on that. `group_id` now
means the same thing for a group as it does for `Signature.freeze()`: the
group the signature belongs to.

Written with help from Claude (AI).

title: Fix chain/group repr mangling task names and arguments
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`repr()` of a `chain`/`group` shortens later task names by removing the first task's module prefix with `remove_repeating_from_task()`, which uses `str.replace()` on the rest of the string. Two cases produce wrong output:

- The prefix is also removed from inside other names: with `app.tasks.a` first, `webapp.tasks.mul(3)` is shown as `webmul(3)`.
- When the first task name has no module part (e.g. `add`), the prefix is `"."`, so every later dot is removed, including in arguments:

```python
>>> add.s(1.5) | mul.s(2.5)   # tasks named "add" and "proj.tasks.mul"
add(1.5) | projtasksmul(25)    # before
add(1.5) | proj.tasks.mul(2.5) # after
```

This only affects `repr()`/log output, but it shows wrong task names and argument values.

The fix returns the string unchanged when the task name has no module, and only strips the prefix where it starts a name (not when preceded by a word character or a dot).

`t/unit/utils/test_text.py::test_remove_repeating_from_task` covers the two docstring examples and both cases above; the two new cases fail on main. `t/unit/utils/test_text.py` and `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py` pass (319 passed, 1 xfailed); flake8/isort clean.

title: Build long chains up to 2,000x faster: chain() of 4,000 tasks in 0.02 s instead of 54 s
body:
## What was slow

Creating a chain with many tasks, like `chain(task.s(1), task.s(2), ..., task.s(4000))`, took almost a minute before anything was sent to a worker.

The time grew with the square of the chain length: twice the tasks took about four times as long.

## Why

`chain(a, b, c, ...)` is built one task at a time, as `a | b | c | ...`. Every time a task is added, all the tasks already in the chain are copied (cloned) again. For 4,000 tasks that adds up to about 8 million copies.

## The fix

When every item passed to `chain()` is a plain task signature, the list of tasks is now built in one go: each task is copied once. Chains that contain groups, chords or other chains still go through the old step-by-step path, because `|` applies special rules to them.

The result is the same as before, including which tasks are copies: the last task is the object you passed in, and the earlier ones are copies.

## How much faster

Time to build `chain(add.s(1, 1), add.s(1), ...)`:

| Tasks | Before | After | Faster by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 500 | 0.70 s | 0.003 s | ~230x |
| 1,000 | 2.88 s | 0.006 s | ~480x |
| 2,000 | 12.6 s | 0.011 s | ~1,100x |
| 4,000 | 54.3 s | 0.024 s | ~2,260x |

## How I checked it

- New test `test_chain_of_signatures_clones_each_task_once`, which fails without the change.
- All tests in `t/unit/tasks/` pass. flake8, isort and bandit are clean on the changed files.
- Built 3,000 random chains (1 to 12 tasks, with links, error callbacks, options and immutable signatures, using both `chain(a, b)` and `chain([a, b])`) the old way and the new way and compared them. The change introduces no differences.

## AI disclosure

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) found this slowdown with a scaling test, wrote the change and the test, and ran the checks above. I reviewed every line and can explain the change.

title: Send the worker hostname as the worker_process_init sender
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #4163.

`worker_process_init` was always sent with `sender=None`, so a handler couldn't tell which worker a pool process belonged to, or connect for one worker only. Now the sender is the worker's hostname, the same as `celeryd_init`:

```python
@worker_process_init.connect(sender='db@example.com')
def setup_db_connection(sender=None, **kwargs):
    ...
```

- **prefork**: `process_initializer` already receives the hostname, so it sends that.
- **solo**: the `Pool` bootstep passes `initargs=(app, hostname)` to every pool class, and the solo pool keeps it in `self.options`, so it sends `initargs[1]`. A `TaskPool()` created without initargs, as some tests do, still sends `None`.

Nothing in the repo connects with `sender=None` (the Django fixup and the smoke handlers connect without a sender), so existing handlers behave as before. I added a `versionchanged:: 5.7` note to `signals.rst`; happy to change the version if this targets a later release.

I kept the solo change to reading `initargs` rather than adding a `hostname` argument to every pool's `__init__`. Let me know if you'd prefer the explicit argument.

Tests: the prefork test checks the sender and that a receiver connected for one hostname only runs for that worker. The solo tests cover both the initargs case and no initargs.

AI assistance (Claude) was used while preparing this; I've reviewed the change, understand it, and will handle the review myself.

title: Fix LimitedSet expiring or evicting a re-added item on its old timestamp
body:
`discard()` removes an item from `_data` but leaves its entry in the heap, so the heap keeps a **stale** entry carrying the item's *original* timestamp. Both `purge()` and `pop()` trusted that stale entry:

* `purge()` read the stale timestamp to decide which item expired,
* `pop()` removed the item named by the stale entry.

As a result a re-added item was expired by `purge()` on its old timestamp, evicted first once `maxlen` was reached, and returned first by `pop()` — even though it had just been added. Those entries were only cleaned up when the heap grew more than 15% larger than the data, which for a few re-added items in a set of realistic size never happens.

**Fix:** skip the heap entries that are no longer the item's current entry (compared by identity against `_data`), and drop such entries from the top of the heap before `purge()`'s expiry check, so a re-added item is treated as the newest one.

This matters for the worker's revoked set (`LimitedSet(maxlen=REVOKES_MAX, expires=REVOKE_EXPIRES)`): ids are re-added on every re-revoke and when mingle merges revoked ids from other workers. A re-revoked id could drop out before `REVOKE_EXPIRES` passed since its latest revoke, letting an ETA or countdown task that should stay revoked run.

The regression test covers all three symptoms (expiry, `maxlen` eviction, `pop()`).

Fixes #10757

title: Accept Pydantic models when calling a pydantic=True task
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #9442

Calling a `pydantic=True` task with a model fails before sending: `x.delay(Arg(value=1))` raises `EncodeError: Object of type Arg is not JSON serializable`, in eager mode too. Callers had to call `model_dump()` by hand.

`Task.apply_async()` now replaces a model passed directly in args or kwargs with its dump when the worker gets an equal model back from it. The caller dumps the model with the task's `pydantic_dump_kwargs` (default `mode='json'`), validates the dump with the annotation, `pydantic_strict` and context the worker uses (the lookup is shared with `pydantic_wrapper`, and this runs the model's validators on the caller too), and compares the result with the original using `==`. `delay()`, signatures, groups, the first task of a chain and eager mode all go through it.

Any other model is left as it is, so the serializer handles it as on main, which usually means `EncodeError`. That includes models that lose a value on the way, such as a `SecretStr` or a field dropped by `Field(exclude=True)` or `exclude_none` that isn't at its default, a subclass passed for its base class, fields that strict mode rejects once `mode='json'` turns them into strings, parameters the worker doesn't validate as a model (no annotation, `Union`, `*args`, `**kwargs`), and models whose serializers or validators raise on the caller. Tasks using the `pickle` serializer and models with kombu's `__json__` hook are left alone too. When no model is dumped, `args` and `kwargs` are passed on unchanged. One change for models made serializable with kombu's `register_type()`: an equal model is now sent as its dump instead of through that encoder.

An equal model can still differ in a few ways, which the docs list: every dumped field counts as set (`exclude_unset=True` in `pydantic_dump_kwargs` keeps `model_fields_set`), aware datetimes arrive with a fixed UTC offset instead of their time zone, a model with its own `__eq__` is only checked as far as that `__eq__` goes, and with `mode='python'` the serializer can still change the dump (tuples arrive as lists, which strict mode rejects).

Out of scope: `.get()` still returns a dict, `send_task()` by name isn't covered, and models inside lists or dicts, in `link` or `link_error`, in a later chain task, a chord body or `map()`, `starmap()` and `chunks()` still raise `EncodeError`. The docs list these.

Testing: 17 new unit tests in `t/unit/app/test_app.py`. The 32 Pydantic tests pass on Python 3.13 with pydantic 2.14.0 and on 3.10 with 2.13.5 (the CI pin). With the source change reverted, 10 of the new tests fail; the other 7 cover behavior main already has. `test_app.py`, `test_tasks.py` and `test_canvas.py` pass apart from `test_setup_security`, which also fails on main because my venvs lack `cryptography`. `test_pydantic_model_arguments` in `t/integration/test_tasks.py` passes against Redis and fails on main with `EncodeError`.

@mathiasertl you offered to review this on the issue, thanks!

title: feat(worker): add task_retry_on_worker_lost to limit requeues after worker loss
body:
## Description

Fixes #9082 (see also discussion #8969)

With `task_reject_on_worker_lost`, a task whose worker dies is requeued with no limit, since the broker doesn't count requeues.

This adds an opt-in `task_retry_on_worker_lost` setting. When it's on, a lost worker retries the task like `Task.retry()` does, so `max_retries` and `default_retry_delay` apply. When retries run out, the task is marked as failed. Default is off, so existing behaviour doesn't change.

One open question: if sending the retry fails, the task is currently marked as failed. Would falling back to requeue be better?

title: Fix prefork write generators raising StopIteration (PEP 479)
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10841

`AsynPool._write_job()` and `AsynPool._write_ack()` are generators driven by
the event loop. Three places in them end the generator with
`raise StopIteration()`:

- `_write_job()`, after `on_not_recovering()` when writing the job header
  fails with EAGAIN more than 100 times in a row;
- `_write_job()`, the same for the job body;
- `_write_ack()`, when the synq fd no longer maps to a process and the ack is
  discarded.

Under PEP 479 (Python 3.7+) this becomes
`RuntimeError('generator raised StopIteration')`. kombu's `Hub.create_loop()`,
`schedule_writes()` and `AsynPool._flush_writer()` only treat `StopIteration`
from `next()` as "writer finished", so the `RuntimeError` propagates out of the
event loop and the worker stops with `Unrecoverable error` and exit code 1,
instead of carrying on after the damaged child has been terminated.

This change replaces the three `raise StopIteration()` with `return`. A
`return` inside the generator makes `next()` raise `StopIteration`, which is
what the old code meant and what the callers already handle. The `finally`
blocks run in both cases, so cleanup is unchanged: `on_not_recovering()` has
already logged the error, terminated the child, removed the fd from the hub
and put the job back in the outbound buffer, and `_write_job()`'s `finally`
removes the writer and marks the fd and generator inactive.

### Tests

Added to `t/unit/concurrency/test_prefork.py` (`test_AsynPool`):

- `test_write_job_stops_when_inqueue_not_recovering[False|True]`: drives
  `_write_job()` through `schedule_writes()` with a `send_job_offset` that
  always raises `OSError(EAGAIN)` (for the header, or for the body after the
  header was written). It asserts that the generator ends with
  `StopIteration`, that `on_not_recovering()` ran (error logged, child
  terminated, job put back in the outbound buffer) and that the fd and the
  generator are no longer active.
- `test_write_ack_stops_when_process_gone`: sends an ack for an fd that has no
  process and asserts the `_write_ack()` generator ends with `StopIteration`
  and is no longer active.

All three fail on `main` with `RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration`
and pass with this change.

title: Build chains in a single pass instead of folding with `|`
body:
## Description

`chain.__new__` builds the chain by folding the tasks with `|`:

```python
new_instance = reduce(operator.or_, tasks, _chain())
```

Every `_chain.__or__` goes through `seq_concat_item(self.unchain_tasks(), other)`, and `unchain_tasks()` is `[t.clone() for t in self.tasks]` — it re-clones every task the chain already holds. Folding *n* signatures therefore performs *n(n-1)/2* clones. For an 800-task chain that is 319,600 calls to `Signature.clone`, and a profile attributes 96% of construction time to cloning.

The composition rules (empty groups are skipped, a group of one is unrolled, a group followed by a task becomes a chord, a task after a chord extends the chord body, consecutive chords collapse) only ever inspect the *last* step, so they can be applied to a list in place rather than by rebuilding the chain each time. `_fold_chain` does one pass and clones each task once. Anything the single pass cannot express — notably an empty chain followed by a group, which yields the group rather than a chain — is handed back to `|`, which knows how those receivers compose.

Building a chain of plain signatures, measured on CPython 3.14 (i7-12700H), with the patch applied and then reverted with `git checkout HEAD` on the same checkout:

| tasks | current main | this PR | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 100 | 10.60 ms | 0.53 ms | 20x |
| 200 | 39.95 ms | 0.96 ms | 42x |
| 400 | 154.41 ms | 1.88 ms | 82x |
| 800 | 631.38 ms | 3.72 ms | 170x |

Current main quadruples per doubling; this doubles. Fewer clones also means proportionally less memory, which is the part #9202 reports as the practical problem.

## One behaviour change

Folding with `|` leaves the **last** task of the finished chain aliased to the signature the caller passed in, because the final `__or__` clones the accumulated tasks but not the incoming one. Every other position is a clone. The single pass clones that one too, so `chain(a, b, c).tasks[-1] is c` is now `False` where it used to be `True`.

I took the consistent behaviour rather than reproducing the asymmetry, since reproducing it means leaving a caller-owned signature in the chain where later composition can mutate it in place. Nothing in the test suite depends on it. Happy to preserve the old aliasing instead if you would rather keep it bit-for-bit.

## Tests

Two added to `test_chain`:

- `test_chain_clones_each_task_once` asserts the number of `Signature.clone` calls stays linear. It fails on current main, where a 40-task chain clones 780 times.
- `test_chain_construction_handles_nested_canvas_shapes` pins the group/chord/nested-chain/empty-group outcomes. It passes both before and after, so it documents the semantics the single pass has to preserve.

`t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`, `test_chord.py`, `test_result.py`, `test_tasks.py` and `t/unit/app/test_builtins.py` all pass (606 tests). `flake8` is clean.

## Scope

This is construction cost only. It does not address the serialized message growth also discussed in #9202, which #10743 covered for chains of implicit chords and #10824 is picking up for standalone chord bodies — hence `Refs` rather than `Fixes`.

title: Reset autoscale keepalive for immediate tasks
body:
## Description

The autoscaler currently measures its keepalive from the last pool growth. After a sustained workload that needs no further growth, a short gap between tasks can shrink the pool immediately, forcing the next burst to start new processes.

Reset the keepalive when a task is accepted for immediate execution, even when the pool already has enough processes. The event loop records receipt through its existing scaling callback; workers without an event loop register a receipt callback. Updating the receipt timestamp does not wait for the pool's resize mutex. Periodic checks do not reset the timestamp.

Keep the existing `_last_scale_up` timestamp for custom autoscaler subclasses and track task receipts separately. Custom autoscaler classes without the receipt hook can still start. The worker guide explains that tasks routed through ETA/countdown or rate-limit scheduling do not reset the timer.

Fixes #8943.

The regressions cover both callback paths, the keepalive boundary, task receipt while the resize lock is held, and custom autoscalers. A smoke test runs repeated pairs of tasks with a prefork worker and verifies that short gaps retain the same pool process IDs after the initial growth keepalive has elapsed.

Validation at `08002e7` (before the subsequent main merge):

- `pytest t/unit`: 4599 passed, 69 skipped, 2 xfailed; 27675 subtests passed.
- `pre-commit run --files celery/worker/autoscale.py t/unit/worker/test_autoscale.py docs/userguide/workers.rst`: all applicable hooks passed, including mypy.
- Documentation codespell and `git diff --check`: passed.


Additional smoke validation:

- The smoke test body passed locally with Redis 7.2.7 and a real prefork worker on the current PR code. It failed on clean main `cf0dc0d` when the pool shrank and replaced a process between bursts.
- `pytest t/unit/worker/test_autoscale.py`: 20 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files t/smoke/tests/test_autoscale.py`: all applicable hooks passed, including mypy.
- Smoke collection includes Redis and RabbitMQ broker cases. The Docker smoke matrix has not been run locally because the Docker daemon is unavailable.

title: Fix errback arity classification with stored signature arguments
body:
## Errback classification

The arity check currently counts arguments already stored on a mutable errback signature. A callback such as `handle_error(task_id, foo, bar, baz)` linked with `.s(1, 2, 3)` is consequently dispatched as a new-style errback and fails with six positional arguments instead of four.

Inspect a partial of the generated header to classify the remaining arguments, including keyword bindings. Immutable signatures and the existing bound-task fallback are unchanged. Regression tests cover eager and queued old-style callbacks with positional and keyword bindings, plus a new-style callback with a stored argument.

Fixes #6430.

title: Pass preload options to commands that do not accept them
body:
Fixes #7894.

Issue #7894 adds a preload option such as `--ini` through `user_options['preload']`. `celery -A example worker --ini app.ini` works. `celery -A example flower --ini app.ini` raises `TypeError: flower() got an unexpected keyword argument 'ini'`. Celery adds those options to every subcommand, and Click passes them as keywords. Flower is a `celery.commands` entry point, and its callback does not accept them.

`handle_preload_options` now removes the preload names, sends `user_preload_options`, and then calls the original function. A subcommand that already carries preload options, and whose callback is not already wrapped, gets the same handling before Click calls it. A plugin callback that uses `@click.pass_context` is not given `ctx` again as a positional argument.

A command's own options, such as `--force`, are still passed through. A callback that already accepts `**kwargs` does not receive `ini`. The preload signal is sent once if that wrapper runs again.

On this commit (`dd8f43a53a840bf78f83eb43e1f5b7e1f5852dff`), Windows, Python 3.13.3: `pytest t/unit/app/test_preload_cli.py t/unit/bin/test_upgrade.py -k "not test_preload_options"` was 13 passed, 2 deselected. Those new tests failed with the `TypeError` before the change. Pre-commit on this diff passed, including isort and mypy. Full tox, bandit, apicheck, configcheck, integration tests, and a real Flower install were not run.

AI-assisted (Cursor).

Cherith reviewed this diff and confirmed it with the person who helped draft it.

title: fix(backends): avoid get_state for plain chain failures
body:
## Description

Fixes #10835

### Problem

When a task in a chain fails and no result backend is configured, `_fail_chain()` unconditionally calls `get_state()` for the failed task.

With `DisabledBackend`, this raises `NotImplementedError` and interrupts the normal failure-handling flow, preventing callbacks such as `on_failure`, `task_failure`, and `link_error` from being triggered correctly.

### Tests

* Verify `get_state()` is not called for plain chain failures.
* Verify `get_state()` is still called for chord members.
* Verify plain chains work with `DisabledBackend`.
* Preserve existing chord failure behavior.

title: Fix IndexError when a chain is an empty group followed by an empty chain
body:
## Summary

Fixes a regression from #10646, reported in https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10646#issuecomment-6042441674:

    optional = chain(group(app=app), chain(app=app), app=app)
    optional.freeze()        # IndexError: list index out of range
    optional.apply_async()   # returns None instead of a GroupResult

Both returned an empty `GroupResult` before #10646.

## Cause

#10646 made `_chain.prepare_steps()` normalise the head of the chain before the reverse walk: leading empty groups are stripped as long as another step follows them, and a nested chain at the head is spliced in place.

"Another step follows" was checked with `len(steps) > 1`. When the following step is an empty chain, the group is stripped and the chain is then spliced into nothing, so no step is left. `prepare_steps()` returns no results, `freeze()` indexes `results[0]`, and `run()` skips the apply and returns `None`.

## Fix

`prepare_steps()` keeps the last empty group it stripped and puts it back if the head normalisation leaves no steps. This is the rule #10646 already applies to a chain made up of empty groups only: one empty group is kept so the chain still yields an (empty) `GroupResult`.

Chains with a real task after the empty steps are unaffected, since the steps are not empty in that case.

## Tests

Added to `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`:

- `test_chain_empty_group_followed_by_empty_chain`
- `test_freeze_empty_group_followed_by_empty_chain`, parametrised over an empty chain, a nested empty chain, two empty chains, and an empty group followed by an empty chain
- `test_apply_async_empty_group_followed_by_empty_chain`

All six cases fail on `main` and pass with this change. `t/unit/tasks`, `t/unit/app/test_app.py` and `t/unit/worker/test_strategy.py`: 1398 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed.

## Not in this PR

These fail the same way on the commit before #10646, so they are not part of this regression:

- `chain().freeze()` and `chain(chain()).freeze()` raise `IndexError`.
- `chain(group(), chain()).apply()` (eager) raises `AttributeError`.

title: Fix chord.apply_async(link=...) raising TypeError on the header group
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10781

`_chord.run()` copies the merged options to the body, then passes the same options to `header.apply_async()`. It already removes `chain`, `chord` and `task_id` for the header, but `link` and `link_error` also got through. `group.apply_async()` always rejects those, so:

1. `chord(header, body).apply_async(link=cb)` raised `TypeError: Cannot add link to group: use a chord` on the client.
2. `chain(a, chord(header, body)).apply_async(link=cb)` failed on the worker. The chain stores its `link` on the last step (the chord), so the error came after `a` finished, and `a` was stored as `FAILURE` even though it returned a value.

The fix removes `link` and `link_error` from the header options. The body already has them from `body.options.update(...)` a few lines earlier. The result matches what `chord.link()` and `chord.link_error()` do, which attach to the body (with the default `task_allow_error_cb_on_chord_header=False`).

## Tests

- Added `test_chord_run_sends_link_options_to_body_only` and `test_chord_apply_async_with_link_option` in `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`. Both fail on `main` and pass with this change.
- Ran the reproducer from the issue with a real worker (memory broker, `cache+memory://` backend):
  - case 1 returns `6`, and the callback runs once with `6`;
  - case 2 returns `34`, the first task is `SUCCESS 2`, and the callback runs once with `34`.
- `t/unit/tasks` and `t/unit/app`: 2013 passed. flake8, isort and codespell are clean on the changed files.

title: fix(cache): keep chords alive past result_expires
body:
## Description

Follow-up to #10827 that fixes #4207 for the memcached backend. This builds on #10827

On the cache backend, a chord's group record and its header results only live for `result_expires`. If the chord runs longer than that, the body never runs. With 5.7.0b1, a chord of three 3-second tasks and `result_expires=1` fails every time.

This makes the cache backend use `result_chord_expires` too:

- The counter and the group record get it when the chord starts.
- Each finished header task refreshes the counter, the group record and its own result.
- A header result never ends up with a shorter TTL than `result_expires`.

Redis avoids the problem by copying the results into one key. I didn't do that here, because memcached caps an item at 1 MB by default and large chords that work today would break.

If the setting isn't set, the only change is a few extra `touch` calls. DynamoDB and GCS share this code but don't implement `expire`, so they aren't affected.

title: Fix duplicate nodes in a chain's as_tuple() after a group
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #9608.

When `prepare_steps` turns a group and the task after it into a chord, the chord's result takes the place of that task's result and has the same id. The next step is still linked to the task's old result, and the old result is then linked to the chord's result. So `as_tuple()` lists the task twice, and with two groups in a row, the second group twice as well.

The repeated id also brings back #8890 on main: `chord([a, b], chain(c, group(d, e), f | g, task_id='x')).freeze()` raises `RuntimeError('Recursive result parents')`, and so does `apply_async()` of a group that holds such a chord. 5.6.3 does not raise.

This change finds the node that is linked to the old result (the next result, or the `GroupResult` of a chord that follows) and links it to the chord's result instead. The `GroupResult` fan-out that #10408 restored is kept.

The example in #9608 has 33 tasks in 2 groups, so its tree should have 35 nodes. Nodes in `as_tuple()` / unique ids:

| | `chain(*tasks)` | `chain(*tasks, task_id=...)` |
|---|---|---|
| 5.3.6 | 35 / 35 | 58 / 35 |
| 5.6.3 | 35 / 35 | 2 / 2 |
| main (a478a2a) | 57 / 35 | 58 / 35 |
| this PR | 35 / 35 | 35 / 35 |

- In 5.3.6 the old result stayed in the tree: nodes were repeated, and freezing such a chain as a chord body raised #8890.
- #8903 (5.4) fixed #8890 by dropping the link, so most of the tree was lost. This is what #9608 reports.
- #10408 restored the link, and with it the repeats and, for chains built with options, the #8890 error.
- `chain()` with any option, `task_id` or `app` included, keeps its steps as written, so the group is upgraded in `prepare_steps`. Since #10743 (in 5.7.0b1), chains built without options reach this code too, because the chord bodies built by `|` are split back into steps (the first column on main).

With this change the tree has the same shape with and without `task_id`, as the issue expects.

## Tests

- Two new tests in `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py` check that `as_tuple()` holds every node exactly once: with and without `task_id`, through `apply_async()` and `freeze()`, under task protocols 1 and 2, and when a chord follows the task that becomes the body. 8 of their 10 cases fail on main; the other two (`freeze()` without options) already pass there.
- `test_group_in_center_of_chain` (#8890) now also runs with a `task_id`; that case raises the `RuntimeError` on main.
- `test_consecutive_groups_in_chain_preserve_group_results_in_as_tuple` from #10408 still passes.
- `t/unit/tasks`: 1132 passed.
- `t/integration/test_canvas.py` against a local Redis (broker and backend): 194 passed, the same as on main.
- flake8 and codespell: clean.

## Notes

- #9713 was suggested on the issue. It changes how task ids are generated, while this tree is built in `prepare_steps`, so I think the two changes are independent.
- Not changed here: for a chain that starts with a group, `chain(group(...), a, b).apply_async().as_tuple()` leaves out `a`, because `chord.run` sets the header result as the parent of the body's last result. `freeze()` keeps `a`, and 5.3.6 behaves the same. I can open a separate issue for it if that helps.

Written with help from Claude (AI); I reviewed it before posting.

title: Don't call setup_defaults twice when creating a Worker
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #7278

**Problem:** When `celery.apps.worker.Worker` is created, `setup_defaults()` runs twice. The second call skips any subclass override of `setup_defaults`, so attributes set in that override get reset. For example, a subclass that sets `self.concurrency = 7` after calling `super().setup_defaults(**kwargs)` ends up with the value from the command line or the config.

**Root cause:** `WorkController.__init__` calls `on_before_init(**kwargs)`, then `setup_defaults(**kwargs)`, then `on_after_init(**kwargs)`. `Worker.on_after_init` then called `super().setup_defaults(**kwargs)` again with the same kwargs, which went straight to `WorkController.setup_defaults` and reset whatever the override had changed.

**Fix:** Remove the redundant `super().setup_defaults(**kwargs)` call from `Worker.on_after_init`. The kwargs `on_after_init` cares about (`purge`, `no_color`, `redirect_stdouts*`) are swallowed by `**_kw` in `setup_defaults` anyway, and the first call already sets `self.logfile` and `self.loglevel`, which `on_after_init` reads afterwards.

One behaviour change to be aware of: a subclass that overrides `setup_defaults` *without* calling `super()` used to get the base defaults filled in anyway by that second call. It no longer does, which is the point of the fix, but it's worth calling out.

**Tests:** Added `test_Worker_setup_defaults` to `t/unit/apps/test_worker.py`:
- `test_setup_defaults_called_once` spies on `WorkController.setup_defaults` and asserts it runs once.
- `test_setup_defaults_override_is_kept` checks that a subclass override survives worker construction.

Both fail on main and pass with this change.

```
python -m pytest t/unit/apps/test_worker.py t/unit/worker -q   # 727 passed, 10 skipped
python -m flake8 celery/apps/worker.py t/unit/apps/test_worker.py
python -m isort --check-only celery/apps/worker.py t/unit/apps/test_worker.py
```

title: fix(redis): add result_chord_expires for chord keys
body:
## Description

Fixes #4207.

On the Redis backend, a chord's size, results and counter keys expire after `result_expires`, measured from the chord's start or from the last header task to finish. If a header task takes longer than that, the size key is gone, so the chord's body never runs and nothing is logged.

This adds `result_chord_expires` for those keys and for the header that a chord with nested groups saves. Unset, it falls back to `result_expires`, as today. `0` means the keys don't expire while the chord is open.

The results of the header tasks themselves still use `result_expires`. The saved header is now written like the other chord keys, so with `result_backend_always_retry` it no longer goes through `GroupResult.save()`'s retry loop.

Tests cover each write and the fallback. An integration test checks the TTLs against Redis and that the saved header still restores.

title: feat(redis): add result_failure_expires setting
body:
## Description

Related to #6936, following the separate expiry for failed results proposed there.

Adds `result_failure_expires`, an optional expiry for the results of failed tasks. It lets failures be kept longer, or shorter, than other results.

- Unset, failed results use `result_expires`, as they do today.
- `0` means failed results never expire.
- Only the `FAILURE` state uses it.

This only covers the Redis backend, which writes the TTL in the same `SETEX` it already sends. The docs say so. Other backends can follow separately if there is interest.

Tests cover the failure and success paths, the default, and `0`. An integration test checks the TTLs against Redis.

title: fix: redact Azure credentials in diagnostic output
body:
## Description

Fix Azure Block Blob credentials being exposed through Celery's diagnostic/configuration output.

`sanitize_url()` previously handled credentials embedded in standard URL authority sections, but Azure Block Blob connection strings store credentials as semicolon-separated key/value pairs such as `AccountKey` and `SharedAccessSignature`. As a result, these credentials could appear in plaintext in `celery report` and other configuration output.

title: saferepr: keep container closing bracket when the last element is truncated
body:
Fix #10760.

## Problem
`saferepr()` drops the container's closing bracket when the budget (`maxlen`) runs out on the *last* element:

```python
>>> saferepr([1, 2, 3, 'abcdefghij'], maxlen=12)
"[1, 2, 3, 'ab...', ..."   # missing ]
```

If more elements follow, the bracket is kept:

```python
>>> saferepr([1, 2, 3, 'abcdefghij', 5], maxlen=12)
"[1, 2, 3, 'ab...', ...]"
```

This affects every task whose final argument is large: `argsrepr`/`kwargsrepr` in the message headers and the logged result repr are built with `saferepr`, so logs/events show an unbalanced repr.

## Root cause
When the token that exhausts the budget is an un-truncatable closing literal, `reprstream` has *already consumed it* from the iterator before `_saferepr` sees `maxlen <= 0`. The iterator pushed back onto the stack then no longer contains that bracket, and the drain loop can't restore it.

## Change
In `_saferepr`'s truncation branch, emit the current token when it is a non-truncatable literal (a closing bracket) before breaking. The outer iterators are unaffected — their brackets are still drained by the existing loop, so nested containers stay balanced.

## Tests
Added three regression tests in `t/unit/utils/test_saferepr.py` covering the last-element case, the three container types (list/tuple/set), and nested containers. All 73 tests in the file pass.

title: Fix Celery Beat relative schedule rounding across DST transitions
body:
## Description

Fixes #10817 

Fix a Beat scheduling regression introduced by #10769 when elapsed-time addition is followed by rounding for `relative=True`.

For example, a daily relative schedule last run at **November 1, 2026, 00:30 EDT** in New York currently:

- Adds 24 elapsed hours, reaching November 1 at 23:30 EST.
- Rounds down to November 1 at midnight.
- Becomes immediately due because the calculated deadline is already past.

The correct deadline is **November 2 at midnight EST**, with **88,200 seconds** remaining.

This change:

- Uses calendar arithmetic for relative intervals of a day or more before rounding.
- Handles partial-hour DST rollbacks where rounding returns a deadline at or before the previous run.
- Preserves elapsed-time arithmetic for shorter intervals and non-relative schedules, including repeated-hour execution.
- Adds regression tests and documents daily relative scheduling.

title: test(consumer): pin reconnect prefetch reduction to green-pool capacity (regression test for #10803)
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Regression test for #10803 (Related: #10361, #7350, #8581).

Before #10361 the gevent `TaskPool` reported `num_processes` as the number of greenlets running *right now* (`len(self._pool)`, 0 when idle) instead of the configured concurrency. On `Connection to broker lost` the consumer therefore computed `max_prefetch_count == 0`, reduced the channel to `prefetch_multiplier` (1), logged *"will be gradually restored to 0"*, and the restore step immediately treated `min(0, qos + 1)` as fully restored — so a gevent worker that reconnected once stayed at prefetch=1 for the rest of its life. Details, log signature and production impact are in #10803.

#10361 fixed the pool side (motivated by autoscale, #4003). Nothing pins the consumer-side outcome, so this adds one parametrized test in `t/unit/worker/test_consumer.py` that runs `on_connection_error_after_connected` against a **real** `celery.concurrency.gevent.TaskPool`:

- `idle`: 0 greenlets running, 0 active requests → `max_prefetch_count == 50`, `initial_prefetch_count == 50`, `_maximum_prefetch_restored is True` (no reduction at all).
- `busy`: 3 greenlets / 3 active requests → `initial_prefetch_count == 47`, `_maximum_prefetch_restored is False` (reduce by in-flight count, restore gradually, as #7350 intended).

The test is skipped when gevent is not installed (`pytest.importorskip`).

Verified locally:

- on `main`: `2 passed`; full `t/unit/worker/test_consumer.py` + `t/unit/concurrency/test_gevent.py`: `141 passed, 40 subtests passed`.
- with `celery/concurrency/gevent.py` swapped to its `v5.6.3` content: both cases fail (`assert 0 == 50`, `assert 3 == 50`), i.e. the test does catch the bug.
- `flake8` (repo `setup.cfg`) and `isort --check-only` clean.

Tests-only change; no behaviour change.

title: fix(graph): keep every node of a cycle in DependencyGraph.topsort
body:
## Summary

`DependencyGraph.topsort` handles cycles by first condensing strongly connected components (Tarjan) and topologically sorting the condensation (Khan) — but then projects every component down to its **first member**:

```python
from celery.utils.graph import DependencyGraph

DependencyGraph([("A", ["B"]), ("B", [])]).toposort()
# -> ['B', 'A']   (correct)

DependencyGraph([("A", ["B"]), ("B", ["A"])]).toposort()
# -> ['A']        (!)  B silently vanished
```

Any node that is only reachable through a cycle disappears from the "objects in the order in which they must be handled" that the docstring promises. The graph drives worker **bootstep ordering** (`celery/bootsteps.py`) and the `AsyncResult.graph` dependencies (`celery/result.py`), where a dependency cycle in declared requirements would silently drop the affected steps/tasks instead of surfacing the problem.

## Fix

Emit all members of each component instead of the first:

```python
# Each strongly connected component is collapsed into one vertex by
# the condensation; emit all of its members, otherwise nodes that
# are only reachable through a cycle silently disappear from the
# result (e.g. a two-node A <-> B cycle used to yield just ['A']).
return [node for component in graph._khan62() for node in component]
```

Acyclic graphs are unaffected (every component is a singleton).

Regression tests: `test_topsort_cycle_keeps_all_nodes` covers the pure two-node cycle and a mixed graph asserting both the full node set and the acyclic ordering constraints. Full `t/unit/utils/test_graph.py`, `t/unit/tasks/test_result.py`, and `t/unit/worker/test_bootsteps.py` suites pass.

## AI Disclosure

This PR was prepared with the assistance of `ZCode (GLM-based coding agent)`: the vanishing-node behavior was found by probing `DependencyGraph`, and the fix, regression tests, and description were drafted by the tool. The change was reviewed and tested by the author, who is responsible for it.

title: fix(text): stop abbr from slicing from the end at tiny widths
body:
## Summary

`celery.utils.text.abbr` abbreviates to `max` characters by slicing `S[: max - len(ellipsis)]` and appending the ellipsis. When `max` is smaller than the ellipsis length (3 by default), `max - 3` goes negative and the slice silently takes characters **from the end of the string**:

```python
from celery.utils.text import abbr

abbr("hello", 4)   # -> 'h...'    (correct)
abbr("hello", 3)   # -> '...'     (correct)
abbr("hello", 2)   # -> 'o...'    (!)  4 chars for width 2, and 'o' is the LAST character
abbr("hello", 1)   # -> 'll...'   (!)  5 chars for width 1
abbr("hello", 0)   # -> 'he...'   (!)  5 chars for width 0
```

Every result is *longer* than the requested width and built from the tail of the string. `abbr` feeds the CLI/inspect table formatting (`celery inspect`, `celery status`), where a computed column width of 0–2 (tiny terminal, long task names) produces exactly this garbled output.

## Fix

Only use the ellipsis form when the ellipsis actually fits in `max`; otherwise cap at `S[:max]`:

```python
if len(S) > max:
    if isinstance(ellipsis, str) and max >= len(ellipsis):
        return S[: max - len(ellipsis)] + ellipsis
    return S[: max]
```

Behavior for `max >= len(ellipsis)` and for strings that already fit is unchanged (covered by the existing parametrized tests, which still pass).

Regression test: `test_abbr_small_width` covers widths 0–4 plus the unchanged fitting/regular-truncation/`ellipsis=False` cases.

## AI Disclosure

This PR was prepared with the assistance of `ZCode (GLM-based coding agent)`: the tail-slicing behavior was found by probing `celery.utils.text`, and the fix, regression test, and description were drafted by the tool. The change was reviewed and tested by the author, who is responsible for it.

title: fix(time): reject unknown kwargs in ffwd instead of a silent no-op
body:
## Summary

`ffwd` is documented as *"Version of ``dateutil.relativedelta`` that only supports addition"*, but its semantics differ in a way that currently fails **silently**: it takes absolute fields (`year=`, `month=`, `day=`, `hour=`, ...) plus relative `weeks=` only. Any other keyword — `months=`, `years=`, `days=`, `hours=`, ... — is swallowed by `**kwargs` and ignored:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from celery.utils.time import ffwd

datetime(2026, 1, 31) + ffwd(months=1)   # expected end of February
# -> datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 31)      # unchanged, no error!
datetime(2026, 1, 31) + ffwd(months=12)
# -> datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 31)      # a whole year, silently dropped
datetime(2026, 1, 31) + ffwd(days=3)     # timedelta-style kwarg
# -> datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 31)      # ignored
```

Anyone migrating `relativedelta` arithmetic to `ffwd` gets date math that silently does nothing — worst case for scheduled/ETA code.

## Fix

Raise a `TypeError` listing the unexpected argument(s) and pointing at the right tool:

```python
if kwargs:
    raise TypeError(
        'ffwd() got unexpected keyword argument(s): '
        f'{", ".join(sorted(kwargs))}. ffwd sets absolute fields '
        '(year=, month=, day=, ...) and only supports relative '
        'addition through weeks=; for relative months/years use '
        'dateutil.relativedelta, for days/hours use timedelta.'
    )
```

All in-tree callers (`celery/schedules.py` and tests) were audited and only use the named fields, so behavior is unchanged for existing code — verified by the full `t/unit/utils/test_time.py` + `t/unit/app/test_schedules.py` suites (209 passed).

Tests: `test_ffwd_unknown_kwargs` covers `months=`/`days=`/`years=`+`hours=` rejection and that every named field plus `weeks=` still works.

title: fix(time): convert datetimes in datetime.timezone.utc in localize
body:
## Summary

`localize()` decides whether an aware datetime can be safely converted with `astimezone()` by checking `dt.tzinfo == ZoneInfo("UTC")`. That comparison only matches a `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("UTC")` instance — an aware datetime carrying `datetime.timezone.utc`, which is the default way plain Python code marks UTC times (`datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, `datetime(..., tzinfo=timezone.utc)`), fails the check and is returned **unchanged** instead of being converted to the target zone:

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from celery.utils.time import localize

utc_dt = datetime(2017, 4, 23, 21, 36, 59, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
localize(utc_dt, ZoneInfo("US/Eastern"))
# -> 2017-04-23 21:36:59+00:00   (unchanged, expected 17:36:59-04:00)

localize(utc_dt.replace(tzinfo=ZoneInfo("UTC")), ZoneInfo("US/Eastern"))
# -> 2017-04-23 17:36:59-04:00   (same instant, ZoneInfo flavor converts fine)
```

So the same wall time silently converts or doesn't depending on which of the two UTC tzinfo objects it carries — a 4/5-hour discrepancy in the worker-local display/ETA paths built on `localize()` (e.g. `_Zone.to_local`, `to_local_fallback`).

## Fix

Treat `datetime.timezone.utc` as the UTC zone it is:

```python
if dt.tzinfo == ZoneInfo("UTC") or dt.tzinfo == datetime_timezone.utc:
    dt = dt.astimezone(tz)  # Always safe to call astimezone on utc zones
```

`datetime.timezone.utc` is a singleton, so `==` is equivalent to `is` here.

Regression test: `test_localize_converts_fixed_offset_utc` asserts the returned datetime actually carries the target tzinfo with the right offset while preserving the absolute instant. The existing `test_localize_changes_utc_dt` / `test_localize_aware_dt_idempotent` compare instants (`==` on aware datetimes), so they are unaffected by the conversion.

## AI Disclosure

This PR was prepared with the assistance of `ZCode (GLM-based coding agent)`: the divergence was found by an empirical probe of `celery.utils.time`, and the guard, regression test, and description were drafted by the tool. The change was reviewed and tested by the author, who is responsible for it.

title: fix(canvas): don't raise in chain.app when the first task's canvas holds a dict
body:
## Description

Follow-up to #10749, fixing the regression @Borzik reported in
https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10749#pullrequestreview (last review comment).

Since #10749, `_chain.app` reads `self.tasks[0].app` instead of
`self.tasks[0]._app`. A group, or a chain built with options, keeps a dict as a
task until it is frozen, and `.app` on such a canvas raises `AttributeError`.
`_chain.app` only caught `LookupError`, so `apply_async()` now fails on chains
that worked before:

    chain(group([dict(add.s(1, 1)), dict(add.s(2, 2))]), tsum.s(), task_id='x').apply_async()
    chain(chain(dict(add.s(1, 1)), echo.s(), task_id='x'), echo.s(), task_id='y').apply_async()
    # AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'app'

This is the case `chord._app_of` already handles. `_chain.app` now catches
`AttributeError` as well, so the chain falls back to `current_app`, which is
what it resolved to before #10749.

## Tests

Chain versions of `test_app_when_header_canvas_has_dict`, parametrized over a
group and a chain as the first task:

- `test_app_when_first_task_canvas_has_dict`: `chain.app` falls back to
  `current_app`.
- `test_apply_async_when_first_task_canvas_has_dict`: `apply_async()` returns
  an `AsyncResult`.

All four cases fail on main with
`AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'app'` and pass with the change.

Verification (Python 3.13.1, macOS):

- `t/unit/tasks`: 1109 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed.
- flake8 and isort pass on the changed files.

title: Stop gating task publishing signals on cached receiver lists
body:
## Description

`before_receivers` and `after_receivers` keep references to signal's receiver lists. `_clear_dead_receivers()` can replace `signal.receivers`, and those variables still point to the old list. If the old list is empty, the sender skips the signal even when new receivers are connected.
https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/3cfe8de4352e665882f2c4e39cded26fe6c65871/celery/utils/dispatch/signal.py#L292-L301
These gates aren't really needed because `Signal.send()` already checks the current receiver list and returns when there are no receivers.

title: Merge signature options in map/starmap apply_async
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #10782

`_basemap.apply_async()` (used by `task.map()` / `task.starmap()`) forwarded only the options passed to that call to `celery.map` / `celery.starmap`, and never merged `self.options`. So anything stored on the signature was silently dropped:

- callbacks added with `.link()` never ran
- the result returned by `.freeze()` never resolved, because a different task id was sent
- `.set(queue=..., countdown=..., priority=...)` was ignored

This contradicts the canvas docs ("Both map and starmap are signature objects, so they can be used as other signatures"). The same options passed directly to `apply_async(...)` worked, and so did the same signature inside a `group`/`chain`, where it is cloned into a plain `Signature`.

The fix merges the stored options with the call options the same way `Signature.apply_async` does: drop `None` values, then `self._merge(options=...)`. Call options override stored ones, and immutable/stamped option handling is unchanged.

### Verification

The reproduction from the issue, run against a real worker (`memory://` broker, solo pool):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `.link(cb.s())` | callback never called | callback called with `[3, 7]` |
| `r = s.freeze(); s.delay(); r.get()` | `TimeoutError` | `[11]` |
| `.set(countdown=3)` | ran after 1.0s | ran after ~3.5s |

### Tests

Added to `test_xmap_xstarmap`, parametrized over `map` and `starmap`:

- `test_apply_async_uses_signature_options`: `queue`/`countdown` from `.set()`, `link` from `.link()` and the `task_id` from `freeze()` reach `celery.map/starmap`'s `apply_async`
- `test_apply_async_call_options_override_signature_options`: an explicit call option wins, and a `None` call option doesn't erase a stored one

All 4 new cases fail on `main` and pass with this change. `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py` passes in full (275 passed, 1 xfailed), and flake8 is clean.

`chunks.apply_async` has a similar shape. It delegates to a `group`, though, and isn't part of this report, so I've left it out of scope here.

title: Docs: correct the default value of worker_task_log_format
