title: fix(canvas): apply stored options in map/starmap apply_async()
body:
## Description

Signatures created with `task.map()` / `task.starmap()` (`xmap` / `xstarmap`) ignore the options stored on them when they are called directly. `_basemap.apply_async()` forwards only the options given to the call and never merges `self.options`, unlike `Signature.apply_async()`. Everything stored on the signature is silently dropped:

```python
add.starmap(items).set(queue='q1', countdown=10).apply_async()
# sent to the default queue and run at once; no ETA

s = add.starmap(items); s.link(cb.s()); s.apply_async()
# cb never runs

s = add.starmap(items); r = s.freeze(); s.delay()
r.get()   # never resolves: the id sent is not r.id
```

The docs describe map/starmap as "signature objects, so they can be used as other signatures". Other code paths already honor these options:
- `add.starmap(items).apply_async(queue='q1', countdown=10)` (options passed to the call) works.
- The same signature inside a `group` or `chain` works, because it is cloned into a plain `Signature` there.
- The eager path (`Signature.apply()`) merges the options.

Only direct calls were affected.

### Fix

Merge the options with `self._merge()`, as `Signature.apply_async()` does. Options set to `None` in the call are dismissed, the rest override the stored ones, and stamped headers stay immutable.

### Before / after (in-process worker, `memory://` broker, `cache+memory://` backend)

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `starmap.link(cb)` | `cb` never called | `cb` called with `[3, 7]` |
| `r = starmap.freeze(); starmap.delay(); r.get()` | `TimeoutError` (never resolves) | `[11]` |
| `starmap.set(countdown=2)` | ran after 0.5 s | ran after 2.0 s |
| `map/starmap.set(queue='q1')` | default queue `celery` | `q1` |

### Tests

`test_xmap_xstarmap::test_apply_async_uses_signature_options[map|starmap]` checks that stored `queue`, `link` and the frozen `task_id` reach the task's `apply_async()`. It also checks that options passed to the call override stored ones and that `None` options are dropped. Both cases fail on `main` and pass with this change. The existing `test_apply` still passes. The full `t/unit` suite passes except for failures that also occur on unmodified `main` in my environment (root user, no broker). flake8, isort and codespell are clean.

### Not changed here

`chunks.apply_async()` has the same pattern, but chunks fans out into a group. A group rejects `link` / `link_error` with `TypeError`, and a frozen single-task id cannot match the `GroupResult` it returns. Forwarding chunks' stored options needs its own discussion, so it is left for a separate change.

Added an entry under *Unreleased* in `Changelog.rst`.

title: fix(canvas): give a chord's link/link_error options to its body only
body:
## Description

A chord given `link` or `link_error` as an *option* (rather than through `chord.link()`) raises `TypeError` instead of attaching the callback to its body.

```python
chord([add.s(1, 1), add.s(2, 2)], tsum.s()).apply_async(link=cb.s())
# TypeError: Cannot add link to group: use a chord

chord([add.s(1, 1), add.s(2, 2)], tsum.s()).apply_async(link_error=eb.s())
# TypeError: Cannot add link to group: do that on individual tasks
```

The same bug also breaks a chain whose last step is a chord, when the chain has a callback. That failure happens on the worker:

```python
chain(add.s(1, 1), chord([add.s(10), add.s(20)], tsum.s())).apply_async(link=cb.s())
```

`_chain.run()` stores the chain's callback in the chord's options, and the chord travels in the first message's `chain` field. After `add(1, 1)` succeeds, the worker applies the chord. That raises the `TypeError`, so `add` is stored as `FAILURE` even though it returned `2`. The chord header is never published, `.get()` raises the `TypeError`, and the callback never runs. `task_always_eager` takes a different path (`chord.apply()`), so eager test suites do not catch it.

### Cause

`_chord.run()` copies the merged options onto the body. That part is correct: the result of a chord is the result of its body, and `chord.link()` and `chord.link_error()` already link to the body. It then passes the same options to `header.apply_async()`. Before that call it removes only `chain`, `chord` and `task_id`, so `link` and `link_error` reach the header group, which always rejects them (`group.apply_async`).

### Fix

In `_chord.run()`, remove `link` and `link_error` from the options and add each callback to the body with `append_to_list_option()`, the helper `Signature.link()` uses. The header no longer receives them. Two properties follow:

- Callbacks already on the body are kept. For example, `chain(a, chord(h, body.link(x))).apply_async(link=y)` runs both `x` and `y` once. A plain `dict.update` would have dropped `x`.
- Callbacks are never duplicated. `chord.apply_async(link=cb)` also clones the body with `link=cb`, so the callback reaches `run()` twice, and the second append is skipped.

Errbacks attached through `chord.link_error()`, which is also how chains attach them (`prepare_steps`), are unchanged, including the `task_allow_error_cb_on_chord_header` behavior.

### Before / after (in-process worker, `memory://` broker, `cache+memory://` backend)

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `chord(...).apply_async(link=cb)` | `TypeError` on the client | result `6`, `cb` called once |
| `chord(...).apply_async(link_error=eb)` with a failing body | `TypeError` on the client | `eb` called once |
| `chain(add, chord(h, body)).apply_async(link=cb)` | `add` stored as `FAILURE`; chord never runs | result `34`, `cb` called once |
| same, with the body's own `.link(own)` | `TypeError` | `own` and `cb` each called once |
| `chain(add, chord(...)).on_error(eb)` | works | works (unchanged) |

### Tests

- `test_chord::test_link_option_goes_to_body_not_header[link|link_error]`: the option is on the body, and no header task gets it.
- `test_chord::test_chain_link_to_chord_step_keeps_body_callbacks`: a chain ending in a chord is JSON round-tripped and applied the way the worker continues a chain. The body keeps its own callback and gains the chain's, and the header gets no `link`.

All 3 new tests fail on `main` with the `TypeError` above and pass with this change. The full `t/unit` suite passes except for failures that also occur on unmodified `main` in my environment (root user, no broker). flake8, isort and codespell are clean on the changed files.

Added an entry under *Unreleased* in `Changelog.rst`.

title: docs: document PGMQ broker with SQLAlchemy results in PostgreSQL
body:
## Description

Add a guide for using PostgreSQL as both Celery's message broker and result store, with PGMQ handling task messages and SQLAlchemy with psycopg handling results.

The guide covers installation, database provisioning through PGMQ SDK 1.1.4's SQL installer or the PostgreSQL extension, connection settings, visibility timeouts, polling, notifications, and a runnable task example. Link it from the broker documentation index.

Closes #5149.

## Validation

- Tested the quickstart with Celery 5.6.3, Kombu 5.7.0a1, PGMQ SDK 1.1.4, SQLAlchemy 2.0.54, and PostgreSQL 18.6.
- Installed PGMQ SQL using a non-superuser database role, ran a prefork worker, and retrieved `5` from `add(2, 3)` through the SQLAlchemy backend. Confirmed the task's `SUCCESS` status in the result table.
- Confirmed SDK 1.1.2 can send, read, and delete messages against preinstalled PGMQ. This was a Python client compatibility check, not a Celery worker run with that SDK version.
- Passed a focused Sphinx build with warnings treated as errors and `git diff --check`.

The documented installation command targets the upcoming Kombu 5.7.0 release. The full Celery documentation build remains for CI.

title: Fix Beat scheduler connection cleanup on shutdown
body:
## Description

Fixes #10775

Stopping embedded Celery Beat leaves the scheduler’s cached publishing connection and channels open while stopped instances remain referenced. `Scheduler.close()` only synchronizes the schedule, and `PersistentScheduler.close()` additionally closes its shelf without releasing broker resources.

Release the existing cached connection during shutdown, including when synchronization fails, and clear the cached producer and connection without creating new resources. Have `PersistentScheduler.close()` delegate to the base cleanup and close its shelf in `finally`.

Add unit tests for cleanup and failure paths, plus a RabbitMQ smoke test that verifies connection, channel, and socket closure across three embedded Beat lifecycle cycles for each scheduler class. The smoke test lets Beat initialize its scheduler on its own thread, preserving compatibility with Python 3.13’s SQLite shelf backend.

title: Stop firstmethod() from swallowing AttributeError
body:
## Description

`AttributeError` is meant to detect whether a class has the requested method, but currently `firstmethod()` also catches it during method execution. This can incorrectly treat an existing method as missing when the error actually comes from the method itself.

title: fix(result): keep EagerResult.name when copied or pickled
body:
Fixes #10762.

#8486 added the `name` field to `EagerResult`, but `__reduce_args__()` still
returned only `(id, result, state, traceback)`. `copy.copy()` and pickling both
go through `__reduce__`, so the restored result had `name=None`:

    r = add.delay(2, 2)                  # task_always_eager
    r.name                               # '__main__.add'
    copy.copy(r).name                    # None
    pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(r)).name   # None

`__reduce_args__()` now includes the name, which `__init__` already accepts as
its fifth argument.

Added a test covering both `copy.copy()` and a pickle round-trip.

title: fix(result): raise TaskRevokedError from EagerResult.get() after revoke()
body:
Fixes #10761.

`EagerResult.revoke()` only set the state to `REVOKED` and left the task's
return value as the result. Since `REVOKED` is a propagating state, `get()`
then raised the return value wrapped in a bare `Exception`:

    r = add.delay(2, 2)   # task_always_eager
    r.revoke()
    r.get()               # Exception(4)

`revoke()` now also stores `TaskRevokedError('revoked')` as the result and
clears the traceback, which is what `Backend.mark_as_revoked()` stores for a
task revoked on a worker. `get()` raises `TaskRevokedError`, and
`get(propagate=False)` / `.result` return it, matching `AsyncResult`.

Added tests for revoking both a successful and a failed eager result.

title: fix(utils): keep the closing bracket when saferepr truncates the last element
body:
Fixes #10760.

When `saferepr()` ran out of `maxlen` on the last element of a container, the
container's closing bracket was dropped:

    saferepr(['v' * 100], 30)         # "['vvv...', ..."
    saferepr({'a': ['v' * 100]}, 30)  # "{'a': ['vvv...', ...}"

`_saferepr()` pulls the next token before checking `maxlen`, and when the
truncated element is the last one, that token is the closing bracket itself.
It was discarded, so the dangling-parens pass never saw it.

This shows up in task `argsrepr`/`kwargsrepr` headers and in the logged result
repr whenever the final argument is longer than the limit (1024 by default).

A closing bracket is now emitted even when `maxlen` is spent, the same way the
dangling-parens pass already emits them. Since nothing was left out in that
case, `', ...'` is not added:

    saferepr(['v' * 100], 30)         # "['vvv...']"
    saferepr(('v' * 100,), 30)        # "('vvv...',)"
    saferepr({'a': ['v' * 100]}, 30)  # "{'a': ['vvv...']}"
    saferepr(['v' * 100, 1, 2], 30)   # "['vvv...', ...]"  (unchanged)

Note this differs slightly from the expected output in the issue, which kept
`', ...'` before the bracket: that would claim more elements follow when none
do, and would render a 1-tuple as `('vvv...', ...,)`.

Added regression tests for list, tuple, set, dict and nested containers.

title: docs: remote control commands get a state object, not ControlDispatch
body:
## Description

The "Writing your own remote control commands" section in the workers guide says handlers take a single argument, a `ControlDispatch` instance. That class has been gone since 2010 (remote control moved over to kombu's pidbox back then). These days handlers get the worker `state` first and then whatever arguments come with the command, and the example right under that sentence already takes `n`.

So I just reworded that one sentence to match. Haven't built the docs locally.

Found this with Striff, a tool I'm working on that checks docs against the code ([celery's report](https://striff.io/celery/celery?utm_source=github&utm_medium=pull_request&utm_campaign=doc-fix&utm_content=celery-celery) if you're curious).

title: Fix countdown, expiration, and Beat intervals across DST transitions
body:
## Description

This fixes relative ETA and expiration calculations across DST transitions in task protocols 1 and 2. In `America/New_York`, adding 90 minutes to `01:30 -05:00` during spring-forward previously produced `03:00 -04:00` (equivalent to `02:00 -05:00`), only 30 elapsed minutes later. It now correctly produces `04:00 -04:00`.

It also fixes Beat interval calculations during fall-back. In `Europe/Paris`, going from `02:59:55 +02:00 to 02:00:05 +01:00` takes 10 elapsed seconds, but Beat previously calculated another hour remaining for a 10-second interval. It now correctly marks the task as due.

Fixes #6438.

title: Finish a half-read child result on prefork shutdown and ack during the join
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes the warm-shutdown case of #3802 (acks of tasks that finish while the pool is being joined). The hang on a half-read result has no issue of its own; the symptoms are the ones #9505 reported for cold shutdown, which #9678 fixed in 5.6.0rc1, but this is a different path. Verified against RabbitMQ only; the ack path is transport-independent but Redis and SQS have not been run.

### Symptom

A prefork worker (5.6.3, `task_acks_late=True`, prefetch 1, AMQP broker) that receives SIGTERM sometimes never finishes its warm shutdown. It sits until it is SIGKILLed by the supervisor (for us, Kubernetes after `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). While it sits:

1. No child result is read any more, so tasks that **finished** seconds after SIGTERM hit their soft and hard time limits on the shutdown timer thread added in 5.6.1 (#9986). `Request.on_timeout` then marks an already-succeeded task as failed and fires its errbacks.
2. Every ack issued during the drain is a `promise(call_soon, message.ack_log_error)` parked on the hub, and nothing runs it. When the process is killed the broker redelivers every unacked message, including the tasks that had finished, so they run twice.

Stack of a wedged production worker (SIGUSR1 "cry" dump, main thread, 186 s after `Warm shutdown`):

```
worker.py:266 _shutdown → bootsteps.stop → prefork.py:176 on_stop → billiard/pool.py:1620 join
→ asynpool.py:369 on_stop_not_started → asynpool.py:397 _flush_outqueue   task = reader.recv()
→ billiard/connection.py:275 recv → :463 _recv_bytes → :425 _recv   chunk = read(handle, remaining)
```

### Root cause

The event loop reads child results through a resumable generator (`ResultHandler._recv_message`, registered on the kombu hub per pipe fd). If the worker starts shutting down while a result message is only partly read, the loop exits with that generator still holding the first half of the message. `Pool.join()` → `ResultHandler.on_stop_not_started()` → `_flush_outqueue()` then does a blocking `reader.recv()` on the same pipe, interprets the remaining body bytes as a 4-byte length header, and blocks forever. The parent holds the pipe's write end, so the child exiting never produces EOF.

The window is one event-loop iteration per result message larger than the pipe buffer. For us that is every `Task.replace()` result: billiard pickles the traceback of the `Ignore` exception including `co_positions` of each frame, which is ~77 KB in production against a 64 KiB pipe, so every such result is written in two fills and is half-read for one loop iteration.

### Changes

**`celery/concurrency/asynpool.py`**: `ResultHandler` keeps the hub it was registered with. `_flush_outqueue` first calls a new `_finish_partial_read(fd, proc)`: if the hub still holds a generator reader for that fd, resume it until the message completes, polling the pipe for `partial_read_timeout` (1 s) between resumes, and give up and drop the fd if nothing arrives and the child is dead, or after `partial_read_deadline` (10 s) in total. When no partial read is in flight (`hub.readers` has no entry for the fd, or the entry is the plain `handle_event` callback) the stock path runs unchanged.

**`celery/concurrency/prefork.py`**: `_run_ready_callbacks(hub)` runs on every tick of the existing shutdown timer thread and once more on the main thread after the thread is joined (for the acks queued by the last results the join itself waited for). It pops `hub._pop_ready()` one entry at a time and runs only the promises wrapping a bound `Message.ack_log_error` / `reject_log_error`, which is what the consumer queues when a request acks. Anything else is put back with `hub.call_soon` for `Hub.close()`: the set can also hold the transport's socket reader, which re-queues itself after every read and would hand new deliveries to the closed pool. Popping one at a time matters because `Consumer.on_send_event_buffered` adds to `hub._ready` without the lock from the main thread, so iterating the drained set from the timer thread could raise `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration` and lose the rest of the batch.

`hub._pop_ready()` is a private kombu API, but `celery/worker/consumer/consumer.py` already reaches into `hub._ready` directly and `_pop_ready` has been stable since kombu 4. Happy to move this behind a public kombu method if you would prefer.

### Reproduction

Linux container (`python:3.13-slim`, celery 5.6.3, billiard 4.2.4, kombu 5.6.2, RabbitMQ 3.13), worker as PID 1, `task_acks_late=True`, prefetch 1, time limits 30/45 s, SIGTERM via `docker kill -s TERM`.

| Scenario | 5.6.3 | with this patch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Child splits one 70 KB result write with a 4 s gap, SIGTERM inside the gap | wedged every time, same stack as above; soft and hard limits fire for the finished tasks; acks never written; everything redelivered at SIGKILL | half-read message completed, both tasks acked (the one finishing during the drain within 1 s), clean exit |
| 2000 real `replace()` tasks, SIGTERM mid-storm, pipes forced to 4 KiB to widen the window | wedged 2 of 3 runs | 3 of 3 clean exits |
| A 600 s task outlives the grace period | every task finished during the drain is redelivered at SIGKILL (acks only flush at `Hub.close()`) | the task finished at +10 s is acked 1 s later; only the still-running task is redelivered |
| Clean drain inside the grace period | all acks written at exit | unchanged |

`-O fair` has no effect. Soft shutdown (`REMAP_SIGTERM=SIGQUIT` + `worker_soft_shutdown_timeout`) still enters the same flush loop and blocks, and killing the mid-write child makes the partial message permanent.

### Tests

Six new tests in `t/unit/concurrency/test_prefork.py`, all failing on the unpatched tree and passing with the patch:

- `test_flush_outqueue_completes_partial_message_instead_of_recv`: a real `os.pipe()`, a real kombu `Hub` holding the `_recv_message` generator mid-body, and a reader whose `recv()` raises instead of blocking. Unpatched this fails with `recv() on a pipe holding the tail of a partly read message would block forever`.
- `test_flush_outqueue_waits_for_a_live_child_still_writing`: the tail lands 50 ms after the first resume, so a resume loop that never re-polls is caught.
- `test_flush_outqueue_drops_fd_when_process_dies_mid_message`
- `test_finish_partial_read_no_generator_registered` / `test_finish_partial_read_not_registered_with_event_loop`: the guard paths are no-ops.

title: Fail the chords after a chord whose header failed
body:
While working on #10743 I found a regression from my earlier #10171: in a flat chain of chords, a header failure leaves the chords after it pending.

Since 5.6.3 a chain of chords is kept flat (#10171). When a header task in one of those chords fails, `chord_error_from_stack` marks only that chord's body as failed. The chords after it sit in the body's `chain` option, and nothing propagated the failure to them, so their results stayed `PENDING`:

```python
group(chain(chord([add, fail], tsum), chord([add, add], tsum)), add)()
res.get()   # main: hangs until timeout, member state PENDING
```

`AsyncResult.get()` on the chain itself re-raises a parent's failure, which is why this went unnoticed; anything that waits on the chain's result id — a group joining it as a member — hangs.

The chain walk that `mark_as_failure` already runs for a task failing in the middle of a chain is moved into `_fail_chain`, and `chord_error_from_stack` runs it after failing the body, for task and group bodies.

Tests: `test_chord_header_failure_fails_the_chain_of_chords` (unit, task and group body), `test_chord_error_from_stack_fails_the_chain_after_the_body` and `..._after_a_group_body` (backend-level), and two integration tests with the chain as a group member. All fail on `main` and pass with the change.

Still pending after a header failure, as on `main`: a chord nested in an enclosing chord's header whose own header fails (the enclosing chord's part is never returned), a chain of chords whose last body is a chain or a group, and a chord whose body is itself a chord. Those need the failure walk to descend into chain and group bodies rather than another branch here. Chained steps are stored without a traceback.

title: Fix invalid Bandit baseline JSON and validate it before commit

title: Don't record FAILURE when on_success raises after SUCCESS was stored
body:
## Description

Refs #10724 (the `on_success` path). #10752 covers the other path in that issue, a pool child lost after the store.

`Task.on_success` and `Task.after_return` run after the task's outcome is recorded. If either hook raised in a worker, the exception reached the tracer's outer `except Exception`, which calls `on_error` again. For a task that succeeded, that meant:

- the errbacks fired, so the app hears both "succeeded" and "failed" for one run
- a chord header was reported as a failure
- `task_failure` and `task_internal_error` were sent, and `task_success` and `after_return` were skipped (for an `on_success` raise)
- on backends without a guard, such as the database backend, the stored SUCCESS was overwritten with FAILURE. Key-value backends keep it, because `KeyValueStoreBackend._store_result` returns early when the stored status is SUCCESS.

For a task that failed, a raising `after_return` recorded the failure a second time.

With this change, a worker logs an exception from either hook at `ERROR` level, with the task name and id, and the recorded outcome stands. That matches how exceptions from signal receivers are already handled. Specifically:

- In eager mode (`apply()`, `task_always_eager`) the exception still propagates to the caller, as on `main`, so test suites keep seeing broken hooks.
- `Reject` raised from a hook still reaches the outer `except Reject: raise`, as on `main`.
- Exceptions from the task body and from storing the result go through the failure path unchanged.

Because broken hooks no longer send `task_failure` or `task_internal_error` in a worker, I added a changelog entry and a sentence to the `on_success` and `after_return` sections of `docs/userguide/tasks.rst`.

## Tests

In `t/unit/tasks/test_trace.py`:

- `test_trace_on_success_raises_after_success_was_stored`: non-eager trace with a raising `on_success`. `handle_failure` isn't called, `task_success` and `after_return` run, and the error is logged. A comment notes that the state check alone also passes on `main` with the cache backend.
- `test_trace_on_success_raises_eager_propagates` and `test_trace_after_return_raises_eager_propagates`: eager mode still raises.
- `test_trace_on_success_raises_reject_is_not_swallowed`: `Reject` still propagates.
- `test_trace_after_return_raises[False/True]`: a raising `after_return` records no failure for a successful task, and exactly one for a failed task.

`t/unit/tasks` and `t/unit/worker` pass locally on the branch after the merge from `main` (1806 passed). flake8 and isort are clean.

title: fix(utils): don't expire or evict re-added LimitedSet items using their old timestamp
body:
Fixes #10757

`LimitedSet.discard()` leaves the item's heap entry behind, so after an item
is re-added the heap still holds its old `(inserted, seq, item)` entry. `purge()`
used that old timestamp to decide expiry, and `pop()` removed the item when it
hit the old entry, so a re-added item was expired early, evicted first at
`maxlen`, and returned first by `pop()`.

This affects the worker's revoked set, where ids are re-added by repeated
revokes and by mingle syncing revoked ids from other workers.

A heap entry is now only acted on if it is still the item's current entry in
`_data`; outdated entries are skipped by `pop()` and discarded by `purge()`.

Added regression tests for expiry, maxlen eviction and pop() after re-adding.

title: Fix(utils): don't cut regen iteration short when consumed elsewhere mid-loop
body:
Fixes #10755

`_regen.__iter__` delegated to a shared look-ahead generator that stops as soon
as the regen's `__done` flag is set. If anything else exhausts the underlying
iterator during an in-progress loop — `len()`, negative indexing, or a nested
loop over the same regen — the outer loop ends early, silently dropping items.
This affects e.g. iterating `group.tasks` while calling `len(group.tasks)`.

`__iter__` now tracks its own index into the concretised items and only pulls
from the underlying iterator when it has caught up, keeping the existing
single-item look-ahead and deferred-exception behaviour.

Added regression tests for len(), getitem and nested iteration during a loop.

`__iter__` only looks ahead once it pulls from the underlying iterator itself;
already-concretised items are yielded without looking ahead, as before. This
keeps generator chord headers lazy (#3021, `test_chord::test_generator`).
Added a unit test for that.

title: Don't fail a task whose SUCCESS was stored before the worker was lost
body:
## Description

Refs #10724 (the lost pool child path).

When a prefork child stores SUCCESS and then dies before handing the result back (OOM kill, SIGKILL, or a crash in `on_success`, a `task_postrun` receiver or `process_cleanup`), the parent gets `WorkerLostError`. `Request.on_failure` then calls `mark_as_failure` unconditionally. That has three effects on a task that already succeeded:

- the errbacks fire, so the app hears both "succeeded" and "failed" for one execution
- `on_chord_part_return` runs a second time, so a chord header is counted twice and the chord can fail on a header recorded as SUCCESS
- with `acks_late` and `reject_on_worker_lost`, the message is requeued and the task runs again

This change reads the stored state before the worker-lost handling. If it's SUCCESS, the request is acknowledged (when `acks_late`) and nothing is recorded as a failure. If the backend is disabled or can't be reached, the existing failure handling runs as before. The lookup only happens on `WorkerLostError`, so the normal path doesn't pay for it.

The other path in #10724, a raising `on_success` hook inside the tracer, lives in `celery/app/trace.py` and isn't covered here. I kept it out to keep this change small.

## Tests

In `t/unit/worker/test_request.py`:

- `test_on_failure_WorkerLostError_after_success_was_stored`: the reproduction from the issue. No errback runs and the state stays SUCCESS.
- `test_on_failure_WorkerLostError_after_success_was_stored_acks_late`: with `reject_on_worker_lost`, the message is acked, not requeued, and `mark_as_failure` isn't called.
- `test_on_failure_WorkerLostError_backend_unavailable`: if reading the state raises, the failure is still recorded.

The first two fail on `main` and pass with the fix. `t/unit/worker` and `t/unit/tasks` pass locally (1803 passed). #10726 adds the first test as a strict xfail, so whichever lands second will need to drop the duplicate.

title: fix(canvas): keep eager group apply off the result backend
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Fixes #4405.

With `task_always_eager` on, `group(a.si(), chain(b.si(), group(c.si(), d.si()))).delay()` connects to the result backend. With Redis down it fails with `Retry limit exceeded while trying to reconnect to the Celery result store backend`. The same canvas without the inner group runs fine.

`group.apply()` gets its members from `_prepared()`, which freezes each one, and then drops the frozen results. Eager execution only needs the unrolled signatures. Freezing a chain that ends in a group runs `prepare_steps`, which builds a `GroupResult` for the inner group. Its `ResultSet` barrier calls `AsyncResult.then()` on each member, and `then()` calls `backend.add_pending_result()`, which subscribes to the Redis result consumer.

`_prepared()` now takes `freeze=True`, and `group.apply()` passes `freeze=False`. Nested groups still flatten, partial args still prepend, and empty chains are still skipped, because that logic is unchanged. `apply_async()` still freezes as before. The eager request does not carry `group_id` or `group_index` (`Task.apply` builds it without them), so skipping the freeze changes no eager result. Each eager member now gets a fresh task id from `Task.apply` instead of the frozen one. Nothing could read the frozen id, because `apply()` discarded the frozen result.

Commits:

- [AI] test(canvas): eager group with a chain ending in a group must not touch the result backend
- [AI] fix(canvas): keep eager group apply off the result backend

## Verification

- `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py::test_group::test_apply_chain_ending_in_group_skips_result_backend` fails on the test commit (`add_pending_result` called 2 times) and passes with the fix. The returned value `[2, [6, 8]]` is the same before and after.
- Script from the issue against an app with `backend='redis://localhost:6399/0'` (nothing listening), eager on: on `main` it raises `RuntimeError: Retry limit exceeded ...`. With the fix it prints `[1, [1, 1]]`.
- `pytest t/unit/tasks t/unit/backends/test_base.py t/unit/backends/test_redis.py t/unit/app/test_app.py`: 1574 passed with the fix. On `main` plus the new test, the new test is the only failure.

title: fix(canvas): resolve the app of a chain or chord through its tasks
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

A chain whose first task is a chord can resolve the wrong app. Built in a thread
other than the one that created the app, `chain(chord(...), task).apply_async()`
raises `NotImplementedError: Starting chords requires a result backend to be
configured.` although the app has one. This is #6197, still reproducible on main.

`_chain.app` reads `self.tasks[0]._app`. A chord built from task signatures has
no `_app` of its own (`chord.app` resolves one through its header and body), so
the chain falls back to `current_app`. That is thread-local: in the thread that
created the app it is the right one, in any other thread (a threaded gunicorn or
uWSGI worker, a `ThreadPoolExecutor`) it is the fallback app with no result
backend, unless the app was made the default with `set_default()`.

`group.app` already reads `self.tasks[0].app`. This makes `_chain.app` do the
same, so the chain resolves its app through the chord's own tasks.

`chord._get_app` read `tasks[0]._app` and `body._app` the same way, so a chord
whose header starts with a chain, group or chord and whose body is one fell back
to `current_app` too. It now resolves both through their own tasks, in the same
order as before: the chord's own app, the header's first task, the body,
`current_app`. This goes through a small `_app_of` helper rather than reading
`.app` directly, because `Signature.app` never returns `None`: for a header task
without an app it returns `current_app`, and the body would never be tried.
`_app_of` treats that fallback as no app. It also treats the `AttributeError`
raised by a nested chain or group whose first task is still a dict (converted
when the canvas is frozen) as no app, so such a header still falls back to the
body instead of raising.

Fixes #6197

Verification (Python 3.14.5, macOS):

- `test_apply_async_in_another_thread_when_first_task_is_chord` builds and
  applies the chain in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` worker, with the test app current
  only in the test's own thread and an app with `backend='disabled'` as the
  default app. The unit suite's `Trap` for `current_app` is one object shared by
  every thread, so the test installs a real thread-local while it runs. With
  `tasks[0]._app` it fails with the `NotImplementedError` above; with the change
  it passes.
- `test_apply_async_in_another_thread_when_header_and_body_are_chains` does the
  same for a chord whose header starts with a chain and whose body is a chain.
  With the old `_get_app`, it fails, and so do
  `test_app_when_header_and_body_are_canvases` (every chain, group and chord
  header and body pair) and `test_app_when_header_has_no_app_and_body_is_canvas`.
  `test_app_when_header_has_no_app` and `test_app_when_header_canvas_has_dict`
  cover the two cases `_app_of` treats as no app; each fails without its branch.
- `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`: 291 passed, 1 xfailed. `t/unit/tasks` also
  passes on Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.15.0b1 and PyPy 3.11.
- A script with an app using the `cache+memory://` backend, building and
  applying canvases in a second thread:

  ```
  main:    chain(chord, task)     app='default'     NotImplementedError: Starting chords requires a result backend to be configured.
  main:    chain(chord, chord)    app='default'     NotImplementedError: Starting chords requires a result backend to be configured.
  main:    chord([chain], chain)  app='default'     NotImplementedError: Starting chords requires a result backend to be configured.
  branch:  chain(chord, task)     app='configured'  apply_async OK
  branch:  chain(chord, chord)    app='configured'  apply_async OK
  ```

title: fix(backends): upsert CosmosDB results so later states are stored
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`CosmosDBSQLBackend.set()` stores results with `CreateDocument`. CosmosDB rejects that with `409 Conflict` when a document with the same id already exists. The key/value backend writes the task's key once for every state it stores, so the second write for a task fails. This happens when a task stores STARTED (with `task_track_started`), RETRY, or a custom state through `update_state()` before it finishes. Storing the final SUCCESS or FAILURE then raises `HTTPFailure: Status code: 409`, and the stored result stays in the earlier state.

This switches `set()` to `UpsertDocument`. In pydocumentdb 2.3.5 (the version pinned in `requirements/extras/cosmosdbsql.txt`, and the last release) it takes the same arguments (collection link, document, options), resolves the partition key the same way, and sends the request with `x-ms-documentdb-is-upsert: true`, so an existing document is replaced. The other key/value backends already overwrite on `set()`: redis SET, Azure Block Blob with `overwrite=True`, the couchbase upsert, the ArangoDB UPSERT, and couchdb catching the conflict and updating.

`_store_result()` still skips the write once SUCCESS is stored. That check is a read followed by a write, so, as on redis and the other key/value backends apart from Elasticsearch, a late state that races the SUCCESS write can still replace it. Before this change the 409 rejected every write after the first one, which is what dropped the final state. A comment in `set()` notes that the guard is not atomic.

Tests: `test_store_result_overwrites_earlier_state` uses a fake client that, like CosmosDB, refuses to create a document whose id already exists. It stores STARTED and then SUCCESS for the same task and reads the result back. On main it fails with `HTTPFailure: Status code: 409`, and with this change it passes. `test_store_result_keeps_success` stores SUCCESS and then STARTED and checks that the result stays SUCCESS without a second write. `test_set` now expects `UpsertDocument`. The same sequences were also run against the Cosmos DB Linux emulator with pydocumentdb 2.3.5. flake8, isort and codespell are clean on the changed files.

title: fix(events): synchronize EventDispatcher shutdown with publishing
body:
## Description
Fixes #10744 

`EventDispatcher.close()` currently releases its mutex whenever it is locked, even if another thread holds it during `publish()` or `flush()`. If close overlaps a publish, the publishing thread can then raise `RuntimeError: release unlocked lock` when it exits its lock context.

This change makes `close()` acquire the mutex normally, so shutdown waits for an in-flight publication before clearing the producer. A closed-state check prevents a previously prepared publish or flush from using the producer after shutdown; `enable()` resets that state when reopening the dispatcher.

The PR adds unit coverage for those interleavings and a broker-backed smoke test that pauses a publish while another thread calls `close()`.

title: Fix geometric message bloat in a chain of implicit chords
body:
This PR fixes geometric message bloat in a chain where groups are followed by tasks, `chain(task, group, task, group, task, ...)`.

Depends on #10767: with the body split, a header failure must propagate down the chain to the steps after the body, which that PR fixes for every flat chain of chords.

Each group followed by a task is upgraded to a chord, but `_chain.__or__` attaches every further step to the trailing chord's body, so `chain(a, group(b, c), d, group(e, f), g)` becomes `chain(a, chord([b, c], chain(d, chord([e, f], g))))`. Every header task carries a copy of the body, and the body carries the rest of the chain, so the first message grows by (header size + 2) per group: ×5 with 3 tasks per group, reaching 9 MB at 6 groups; ×12 with 10 tasks per group, 10 MB at 4 groups. A chain of 10 groups of 2 tasks produced a 2 GB message that failed to publish. The explicit form `chain(a, chord([b, c], d), chord([e, f], g))` has been flat since #10171. This is the inflation the serializer warning in the canvas user guide describes: the body is one shared object, which pickle writes once and JSON writes per reference.

With this update `prepare_steps` splits a chord whose body is a chain, `chord(header, chain(a, b, c))` → `chord(header, a), b, c`, so the chain is unpacked into the same flat chain of chords as the explicit form. The first message now grows by about 2 KB per group: 13 KB for 6 groups of 3 tasks, 21 KB for 4 groups of 10.

A chord body's `parent_id` is now the header task that fires it for every body shape. A single-task body previously reported the task before the chord, a chain body the header task.

Not covered: a chain of implicit chords used as a chord *body* is frozen as written and serialised into every header task, so that message is still nested (678 KB at 5 two-task groups, as on main). Chains run on their own, or as members of a group or chord header, are flat. The construction-time shape is a separate change.

Script to reproduce:
```python
import json

from celery import Celery, chain, group

app = Celery("repro", backend="cache+memory://")


@app.task
def noop(x=None):
    return None


def first_message_size(num_groups, tasks_per_group):
    steps = [noop.si()]
    for _ in range(num_groups):
        steps.append(group(noop.si() for _ in range(tasks_per_group)))
        steps.append(noop.si())
    canvas = chain(*steps)
    tasks, _ = canvas.prepare_steps((), {}, canvas.tasks, app=app)
    return len(json.dumps([task.__json__() for task in tasks]))


for n in range(1, 7):
    print(n, first_message_size(n, 3))
```

title: Ensure worker shutdown state is set even if the shutdown handler's logging/signal dispatch raises
body:
## Description

`_shutdown_handler`'s signal handler (`_handle_request`) currently runs the `callback`, `safe_say`, and `signals.worker_shutting_down.send()` calls *before* setting `state.should_stop` / `state.should_terminate`:

```python
def _handle_request(*args):
    with in_sighandler():
        from celery.worker import state
        if current_process()._name == 'MainProcess':
            if callback:
                callback(worker)
            if verbose:
                safe_say(f'worker: {how} shutdown (MainProcess)', sys.__stdout__)
            signals.worker_shutting_down.send(
                sender=worker.hostname, sig=sig, how=how, exitcode=exitcode,
            )
        setattr(state, {'Warm': 'should_stop', 'Cold': 'should_terminate'}[how], exitcode)
```

`in_sighandler()` (`celery/utils/log.py`) is a bare `try/finally` — it does not suppress exceptions raised inside the `with` block. So if anything in the callback/say/signal-dispatch block raises, the exception propagates out of the signal handler and **the state flag is never set** — the worker receives the signal but never actually stops accepting new work.

We hit this in production: `safe_say()` writes to a raw fd via `_original_os_write()`, which can still raise `OSError` under some conditions (closed/invalid fd, `EPIPE`, etc.), and on the code as it stands today that silently prevents shutdown from ever taking effect. This is a narrower version of the same class of problem that motivated switching `safe_say` to `_original_os_write` in the first place (avoiding the eventlet/gevent `RuntimeError` case) — same function, an adjacent failure mode that fix didn't fully close.

## Fix

- Move `setattr(state, ...)` to the top of `_handle_request`, before the callback/say/signal-dispatch block, so the shutdown flag is set unconditionally and can't be skipped by anything that runs after it.
- Wrap `safe_say`'s `_original_os_write()` call in `try/except OSError` — it's a best-effort human-readable banner and must never be able to abort a caller's control flow.

## Testing

Added to `t/unit/apps/test_worker.py`:
- `should_stop`/`should_terminate` still gets set when `safe_say` raises.
- `should_stop`/`should_terminate` still gets set when the shutdown `callback` raises.
- Existing behavior unchanged (normal say/signal dispatch, Cold vs. Warm, non-MainProcess still sets state but skips say/callback).

Confirmed these are real regression tests, not tautologies, by reverting only the `celery/apps/worker.py` change and checking the new tests fail against unpatched `main`.

title: fix(canvas): apply countdown and eta to the chord header
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`group | task` is a chord. `apply_async(countdown=…)` / `eta=` was bound to `chord.run(countdown=)`, which is the **chord.unlock retry interval** (default `1`). The header therefore ran immediately and only the callback was delayed.

That matches #7851: a canvas that starts with a `group` and is chained further executes the group right away; the countdown applies only afterwards.

This change:

- strips `countdown` / `eta` off the body clone and off `chord.run`'s kwargs so they do not collide with the unlock retry
- applies those delay options to the header via `header.apply_async`
- leaves `apply_chord(..., countdown=1)` as the unlock retry default

Fixes #7851

## Tests

`t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`: header tasks receive the user delay; `apply_chord` keeps countdown `1`.

```
pytest t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py::test_chord t/unit/tasks/test_chord.py t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py::test_chain t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py::test_group
```

title: fix(consumer): preserve pending operation order
body:
## Description

Deferred consumer operations currently execute in reverse order in hub-less workers.

`Consumer.call_soon()` appends callbacks to `_pending_operations`, while `perform_pending_operations()` removes them with `pop()`. This creates LIFO behavior. For example, an `add_consumer` followed by `cancel_consumer` before the next synchronous-loop cycle executes as cancel-then-add, leaving the queue enabled.

This PR:

- Replaces the pending-operation list with a `deque`.
- Drains operations with `popleft()` to preserve FIFO scheduling order.
- Adds a regression test covering callback execution order.
- Preserves the existing deferred-execution and exception-handling behavior.

Fixes #10733

title: Pin cassandra-driver version specification
Limit the Django fixup's signal handlers to its own app
body:
## Description

Alternative to #10722 that works on `main` without depending on #10699.

`DjangoFixup` connects `on_import_modules` and `on_worker_init` without a sender. With several Django-enabled apps in one process:

- every fixup's `on_import_modules` runs for every app's `import_modules` signal
- `worker_init` has a worse problem: all fixups' `on_worker_init` bound methods get the same receiver key, so only the **first** fixup's receiver is registered. It then installs its `DjangoWorkerFixup` for every app's worker, and the other apps' fixups never see their own worker.

### Changes

- `import_modules` is sent with `sender=app`, so it is now connected with `sender=self.app`. The lookup key includes the sender, so each app's fixup gets its own receiver.
- `worker_init` is sent with the worker as sender, so it can't be filtered by app. Each fixup now connects it with its own `dispatch_uid`, and `on_worker_init` returns early when `worker.app is not self.app`.

Because of the per-fixup `dispatch_uid`, this doesn't rely on #10699's change to `_make_id()`, and it keeps working if #10699 is merged.

| Two apps with the fixup, signals sent for app2 | app1 fixup | app2 fixup |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | runs | not called |
| this PR | not called | runs |

### Tests

- `test_install` now checks the `sender=` and `dispatch_uid=` arguments.

title: Limit the Django fixup's signal handlers to its own app
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Follow-up to #10699, opened as a draft as requested there. It is stacked on that branch, so only the last commit (`3f61343`) is new here.

`DjangoFixup` connects `on_import_modules` and `on_worker_init` without a sender. Once #10699 lets each fixup instance register its own receiver, a process with several Django-enabled apps runs both handlers once per app, and every app's fixup reacts to every worker's `worker_init`.

This change limits each fixup to its own app:

- `import_modules` is sent with `sender=app`, so it is connected with `sender=self.app`.
- `worker_init` is sent with the worker as sender, so `on_worker_init` returns early when `worker.app is not self.app`.

Two apps with the fixup installed, sending `import_modules` and `worker_init` for the second app only:

| | app1 fixup | app2 fixup |
|---|---|---|
| main | runs (for app2's signals) | nothing |
| #10699 | runs | runs |
| #10699 + this | nothing | runs |

This depends on #10699. On main alone, `worker_init` would reach only the first fixup's receiver, which now ignores other apps' workers, so app2's worker fixup would never be installed.

Tests: the `install()` test now checks the `sender=` argument, and two new tests cover a worker and an `import_modules` signal from another app. Without the fixup change, three tests fail. With it, all 37 in `t/unit/fixups/test_django.py` pass.

title: ci: stop installing sphinx-autobuild in test envs and harden pip against index timeouts
body:
## Summary

The latest `main` CI run (#36402288507, commit for #10716) failed 125 of 300 jobs — nearly every integration and smoke test matrix entry. No test actually ran: dependency installation aborted in the tox setup step.

### Root cause

On the Blacksmith runners, pip timed out five times in a row (15s default read timeout) fetching `https://pypi.org/simple/watchfiles/`. pip then treated `watchfiles` as having no distributions and failed with:

    sphinx-autobuild 2025.8.25 depends on watchfiles>=0.20
    ...
    ERROR: ResolutionImpossible

The job's retry action hit the same timeout on all three attempts.

`watchfiles` only reaches the test environments because `requirements/docs.txt` includes `extras/sphinxautobuild.txt`, and tox installs `docs.txt` for every `3.11`–`3.15` env, including integration and smoke. `sphinx-autobuild` is only used by `make livehtml` (the docs Docker image); no test needs it.

### Changes

- `requirements/docs.txt`: drop `-r extras/sphinxautobuild.txt`, so test envs no longer pull `sphinx-autobuild` / `watchfiles`.
- `docker/docs/Dockerfile`: install `requirements/extras/sphinxautobuild.txt` explicitly, so `make livehtml` / `docker compose up docs` keeps working.
- `tox.ini`: set `PIP_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=60` and `PIP_RETRIES=10`, so a slow package index degrades into a slower install instead of a failed job.

### Verification

- `pip install --dry-run` of the exact tox integration install set (`test.txt`, `pkgutils.txt`, `test-ci-default.txt`, `docs.txt`, `test-integration.txt`) on Python 3.12 resolves 164 packages; `watchfiles` and `sphinx-autobuild` are no longer among them.
- The docs image install set (`docs.txt` + `extras/sphinxautobuild.txt` + `default.txt`) still resolves `sphinx-autobuild`.
- `tox config -e 3.12-integration-redis -k setenv` shows the new `PIP_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` / `PIP_RETRIES` values.

title: Avoid calling isoformat() on protocol v1 ETA and expiration strings
body:
## Description

Protocol v1 calls `isoformat()` on `eta` and `expires` unconditionally. When a task with an expiration is retried, the expiration is already an ISO8601 string, so building the retry message fails.

This follows the approach in #4565.

title: Make ArangoDbBackend.delete() a no-op for a missing key
body:
Closes #10700.

`ArangoDbBackend.delete()` runs a bare `REMOVE`, so deleting a result that is not in the collection makes ArangoDB raise `ERROR_ARANGO_DOCUMENT_NOT_FOUND` (1202), surfaced by pyArango as `AQLQueryError`. `AsyncResult(task_id).forget()` therefore raises whenever the result has already expired or been forgotten, where every other backend treats it as a no-op.

The query now carries `OPTIONS {ignoreErrors: true}`, which is ArangoDB's own way to say a `REMOVE` may find nothing. That keeps it one round trip and leaves the "document exists" case identical, rather than catching `AQLQueryError` here and having to tell 1202 apart from a real failure such as a missing collection or a bad bind parameter.

## Tests

`test_delete_missing_key_is_a_no_op` drives `delete()` with an `AQLQuery` stub that raises 1202 unless the query opts out of errors, which is what the server does. It fails on `main` and passes with the change, as does the updated `test_delete`. `t/unit/backends/test_arangodb.py`: 14 passed.

I have no ArangoDB instance to hand, so the server behaviour is from the AQL documentation for `ignoreErrors`, not from a live run.

`docs/userguide/calling.rst` gives `interval_max` a default of 0.2, in the field description and in the "the default policy correlates to" example. The shipped default is 1:

```python
>>> Celery("x").conf.task_publish_retry_policy
{'max_retries': 3, 'interval_start': 0, 'interval_max': 1, 'interval_step': 0.2}
```

title: fix(redis): defer re-entrant cancel_for to avoid GC-driven pub/sub deadlock
body:
Supersedes / builds on #10326 (credit to @wckao for the diagnosis and reproducer).

## Problem

`ResultConsumer` shares one redis-py `PubSub` connection. CPython's cyclic GC can run `AsyncResult.__del__` → `remove_pending_result` → `cancel_for` while the **same thread** is still inside a SUBSCRIBE (e.g. `chain.apply_async()` → `freeze()` → `add_pending_result`) or an UNSUBSCRIBE (another `__del__`). The existing `_pubsub_lock` is an `RLock`, so it lets that thread straight back in; the nested command wedges the connection and the caller hangs forever. See #10326 for the production py-spy stacks and a standalone reproducer.

## Fix

- `ResultConsumer` tracks pub/sub nesting per thread (`_PubSubReentryState`, a `threading.local`).
- `_consume_from` and `cancel_for` run inside `_reentry_guard()`. A `cancel_for` that arrives while this thread is already mid-operation is queued, and the queue is drained once the outermost operation returns. Cancels triggered during the drain are queued behind it too.
- Failure policy while draining:
  - an ordinary exception for one cancel is logged and the drain continues;
  - `RuntimeError` from `reconnect_on_error` (retry limit exceeded, Celery must restart) propagates, and the cancels not yet processed stay queued;
  - if the outer operation itself raised, a failing drain is logged and the original exception is re-raised.
- Other threads are unaffected; they are still serialized by `_pubsub_lock`.
- `on_after_fork` resets the re-entry state along with the lock.

Changes relative to #10326: the duplicated drain/log/re-raise blocks are merged into one context manager; the outer exception can no longer be masked by the drain; pending cancels are not dropped on `RuntimeError`; state is reset after fork; merge-conflict leftovers removed.

## Tests

- Unit (`t/unit/backends/test_redis.py`): re-entry during SUBSCRIBE, during UNSUBSCRIBE and during the drain itself; an ordinary drain error is logged and the rest continue; `RuntimeError` propagates with depth reset and the remainder kept; outer error not masked by a failing drain; outer error still drains; other threads are not deferred; fork reset. All fail on `main`.
- Integration (`t/integration/test_redis_backend.py::test_pubsub_reentrant_cancel_from_finalizer`): against a real Redis, re-enters `cancel_for` from inside every SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE and asserts no nested command is issued, nothing hangs, and no `celery-task-meta-*` channels remain on the server. Fails on `main`.

title: Redis result backend: don't hold the pubsub lock while waiting for messages
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

Since #10671, a gevent-patched client using the Redis result backend can hang in `result.get()`, and the timeout doesn't help. `drain_events()` holds `_pubsub_lock` while it blocks in `get_message(timeout=1)`, and the greenlet drainer takes the lock again right after releasing it because gevent's lock doesn't hand off. `consume_from()` in the calling greenlet never gets it. I described this in https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10671#issuecomment-5760253095.

This keeps the lock around every pubsub call, so the race #10671 fixed stays fixed, but waits for the socket outside it:

- `drain_events()` only takes the lock to read. It waits on the raw socket, or on `subscribed_event` when nothing is subscribed, without it. Only one thread waits on the socket at a time. The others wait on a condition that is notified after each read, because the message it reads may be theirs.
- `cancel_for()` never blocks, since it runs from `AsyncResult.__del__` where a greenlet can't switch. If the lock is busy, the key is queued and the holder unsubscribes it when it releases.

With a real Redis, a solo worker and a monkey-patched client, `get(timeout=8)` on 20 tasks went from 0/20 on main to 20/20 in about 0.1s. `get(timeout=2)` on a pending task now raises at 2s instead of hanging. Clients without gevent behave the same as before. A subscribe/unsubscribe stress with a drainer running under gevent gets through about 50k operations in 4s with every published message drained. On main it manages 4.

The new unit tests fail on main. This doesn't touch the same-thread GC re-entrancy case from #10326.

title: fix(backends): keep forget() idempotent on azureblockblob and cosmosdb
body:
Fixes #10713

`result.forget()` on a missing result should be a no-op on every KV result
backend. Following the pattern established by #10697 (elasticsearch and
couchdb), this makes the two remaining backends idempotent as well:

- `celery/backends/azureblockblob.py`: `delete_blob()` raising
  `azure.core.exceptions.ResourceNotFoundError` for a missing blob is now
  caught and treated as a no-op.
- `celery/backends/cosmosdbsql.py`: `DeleteDocument()` raising `HTTPFailure`
  with status 404 (`ERROR_NOT_FOUND`) for a missing document is now caught
  and treated as a no-op, mirroring the existing handling in `get()`.

Together with #10697, #10701 and #10702 this completes `forget()`
idempotency across all KV result backends.

**Tests:** two new unit tests per backend
(`test_forget_missing_task_is_noop`, `test_forget_twice_is_noop`) mirroring
the couchdb tests from #10697; `t/unit/backends/test_azureblockblob.py` and
`t/unit/backends/test_cosmosdbsql.py` pass (28 passed, 1 skipped).

title: Docs: broker_heartbeat_checkrate default is 3.0, not 2.0
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

The configuration reference says `broker_heartbeat_checkrate` defaults to `2.0`, but the registered default is `3.0`:

```python
# celery/app/defaults.py:96
heartbeat_checkrate=Option(3.0, type='int'),
```

`Consumer` always passes this setting into the event loop (`celery/worker/consumer/consumer.py:215` and `loop_args`), so the `hbrate=2.0` fallback in `celery/worker/loops.py` never applies in a normal worker. The setting default has been `3.0` in every release since 3.0 (checked `defaults.py` at v3.0.24, v3.1.0, v4.0.0, v5.0.0 and main).

Changes in `docs/userguide/configuration.rst`, in the `broker_heartbeat` and `broker_heartbeat_checkrate` sections:
- `Default: 2.0.` -> `Default: 3.0.`
- The 10-second worked examples: "checked every 5 seconds" (double) -> "about every 3.33 seconds" (triple), i.e. 10 / 3.0.

Docs-only change; no behaviour change.

title: Fix cache directory ownership in Docker builds
body:
## Description

PyPy 3.11 Docker builds started failing after the base image switched to the `pp80` ABI. The pinned `cryptography==50.0.1` release has no matching wheel, so pip falls back to building from source. The build tooling then attempts to install Rust, but fails because the `developer` user cannot create `~/.cache/puccinialin` inside the `.cache` directory owned by root.

This change creates `.cache` with `developer` as its owner before installing dependencies, giving the Rust installer permission to write there.

title: Replace deprecated codecs.open in celery upgrade settings
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`codecs.open()` is deprecated as of Python 3.14, and `celery/bin/upgrade.py` uses it four times, so `celery upgrade settings` emits `DeprecationWarning: codecs.open() is deprecated. Use open() instead.` for each file it touches.

This replaces it with the built-in `open()`. `celery upgrade settings` rewrites the user's own settings file (and writes a `.orig` backup), so it matters that nothing else changes: `codecs.open()` never translated newlines, so `open()` is given `newline=''` to keep line endings exactly as they were.

The `upgrade` command had no tests, so this adds `t/unit/bin/test_upgrade.py` covering:

- renaming old setting names (e.g. `BROKER_URL` → `broker_url`) and writing the `.orig` backup,
- `--django` (the `CELERY_` prefix) together with `--no-backup`,
- a file that needs no changes (left untouched, no backup),
- that CRLF line endings and non-ASCII text are preserved byte-for-byte.

The new tests pass on `main` too (apart from the deprecation warnings), since behaviour is unchanged. With `-W error::DeprecationWarning` they fail on `main` and pass here. A plain `open()` without `newline=''` fails the byte-for-byte checks, so they also guard against that regression.

`flake8` and `isort` pass.

*I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help find this, write the change and tests, and draft this description. I reviewed the change and ran the tests myself.*

title: fix(utils): BufferMap ignores bufmaxsize and miscounts total
body:
## Problem

`celery.utils.collections.BufferMap` (used for `BaseBackend._pending_messages`) has three defects in its size accounting, reproducible on current `main` (eb3dfa3):

```python
>>> from celery.utils.collections import BufferMap

# 1. the bufmaxsize parameter is silently ignored (hardcoded 1000)
>>> b = BufferMap(None, bufmaxsize=3)
>>> b.extend(1, list(range(10)))
>>> b.total, len(b[1])
(10, 10)          # expected (3, 3)

# 2. total computed over self.items() -> 2 * number of keys
#    (and maxsize therefore never enforced on construction)
>>> b2 = BufferMap(4, {'a': list(range(50))})
>>> b2.total
2                 # 50 items are really buffered; expected 4 after eviction

# 3. initial iterable stored raw, not wrapped in Messagebuffer
>>> b2.take('a')
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'take'
```

`total` is what `Evictable._evictcount` returns, so a wrong `total` makes `maxsize` eviction fire at the wrong point (or never).

Once the per-buffer cap is actually honored, `put()`/`extend()` also over-count: they add `len(it)` (or 1) to `total` even when `bufmaxsize` eviction drops items from the buffer, so `total` drifts above the real buffered-item count.

On `main` this is not just theoretical: `BaseBackend._pending_messages` is a `BufferMap(8192)`, and a single key pushed past the hardcoded 1000-message buffer cap inflates `total` above the real buffered count — after 1500 `put()` calls to one key, `total == 1500` while the buffer holds 1000 — so the 8192 limit starts evicting *other tasks'* pending messages earlier than it should.

## Changes

- honor the `bufmaxsize` parameter
- wrap initial-iterable values in `Messagebuffer` (via `_get_or_create_buffer`) and compute `total` from the actual buffer lengths; enforce `maxsize` on construction
- `put()`/`extend()` now add the buffer's actual length delta to `total`

## Testing

New cases in `t/unit/utils/test_collections.py` (`test_BufferMap`):

- on unpatched `main`: 5 tests fail (outputs above)
- with this patch:

```
$ pytest t/unit/utils/ -q
608 passed, 1 xfailed, 6 subtests passed
```

title: Tell apart signal receivers bound to different instances
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

`Signal` identifies a bound-method receiver by its function alone, so the same method of two instances gets the same lookup key:

```python
from celery.utils.dispatch import Signal

class Listener:
    def on_signal(self, sender=None, **kwargs):
        ...

sig = Signal()
a, b = Listener(), Listener()
sig.connect(a.on_signal)
sig.connect(b.on_signal)     # skipped: same key as a.on_signal
len(sig.receivers)           # 1
sig.disconnect(b.on_signal)  # True, but it removes a.on_signal
```

`b.on_signal` is never connected, `disconnect(b.on_signal)` removes `a`'s receiver instead, and once `a` is garbage collected nothing receives the signal. Receivers connected with `retry=True` are affected the same way, since their default `dispatch_uid` is the same id.

`_make_id()` used to return `(id(target.__self__), id(target.__func__))`, as Django does. #4645 (4.2.0) changed it to `id(target.__func__)` while removing `Task.__self__` for `task_method`. That PR also removed the `WeakMethod` handling of bound methods, which #4719 restored for #4699, but `_make_id()` stayed as it was.

This puts the instance back into the id. `getattr()` is there because a `staticmethod` has `__func__` but no `__self__`, and one connected with `weak=False` works today.

The two new tests fail without the change: only one of the two receivers gets registered, and after `disconnect(b.a)` nothing responds. The rest of `t/unit` gives the same results as on `main`.

title: fix(backends): keep forget() idempotent on elasticsearch and couchdb
body:
## Problem

`AsyncResult(task_id).forget()` raises on two KV result backends when the result is absent — expired, cleaned up, already forgotten, or never stored:

```python
res = app.AsyncResult("8bed31f4-...")   # never stored, or already forgotten
res.forget()
# ElasticsearchBackend -> elasticsearch.exceptions.NotFoundError
# CouchBackend         -> pycouchdb.exceptions.NotFound
```

`forget()` is documented as removing the result and is expected to be idempotent ("forget about it"), and every other KV backend already tolerates an absent key: filesystem was fixed in #10678, couchbase in #10680, and redis's `delete` is a no-op for missing keys.

## Root cause

`KeyValueStoreBackend._forget` (`celery/backends/base.py:1257`) calls `self.delete(self.get_key_for_task(task_id))`, and both backends let their client's missing-document exception propagate out of `delete()`:

- `celery/backends/elasticsearch.py:260` — `self.server.delete(...)` raises `elasticsearch.exceptions.NotFoundError` (404) for an absent doc (the `get()` path at lines 112/184 already handles this exception, only `delete()` leaks it)
- `celery/backends/couchdb.py:98` — `self.connection.delete(key)` raises `pycouchdb.exceptions.NotFound`

## Fix

Catch the backend-specific NotFound inside each `delete()` and return, so `forget()` is idempotent — same shape as the filesystem and couchbase fixes. `get()`/`mget()` and every other path are unchanged.

```python
     def delete(self, key):
+        try:
+            if self.doc_type:
+                self.server.delete(index=self.index, id=key, doc_type=self.doc_type)
+            else:
+                self.server.delete(index=self.index, id=key)
+        except elasticsearch.exceptions.NotFoundError:
+            # deleting an already-expired, already-forgotten or never-stored
+            # result must keep forget() idempotent, like the other KV backends
+            pass
```

(analogous for `couchdb.py` with `pycouchdb.exceptions.NotFound`)

## Tests

Two regression tests per backend in `t/unit/backends/test_elasticsearch.py` / `test_couchdb.py`:

- `test_forget_missing_task_is_noop` — forget a task whose document does not exist
- `test_forget_twice_is_noop` — forget the same stored task twice

Red/green verified: with the fix reverted all 4 new tests fail with the exception propagating out of `forget()`; with the fix all 58 tests in both files pass. `pre-commit run --files` (pinned hooks: flake8, isort, mypy, pyupgrade, codespell) passes on all changed files.

Note on CI: the elasticsearch/couchdb extras are not part of the default CI requirements, so these tests are `importorskip`'d there (same situation as couchbase before #10680) — they were run locally against elasticsearch 8.19.3 / pycouchdb 1.17.1 (extras' pinned range).

title: Bump version: 5.6.3 → 5.7.0a1
Preserve propagate in nested native result joins
body:
With native joins, `GroupResult.get(propagate=False)` still raises when a task inside a nested group fails. `join_native()` calls each child's `get()` without passing `propagate`, so it falls back to the default of `True`.

This PR forwards `propagate` and `disable_sync_subtasks` to child results. The regression tests cover nested failures with propagation both enabled and disabled, as well as explicit opt-out of the synchronous-subtask guard and its default behavior.

I also looked into the dropped `timeout` argument, but simply passing it to each child would give each one a fresh timeout rather than enforcing a timeout for the whole join.

One option would be to use a shared deadline and pass the remaining time to each child:

```python
deadline = None if timeout is None else time.monotonic() + timeout

...

remaining = (
    None if deadline is None
    else max(deadline - time.monotonic(), 0.0)
)

value = children_result.get(
    timeout=remaining,
    propagate=propagate,
)
```

This is just a sketch, though. Backend waits would need to share the same timeout budget, and we'd need tests to make sure ready results still work with `timeout=0`.

I've kept this PR focused on preserving these two flags. Timeout handling and the other backend options are left for a follow-up with backend-specific tests.

Fixes #10692
