title: Expect the prefetch reduction to be skipped under per-consumer QoS
body:
Since the Kombu 5.7.0a1 bump (#10677), `t/smoke/tests/test_consumer.py` fails on `rabbitmq:latest` in six cases: `test_reducing_prefetch_count[rabbitmq-1..5]` and `test_prefetch_count_restored[rabbitmq]`. Kombu 5.7 reports per-consumer QoS for RabbitMQ 4 (celery/kombu#2481), and in that mode the worker skips the prefetch-count reduction after a connection restart (#9512), so the "Temporarily reducing…" and "restored to the maximum" log lines the tests wait for never appear.

This makes the expectation conditional on the QoS mode, decided the same way `Tasks.qos_global()` decides it (`not connection.qos_semantics_matches_spec`): under per-consumer QoS the tests expect the "Skipping prefetch count reduction after connection restart" log; under global QoS the existing assertions run unchanged.

Verified locally against `rabbitmq:latest` (4.3.5): the whole module passes with Kombu 5.7.0a1 (10 passed, the 8 pre-existing Redis xfails unchanged), the six cases going through the skip branch, and `test_reducing_prefetch_count[rabbitmq-2]` and `test_prefetch_count_restored[rabbitmq]` still pass through the global branch on a tree pinned to Kombu 5.6.2.

Background in #10679; this keeps that PR on the revoke fix only, as requested.

title: fix(backends/couchbase): missing document raises instead of returning None
body:
## Description

The `KeyValueStoreBackend` contract across celery is: `get()` returns `None` for an absent key, and `delete()`/forgetting an absent key is a no-op — that's how redis, memcached, filesystem, etc. behave (mongodb reaches the same observable behaviour at the result layer even though it isn't a `KeyValueStoreBackend`), and it's what `get_task_meta()`/`AsyncResult` rely on to render an expired or unknown task id as a state rather than crashing.

`CouchbaseBackend` violates both halves:

- `get()` does `self.connection.get(key).content` with no guard. When the document has expired (auto-expiry is on: `supports_autoexpire = True`) or was never stored, the SDK raises `DocumentNotFoundException`, which propagates out of `get_task_meta()` — so `AsyncResult(id).state` on a purged id raises `DocumentNotFoundException` instead of reading as unknown/PENDING.
- `delete()` does `self.connection.remove(key)` with no guard, so `AsyncResult.forget()` on an already-expired or already-forgotten result raises `DocumentNotFoundException`.

Reproduce (against a reachable Couchbase with an empty/default collection):

```python
from celery import Celery, uuid
app = Celery('t', backend='couchbase://localhost/default')
app.AsyncResult(uuid()).state          # DocumentNotFoundException, not 'PENDING'
app.AsyncResult(uuid()).forget()       # DocumentNotFoundException
```

## What does this fix

Bug fix — `get()` now catches `DocumentNotFoundException` and returns `None`; `delete()` catches it and returns. The `DocumentNotFoundException` import lives in its own `try` with a stand-in exception class when the SDK is absent (mirroring `mongodb.py`), so a future SDK rename can't take `Cluster` down with it and no `except None` can arise.

Because `KeyValueStoreBackend` routes more than `get_task_meta()` through `get()`, this also fixes on this backend:

- `GroupResult.restore()` on a missing/expired group (`_restore_group()` → `get()`),
- `AsyncResult.exists()` (added in 5.7.0; `task_result_exists()` is `bool(self.get(...))`), which currently raises for never-stored ids.

Four mock-based regression tests added to `t/unit/backends/test_couchbase.py`, following the file's existing mock-the-connection pattern: `test_get_missing_document_returns_None`, `test_delete_missing_document_is_noop`, `test_get_task_meta_pending_for_missing_document` (asserts the user-visible `PENDING` contract through `get_task_meta()`), and `test_get_unrelated_sdk_errors_propagate` (pins the catch width: a timeout still propagates).

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Verification

- With the fix: `pytest t/unit/backends/test_couchbase.py` → 24 passed (couchbase SDK 4.6.3).
- Fix reverted, tests kept: the missing-document tests fail (`DocumentNotFoundException` propagates through `get()`/`get_task_meta()`), the other tests pass — they fail for exactly this behavior, not incidentally.
- Repo-pinned `pre-commit run --files celery/backends/couchbase.py t/unit/backends/test_couchbase.py` (flake8, isort, mypy, yesqa, codespell, pyupgrade): all pass.

Follow-up commits (requested in review):

- `mget()` fixed for the 4.x SDK: `get_multi`'s `MultiGetResult` has neither `.items()` nor iteration and by default raises on the first failed key, so `get_many()`/`GroupResult.restore()` died with `TypeError`. Now translated via `GetMultiOptions(return_exceptions=True)` into the plain dict the KV contract expects (missing document → `None`, other per-key errors re-raised). Five regression tests added, `Fixes #10694`.
- The unit-test CI job now installs the couchbase SDK (`requirements/test-ci-default.txt`), so `t/unit/backends/test_couchbase.py` actually runs; markers exclude exactly the matrix cells where the SDK publishes no wheels (PyPy, CPython 3.15, Windows/3.14).


also fix https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/10694

title: Keep a finished result when a revoke arrives for the task
body:
Since #9869 the revoke command writes `REVOKED` to the result backend for every id the worker isn't currently running. When a chord header fails and the body is a group, `_handle_group_chord_error()` revokes the body ids and stores `FAILURE` for each of them; the revoke is a broadcast, so the worker's main process writes `REVOKED` a few milliseconds later and replaces that `FAILURE`. Whichever write lands last wins, and callers get `TaskRevokedError` instead of the header's exception. This is what makes `test_chord_error_propagation_with_different_body_types[body is a group]` fail on #10677: Kombu 5.7.0a1 only changes the broadcast timing enough for the wrong write to land last on CI.

Skip the `REVOKED` write when the backend already holds a ready state for the task, and store the chord failures before broadcasting the revoke so that check always sees them. Pending tasks, the case #9869 was about, are still marked. The check is one extra backend read per revoked id in the control command.

Checked with Kombu 5.7.0a1 pinned: the `body is a group` case passes 3 out of 3 runs where it failed every time before, all four body types pass on both brokers, and `t/unit/worker` is unchanged apart from the new test.

Fixes the smoke failure that came with the Kombu 5.7.0a1 bump (#10677).

title: Update kombu version to 5.7.0a1
Add a smoke test workflow that runs against py-amqp, Kombu and Billiard main
body:
Closes #10675.

Adds `.github/workflows/smoke-tests-dev.yml`, a separate workflow on the same push/PR triggers as the main one. It calls the reusable `smoke-tests.yml` with a new `dev_requirements` input, which selects the `smoke-dev` tox env: the `smoke` env plus `requirements/dev.txt`, so the host gets py-amqp, Kombu and Billiard from Git `main`. That env also sets `CELERY_DEV_REQUIREMENTS=1`, which `SmokeWorkerContainer.buildargs()` passes to the worker image, where a new build arg installs `dev.txt` on top of the editable Celery install. Without the flag the image build is unchanged, and `python-package.yml` is untouched.

The job covers `test_worker.py` and `test_tasks.py` (the two files that caught the Billiard 4.3.0 changes in #10659) on one Python version, so it is two extra jobs rather than another full matrix.

Checked locally on macOS with Docker: the `3.12-smoke-dev` tox env ends up with py-amqp, Kombu and Billiard from Git (`direct_url.json` points at the three repos), the worker image does too with the build arg and stays on PyPI without it, and both files pass in that mode (`test_tasks.py` 22 passed, `test_worker.py` 62 passed / 6 skipped, same as with the released versions).

Two things worth knowing. The image install needs `--force-reinstall`: pip clones the three repos but keeps the PyPI copy when the checkout reports the same version string. And `default.txt` pins `billiard==4.3.0`, so once Billiard `main` bumps its version the dev job will fail at install time until the pin moves, which is the kind of thing this job exists to surface.

title: Wait for the replacement child in the smoke respawn test
body:
`test_child_process_respawn` waits until the worker container is back to two `celery` processes and then checks that a new pid appeared. The old child can still be alive at that point, so the wait passes early and the check fails with `assert 2 == 3` (the pid sets are identical). On current `main` the `DELAY_TIMEOUT` case fails 3 out of 10 runs for me locally; CI only hides it behind `--reruns 5`.

Wait for a pid that was not there before the task instead, and take the "after" snapshot from that same poll. With the change the same case passes 10 out of 10 runs.

title: Refresh AMQP task routes for all configuration update forms
body:
## Description
`AMQP._handle_conf_update()` only recognizes `task_routes` when `app.conf.update()` is called with keyword arguments. When a mapping or iterable of pairs is passed instead, the cached routes and router are not refreshed.

https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/0ec71f929742938cbcbe996b74cabf5b6cd54655/celery/app/amqp.py#L660-L664

For example:
`app.conf.update({'task_routes': routes})`
Here, args is:
```python
({'task_routes': routes},)
```
  It is a tuple containing the mapping, so `'task_routes' in args` is False.

title: Store failures raised as BaseException subclasses with the JSON serializer
body:
`Backend.encode_result()` only runs `prepare_exception()` when the result is an `Exception`, so a task that fails with a bare `BaseException` or `asyncio.CancelledError` reaches the JSON encoder as the raw object and `mark_as_failure()` dies with `EncodeError: Object of type BaseException is not JSON serializable`. No result is written and the caller waits for its own timeout. Pickle is unaffected since it serializes the object as is.

This came up while looking at Billiard 4.3.0 in #10659: the worker loop now reports any `BaseException` a task raises instead of turning it into `WorkerLostError`. `SystemExit` and `KeyboardInterrupt` are handled in #10667; this covers the rest.

Checking `BaseException` instead is enough, `exception_to_python()` already accepts them on the way back. With a prefork worker against Redis, both cases now come back as the raised exception in well under a second where they used to time out.

title: Redis result backend: serialize pubsub access between the drainer and result cleanup
body:
## Description

Got bitten by the #4670 race again on 5.5.x: `AsyncResult.__del__` runs on whatever thread the GC happens to pick, and it walks into `remove_pending_result` -> `cancel_for` -> `pubsub.unsubscribe()` while the result drainer is sitting in `get_message()` on the very same pubsub object. redis-py pubsub isn't safe for concurrent use, and with gevent this blows up as `ConcurrentObjectUseError: This socket is already used by another greenlet` (AssertionError on older versions). The #4666 / #6416 fixes added the unsubscribe but never serialized it against the reader, so the race just moved around.

What I did: gave `ResultConsumer` an RLock and took it around every touch of the shared pubsub — start/stop, subscribe, unsubscribe, the `get_message` poll in `drain_events`, reconnect, and the fork cleanup. RLock because the drainer itself calls `cancel_for` from `on_state_change` when a ready meta comes in, and the reconnect path re-enters from the error handler. The idle sleep when there's no pubsub yet stays outside the lock so `apply_async` isn't stalled by nothing.

One thing I wasn't 100% sure about: fork safety. The child inherits the lock possibly still held by a thread that didn't survive the fork, so `on_after_fork` swaps in a fresh one before closing the old pubsub.

There's a real trade-off here worth spelling out: while the drainer is mid-poll (up to its 1s timeout), a subscribe/unsubscribe from another thread has to wait. I think that's strictly better than crashing, and in the pure fire-and-forget producer case the drainer isn't running so there's no contention at all. If maintainers would rather have the drainer own the pubsub exclusively via a command queue, that's a bigger redesign — figured I'd start here.

Tests: the main one is a race test that hammers subscribe/unsubscribe from 4 threads while a drainer thread polls; the fake pubsub records any overlapping calls. It fails immediately on main (`assert not ['subscribe', 'subscribe', 'get_message', 'unsubscribe', ...]`) and is clean with the lock. Plus deterministic checks that each pubsub op holds the lock, that the idle sleep doesn't, and that `on_after_fork` replaces the lock. `t/unit/backends/test_redis.py` + `test_asynchronous.py` pass locally (167 passed, 9 skipped), flake8 clean.

title: Update billiard dependency in dev requirements
body: Updated billiard dependency to the latest version.

title: Queues.__setitem__() should apply the default routing key
body:
## Description

`Queues.add()` applies the default routing key, but `Queues.__setitem__()` doesn't. I think these two operations should behave the same.

`_add()` also replaces an empty-name exchange with `self.default_exchange`, even when the default exchange is None. An empty exchange name means RabbitMQ's built-in unnamed exchange, not "no exchange" so the fallback should only be applied when self.default_exchange is not None.

title: Fix revoked tasks running anyway after mingle merged revoke stamps from another host
body:
## Description

Fixes #4300 — a revoked task with an ETA/countdown runs anyway, although the worker logged `Tasks flagged as revoked` for it. This is the mechanism @tahamr83 guessed at in https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4300#issuecomment-951743011, confirmed on a production cluster and reproduced in unit tests at the `hello`, mingle and `--statedb` levels.

### The bug

`celery.worker.state.revoked` is a `LimitedSet`, and `LimitedSet.add()` stamps every item with `time.monotonic()` — seconds since the boot of *this* host. `mingle` copied the whole set between workers on start-up (`hello` sent and received `revoked._data`, stamps included), and the stamps were merged as they were.

A stamp taken on a host with a longer uptime is ahead of the local clock of the worker that receives it, so for that worker:

- it never expires — `purge()` stops at the first item whose `stamp + expires > now`, and these are forever "not expired yet";
- once such stamps fill the set up to `maxlen`, every `add()` triggers `purge()`, which drops the item with the *smallest* stamp — the id just revoked locally.

So the revoke is logged and lost in the same call. Any worker started while the cluster is in this state inherits the stamps on mingle, so a rolling restart never clears it; it recovers only when the local uptime catches up with the foreign stamps (which is why the reporter saw it "disappear the next morning"). A state db (`--statedb`) read after a reboot of the host does the same to a single worker.

Observed on Celery 5.6.3, Kubernetes, ~3800 revokes/hour cluster-wide: every worker had exactly `maxlen` (50 000) revoked ids, the oldest 15 days old with `worker_revoke_expires` at 3 hours, and 8 out of 8 revoked ETA tasks whose ETA fell inside the hour I looked at ran anyway, with no `Discarding revoked task` in the log.

### The fix

Foreign stamps are never merged: a set received on mingle or read from the state db contributes its **ids only**, stamped with the local clock (`merge_revoked()` in `celery.worker.state`, used by the `hello` command, `Mingle.on_revoked_received` and `Persistent`). `hello` and `Mingle.send_hello` send only the ids as well, which halves the payload.

- `LimitedSet` keeps `time.monotonic()`, so a step of the wall clock cannot reproduce the bug on a single host.
- The ids received live `REVOKE_EXPIRES` seconds from their receipt rather than from the revoke — the concern of the `# XXX AVOID THIS` comment on that path of `LimitedSet.update()`, and a far better failure than losing revokes. Documented in the workers guide.
- A mixed cluster is safe in both directions: an older worker merges a list of ids through the same iterable path (stamping them with its clock), and a newer worker takes the ids out of the dict an older one sends. Same for a state db written by either version.

Independently of the clock, the heap entries of `LimitedSet` are now ordered by `(stamp, sequence number, item)`: items added within the clock resolution keep their insertion order, and the heap never compares the items themselves (a tie between an `int` and a `str` raised `TypeError` — the flakiness #3892 papered over). `add()`/`purge()` take `now=0` as a time rather than as "unset", and `__eq__` returns `NotImplemented` for a non-`LimitedSet` operand.

### Tests

- `test_hello_stamps_received_revoked_items_locally` (`test_control.py`), `test_start_stamps_received_revoked_items_locally` (`test_consumer.py`) and `test_merge_stamps_saved_items_locally` (`test_state.py`) reproduce the bug on the real paths: ids arriving with stamps a million seconds ahead of the local clock are stamped locally, expire with the local ones, and — at the mingle level, with `maxlen=1` — no longer evict an id revoked afterwards.
- `test_add_orders_items_within_the_clock_resolution`, `test_add_at_time_zero`, `test_update_from_another_clock` and `test_eq` cover the `LimitedSet` changes.

All of them fail on `main`. `t/unit` passes with the same set of failures as `main` on my machine (15 pre-existing `test_prefork` failures on macOS, unrelated); `pre-commit` is clean on the changed files, `apicheck`/`configcheck` report nothing new.

### Notes for the 5.7 changelog

- Fixes #4300: revoked tasks ran anyway once `mingle` had filled a worker's revoked set with stamps from a host with a longer uptime. Ids received on mingle or read from `--statedb` are now stamped with the local clock and expire `CELERY_WORKER_REVOKE_EXPIRES` seconds after receipt.
- The `revoked` value in the `hello` remote-control request and reply is a list of ids, not a `{id: [stamp, id]}` dict; both versions merge the other's format, so a rolling upgrade is safe.
- `LimitedSet._data`/`_heap` entries are `(stamp, seq, item)` 3-tuples; `now=0` is a time, not "unset"; `__eq__` returns `NotImplemented` for other types. `as_dict()`, pickling and `update()` are unchanged.

title: Keep a cancelled task unacked when the child reports SystemExit
body:
Follow-up to the investigation in #10659.

With Billiard 4.3.0 the `test_reset_visibility_timeout` smoke tests fail: after `worker: Cold shutdown (MainProcess)` the worker never logs `Restoring 1 unacknowledged message(s)`. The worker isn't stuck. It exits normally, and the task that was still running has been acknowledged and dropped instead of being requeued.

Cold shutdown cancels the active request by sending `SIGTERM` to the child running it, and Billiard's signal handler in the child raises `SystemExit`. Up to Billiard 4.3.0rc1 that killed the child, the job came back as `Terminated`, and `Request.on_failure` returned early for it, so the message stayed unacked and kombu restored it on close. Since celery/billiard#452 the worker loop catches `BaseException`, so the same `SystemExit` is marshaled back as an ordinary task failure. `on_failure` then takes the `acks_late` branch, `acks_on_failure` is on by default, and the message gets acked. Bisecting Billiard between rc1 and 4.3.0 lands on that commit.

This change treats a `SystemExit`/`KeyboardInterrupt` result like `Terminated` when the request was cancelled or revoked by the worker itself. A task that exits on its own is still a failure and goes through the usual path.

Checked with Billiard 4.3.0 pinned: the five failing `test_reset_visibility_timeout` cases pass, the full `t/smoke/tests/test_worker.py` passes, and `t/unit/worker` is unchanged apart from the three new tests. Also reproduced and re-checked on macOS with a plain prefork worker against Redis, where the in-flight message now comes back to the queue after a cold shutdown.

Fixes the smoke failures blocking #10659.

title: Fix escaped percent signs in node formatting
body:
## Description

Recognize `%%` as an escaped percent sign in `simple_format()`. The formatter already registers `%` as a literal value, but its pattern only matches word characters, so `%%n` expands the node name and `%%x` raises an unknown-format error.

`host_format("logs/%%n-%n.log", host="worker.example.com")` now returns `logs/%n-worker.log`. Log and pid file options passed through `celery multi` are expanded twice, so they require `%%%%` to preserve a literal percent sign in the final worker path. The worker guide and changelog document this behavior.

`Node.pidfile` now applies the worker's second formatting pass too. For example, `--pidfile=%%%%n-%n.pid` is both written and located as `%n-worker.pid`, allowing multi's stop/stopwait commands to find the worker.

Tests cover the final multi argv, reading real pidfiles for both `--pidfile` and `-p`, and actual logfile creation through Celery's logging subsystem in isolated subprocesses.

## Validation

- 67 focused unit tests passed, including ten pidfile cases. The six standalone subprocess logfile checks also pass (`pytest --noconftest t/integration/test_logfile_format.py`).
- Before the pidfile fix, eight escaped-path cases failed to locate the pidfile; they pass with the fix.
- All configured pre-commit hooks passed for changed files, including YAML validation and mypy.
- Docker and smoke-workflow changes are now provided by upstream #10707 and #10709; this PR contains only the percent-formatting fix, documentation, and tests.

title: Apply index lists like -c:1,2 to named nodes in celery multi
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

I was reading `MultiParser.parse` after #10643 and noticed that an index list is silently dropped when the nodes have names. `celery multi start foo bar baz -c 3 -c:1 10` gives `foo` 10 processes, as the comment in `_update_ns_opts` describes, but `celery multi start foo bar baz -c 3 -c:1,2 10` leaves all three nodes at 3, with no error. The docstring of `celery multi` says `-c:1-3` can also be written as `-c:1,2,3`, and it shows lists working with node names (`-c:foo,bar,baz`), so a list of indexes should reach the named nodes the same way a single index does.

The cause is the order of the two passes: `_update_ns_opts` maps numeric namespaces to node names first, and only then does `_update_ns_ranges` split `1,2` into `1` and `2`. By that point the mapping has already run, so the new namespaces never reach `foo` or `bar`. When the arguments are node names, I now split the lists first and map the indexes afterwards. The order stays the same when the nodes are given as a count (`celery multi start 3 ...`), because there the node names are the indexes themselves, so the out-of-range handling for that form is unchanged. With named nodes, an out-of-range index inside a list (`-c:1,5` with two nodes) now raises the same `KeyError` that `-c:5` already raised, instead of being ignored.

The new test in `t/unit/apps/test_multi.py` fails on main with `assert ['3', '3', '3'] == ['10', '10', '3']` and passes with the change. The rest of `t/unit/apps/test_multi.py` and `t/unit/bin` still pass, and flake8 is clean on both files.

Found by a defect-hunting pipeline I build and run ([Dev-next-gen](https://github.com/Dev-next-gen)), using Claude Code with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.

title: Publish the Cassandra session only once the connection is ready
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

I was reading `CassandraBackend._get_connection()` and noticed that callers leave early as soon as `self._session is not None`, before taking the lock. Inside the lock, though, `self._session` is set right after `Cluster.connect()`, and only then are the write/read statements prepared and, for writers, `CREATE TABLE` issued. So another thread (a `threads` pool worker where several tasks finish right after start, for instance) can see the session and run `_store_result` while the first thread is still waiting on `CREATE TABLE`, which on a fresh keyspace means an insert into a table that doesn't exist yet. It can also land in the short window where `_write_stmt` is still `None`.

The fix builds the session and the statements in local variables and assigns `_write_stmt`, `_read_stmt` and `_session` at the end, once the table exists. Nothing else changes: the statements, the order in which they run and the lock are the same, and only private attributes are involved. As a side effect, an `OperationTimedOut` raised by `CREATE TABLE` now leaves `_session` unset, which is what the `except` branch was already trying to do.

The new test starts a second thread from inside the fake `CREATE TABLE` call. Before the change it fails with `assert ['INSERT', 'CREATE'] == ['CREATE', 'INSERT']`: the second thread wrote first. After the change the second thread waits on the lock, and `t/unit/backends/test_cassandra.py` passes (17 tests), as does the rest of `t/unit/backends` (635 passed, 19 skipped).

A review pointed out that the barrier was still bypassed when the first caller was a read: `_get_connection(write=False)` published the session without issuing `CREATE TABLE`, and the early return only looked at `self._session`, so the first `_store_result` behind a read-opened session returned before the table existed. The second commit tracks that with a `_table_created` flag, checked in the early return and assigned after `_session`, so a writer takes the lock while the flag is false. `test_table_is_created_for_a_write_through_a_read_session` reads then writes and fails without it with `assert ['SELECT', 'INSERT'] == ['SELECT', 'CREATE', 'INSERT']`.

Found by a defect-hunting pipeline I build and run ([Dev-next-gen](https://github.com/Dev-next-gen)), using Claude Code with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.

title: Keep the Azure Block Blob backend picklable
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

I noticed that the Azure Block Blob result backend can't survive a pickle round trip. `AsyncResult.__reduce_args__` includes `self.backend`, and `unpickle_backend` rebuilds the backend from whatever kwargs its `__reduce__` returns. `AzureBlockBlobBackend` never overrides `__reduce__`, so it gets rebuilt with `url=None`, and `_parse_url` fails on `None[len(prefix):]`. This is the same failure #6108 reported for the filesystem backend (fixed in #6120).

This is enough to trigger it, with azure-storage-blob 12.30.1 installed and no network needed:

```python
import pickle
from celery import Celery
from celery.result import AsyncResult

app = Celery(set_as_current=True)
app.conf.result_backend = (
    'azureblockblob://DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=name;'
    'AccountKey=key;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net')
pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(AsyncResult('some-task-id', app=app)))
```

On main it raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. With this change it gives back an `AsyncResult` backed by an `AzureBlockBlobBackend`. In practice, this breaks a task that returns an `AsyncResult` when `result_serializer='pickle'`: the result is stored fine, but `.get()` fails with a `DecodeError` when it's read back.

The fix passes the connection string (with its `azureblockblob://` prefix) and the container name through `__reduce__`, the same way the filesystem, redis and mongodb backends pass their URL. The signature matches `Backend.__reduce__`. The pickle format of this backend does change, but before this change unpickling it always failed, so nothing that used to load can stop loading. As with redis and mongodb, the pickled backend carries its credentials, since it can't reconnect without them.

I added two tests to `t/unit/backends/test_azureblockblob.py`: a plain pickle round trip, and an `AsyncResult` encoded and decoded through the backend with the pickle serializer. Without the fix, both fail with the `TypeError` above (the second one wrapped in `DecodeError`). With the fix, the file passes (24 tests), `t/unit/backends/` passes (636 passed, 19 skipped), and flake8 reports nothing on the two files.

Found by a defect-hunting pipeline I build and run ([Dev-next-gen](https://github.com/Dev-next-gen)), using Claude Code with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.

title: Fix empty group/chain handling in chains and group headers (#9772)
body:
## Summary

Supersedes #10245 by @kaiisfree, rebased on current `main` and reconciled with #10321 ("Skip empty groups in chains"), which landed after that PR was opened and already fixes the crash reported in #9772 for the common `chain(group([...]), group(), group())` case. The original commits are kept; the final merge commit carries the conflict resolution.

Two problems remained on `main` after #10321:

- **Partial args are silently dropped** when a chain starts with an empty group, an empty chain, or a nested chain that starts with an empty group. `prepare_steps()` detects the chain's first task via `not steps` during its reverse walk, and the in-loop skip from #10321 removes the leading empty group *after* that check, so no task receives the args. `_chain(group(), add.s(10))(1, 2)` ran `add(10)`.
- **Empty chains inside a group or chord header raise `IndexError`** from `_chain.freeze()`, e.g. `group(chain(), add.s(1, 2)).apply_async()` and the previously `xfail`ed `test_apply_contains_chords_containing_empty_chain`.

## Changes (`celery/canvas.py`)

- `_chain.prepare_steps()`: normalise the head of the chain before the reverse walk. Leading empty groups are stripped (same list/tuple predicate as #10321) and a nested chain at the head is spliced in place, so the first real task is the last one popped and receives the partial args. A chain made up of empty groups only keeps a single one, matching #10321's in-loop behaviour, so it still yields an (empty) `GroupResult` rather than a placeholder result that never completes.
- `group._prepared()`, `group._freeze_unroll()`, `group._freeze_tasks()`: skip empty chains so they neither crash `freeze()` nor produce a frozen result with no task behind it. `_chord._descend()` already counted them as 0.

Compared with #10245, the following were dropped because #10321 made them redundant or they conflicted with its semantics: the second in-loop empty-group skip and splice reordering, the `applied_first_args` post-loop fallback, the `res is not None` guard (chord bodies are always frozen now, see `_chord.freeze`), the placeholder `AsyncResult` returned from `_chain.freeze()` for all-empty chains, and the `_chain_effectively_empty()` helper.

## Tests

- All regression tests from #10245 carried over. `test_chain_only_empty_groups*` updated to the reconciled behaviour (one empty group is kept). `test_group_prepared_skips_effectively_empty_chain` removed since that semantic no longer exists.
- New: `test_chain_leading_empty_chain_passes_args`, `test_group_freeze_skips_empty_chain`, `test_group_freeze_skips_empty_chain_in_generator`.
- `test_apply_contains_chords_containing_empty_chain` is no longer `xfail` and asserts the chord bodies are applied immediately.
- `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`: 250 passed, 1 xfailed (pre-existing `test_apply_contains_chords_containing_empty_group`). Full `t/unit`: 3826 passed, 36 skipped.

Fixes #9772

title: Set default max priority in Queues.__setitem__() when the queue has none
body:
## Description

There is a discrepancy between `Queues.add()` and `Queues.__setitem__()` where `add()` applies the default `x-max-priority`, but `__setitem__()` doesn't. I think users would expect these two ways of adding a queue to handle priority the same way.

title: Skip empty groups in eager chains
body:
## Description

Follow up to #10321 (which fixed #9772 for the worker path).

`_chain.prepare_steps()` skips empty groups when preparing a chain for execution, but `_chain.apply()`, the eager execution path, did not. The same canvas therefore produced different results depending on how it was executed:

```python
chain(add.s(2, 2), group())
# eager: []  vs  worker: 4
```

This change extracts the empty group check into a shared `_is_empty_group()` helper, used in three places. `_chain.__or__` drops empty groups at construction time, so `chain(a, group(), b)` no longer builds a chord with an empty header. Both execution paths, `_chain.prepare_steps()` and `_chain.apply()`, skip them, mirroring the worker behavior: an empty group is skipped unless it is the only task in the chain.

## Verification

- Repro scripts confirmed the divergence on current `main` and agreement after the fix (trailing, middle, and leading empty groups, plus the canonical `chain()` spelling).
- Added two regression tests in `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`, written failing first.
- `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`: 231 passed, 2 xfailed. Full `t/unit/tasks/`: 1029 passed, no regressions.

title: Fix celery multi crashing on a single node name containing a dash
body:
## Description

I was reading `celery/apps/multi.py` and noticed that `MultiParser.parse()` decides whether the
arguments describe a range *before* it knows what the single argument actually is:

```python
ranges = len(names) == 1
...
if ranges:
    try:
        names, prefix = self._get_ranges(names), range_prefix
    except ValueError:
        pass
self._update_ns_opts(p, names)
self._update_ns_ranges(p, ranges)
```

`_get_ranges()` calls `int(names[0])`, so for `celery multi start worker-1` it raises `ValueError`
and the names are left alone — but `ranges` is still `True`. `_update_ns_ranges()` then hands that
flag to `_parse_ns_range()`, which treats any dash in a namespace as a range separator and calls
`int()` on both halves.

So starting a single worker whose name contains a dash, with a namespaced option for it, crashes:

```
$ celery multi show worker-1 -c:worker-1 5
...
  File "celery/apps/multi.py", line 363, in _parse_ns_range
    str(n) for n in range(int(start), int(stop) + 1)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'worker'
```

The same thing happens with the index form (`-c:1`), because `_update_ns_opts()` copies the options
onto the `worker-1` namespace first. Two or more node names on the command line are fine, since
`ranges` is then `False`.

The fix is to clear the flag when the range expansion didn't apply — if the lone argument isn't a
node count, it's a plain node name and its dashes aren't range separators.

After the change:

```
$ celery multi show worker-1 -c:worker-1 5 --pidfile=/tmp/%n.pid --logfile=/tmp/%n.log
python -m celery worker --detach --pidfile=/tmp/worker-1.pid --logfile=/tmp/worker-1.log \
    -c 5 -n worker-1@shwp-ai --executable=python
```

and the numeric form still expands as before:

```
$ celery multi show 3 -c:1-2 10 ...
... -c 10 -n celery1@shwp-ai ...
... -c 10 -n celery2@shwp-ai ...
... -n celery3@shwp-ai ...
```

I added a unit test in `t/unit/apps/test_multi.py` that reproduces the crash: it fails with the
`ValueError` above on main and passes with the fix. `t/unit/apps/` and `t/unit/bin/` are green
(62 passed).

Found by a defect-hunting pipeline I build and run ([Dev-next-gen](https://github.com/Dev-next-gen)), using Claude Code with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.

title: Rebuild the GCS storage client after a fork when Firestore is touched first
body:
## Description

`GCSBackend` holds two clients: the Cloud Storage one on `_client` and the
Firestore one used for the chord counter on `_firestore_client`. Both
properties guard against a fork with the same check — compare `self._pid` to
`getpid()`, and rebuild if they differ — and both of them wrote back to that
one `_pid` attribute. So whichever client is rebuilt first clears the fork
flag for the other one:

```python
backend.firestore_client   # rebuilds, and sets _pid to the child's pid
backend.client             # _pid now matches, so the parent's client is returned
```

I ran into this reading `on_chord_part_return`, because that is the order it
uses: `incr()` reaches Firestore first through `_firestore_document`, then
`_restore_deps` reaches GCS through `client`. In a prefork worker the child
therefore keeps using the storage client the parent built, along with the
`requests` session and the sockets mounted on it in the `client` property —
which is the situation the pid check exists to avoid.

The fix is to give the Firestore client its own `_firestore_pid`, so the two
properties stop overwriting each other's marker.

There are already two tests for this, `test_new_client_after_fork` and
`test_new_firestore_client_after_fork`, but each one only ever asks for a
single client, so neither can observe the interaction. I added one that asks
for both after the pid changes; it fails on main with

```
assert backend.client is not storage_client
E  AssertionError: assert <MagicMock name='Client()' id='...'> is not <MagicMock name='Client()' id='...'>
```

and passes with the change. `t/unit/backends/` is green (633 passed, 19
skipped). I also moved the two `_pid` assertions in
`test_new_firestore_client_after_fork` onto `_firestore_pid`, since that is
the attribute that test is actually about.

Found by a defect-hunting pipeline I build and run ([Dev-next-gen](https://github.com/Dev-next-gen)), using Claude Code with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Support for Closed TypedDicts (PEP 728)

Mypy now supports closed TypedDicts as specified in PEP 728. A closed TypedDict cannot have extra keys beyond those explicitly defined. This allows the type checker to determine that certain operations are safe when they otherwise wouldn't be due to the potential presence of unknown keys.

You can use the closed keyword argument with TypedDict:

HasName = TypedDict("HasName", {"name": str})
HasOnlyName = TypedDict("HasOnlyName", {"name": str}, closed=True)
Movie = TypedDict("Movie", {"name": str, "year": int})

movie: Movie = {"name": "Nimona", "year": 2023}
has_name: HasName = movie  # OK: HasName is open (default)
has_only_name: HasOnlyName = movie  # Error: HasOnlyName is closed and Movie has extra "year" key

title: Return the exact fractional utcoffset() instead of rounding it
body:
## Description

`celery.utils.time.utcoffset()` computes the local UTC offset in whole hours
from `time.timezone`/`time.altzone` (seconds *west* of UTC) using floor
division (`// 3600`). For any fractional-hour, **east**-of-UTC timezone
(India, Sri Lanka, Iran, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Nepal, parts of Australia, all
at a 30- or 45-minute offset), this rounds the magnitude *up* instead of
truncating:

```python
>>> -19800 // 3600      # UTC+5:30 (India), floor-divided
-6                       # implies UTC+6:00, a full hour off
```

That's a full-hour error for east-of-UTC zones. West-of-UTC fractional zones
don't hit this specific floor-vs-truncation asymmetry (floor and truncation
agree for positive dividends), but they're not correct on `main` either —
they're still truncated to a whole hour, which is 15-30 minutes off from the
real offset. `main` is only exact for whole-hour zones.

This PR fixes both: instead of rounding to a whole hour at all, `utcoffset()`
now returns the exact fractional offset via true division:

```python
>>> -19800 / 3600
-5.5                     # exact, matches UTC+5:30
```

`utcoffset()` feeds `celery/events/dispatcher.py` (attached to every worker
event) and `celery/events/receiver.py`'s `adjust_timestamp()` (used to
normalize event timestamps across workers in different timezones), and
`adjust_timestamp()` does pure arithmetic on this value, so keeping it exact
rather than rounded avoids skewing cross-timezone timestamp correction for
any fractional-hour zone, east or west.

Whole-hour zones now get a `float` back (e.g. `5.0` instead of `5`) rather
than an `int`. This doesn't change the arithmetic anywhere `utcoffset()` is
consumed, and the function was already annotated `-> float`, so this brings
the implementation in line with the type it already claimed to return.

This is a different function from `LocalTimezone.fromutc()` (fixed in #10519
for a related but distinct negative-offset bug; that one lost the sign
entirely via `timedelta.seconds`, this one mis-rounds the magnitude for
fractional hours via `//`). `LocalTimezone.__repr__` a few lines above the
function I'm fixing already reports the equivalent seconds-to-hours
conversion without floor-dividing (`int(x.total_seconds() / 3600)` truncates
toward zero rather than flooring); this fix goes one step further for
`utcoffset()` and skips rounding entirely.

## Testing

Added `test_utcoffset_whole_hour_unaffected` (confirms no behavior change for
ordinary whole-hour zones, aside from the `int` → `float` type), plus
`test_utcoffset_fractional_hour_offset` and
`test_utcoffset_quarter_hour_offset` (regression tests for 30- and 45-minute
offsets, covering both STD and DST branches) to `t/unit/utils/test_time.py`.

```
$ pytest t/unit/utils/test_time.py -q
65 passed
$ pytest t/unit/events/ -q
100 passed, 1 skipped
```

Confirmed the new fractional-hour tests fail on current `main` and pass with
this fix.

`flake8` and `isort --check-only` clean on both changed files.

title: Prevent apply_async() from mutating cached execution options
body:
## Description

When `apply_async()` receives an empty `options`, it reuses and mutates the task's cached options 
https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/ea1db4a551a40c3ec1192abeed4785853833cda5/celery/app/task.py#L686-L687
while adding value such as ignore_result and priority
https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/ea1db4a551a40c3ec1192abeed4785853833cda5/celery/app/task.py#L689-L691

Subsequent `send_task()` calls can then behave differently depending on earlier dispatches because they use the
mutated cached options as defaults.

This change always copies the cached options before adding defaults.

title: Preserve configuration when copying settings
body:
## Description

Copying `app.conf` produces a settings object that cannot be read:

```python
from celery import Celery

app = Celery('example')
app.conf.task_always_eager = True
assert app.conf.task_always_eager is True

copied = app.conf.copy()
assert copied.task_always_eager is True  # TypeError: 'str' object is not callable
```

`copy.copy(app.conf)` fails in the same way. The inherited `ChainMap.copy()` expands the default mappings into positional arguments, but `ConfigurationView` expects a list of defaults followed by key converters and a prefix.

This adds a copy implementation that matches `ConfigurationView`'s constructor and preserves its key conversions. Changes get their own mapping, while default mappings and nested values remain shared. `Settings` also loads pending configuration before copying and preserves the deprecated-settings value without adding it back after `clear()`.

## Validation

- The 30 new cases give **26 failures and 4 passes** on main at `cdd516f71d98121d8a4a659d90d400a78b13dcd3`, and **30 passes** with the fix.
- `pytest -p celery.contrib.pytest t/unit/utils t/unit/app t/unit/test_generics.py`: **1,301 passed, 14 skipped, 1 xfailed**, with 6 subtests passed.
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: passed, including mypy.
- Four memory-broker worker checks using copied settings passed, covering both copy APIs before and after configuration was loaded. Changes to the copy left the original settings unchanged.
- The new copy methods have full line and branch coverage in the focused tests.

These checks used CPython 3.12.13 on macOS. I also ran `apicheck`, `configcheck`, and Bandit; the base and this branch reported the same documentation failures and Bandit findings. The existing `bandit.json` could not be parsed in either tree. I have not run the full upstream platform matrix locally.

title: added new regression test to check issue #3885
Prevent add_defaults() from crashing when config_from_object() fails on an already configured app
body:
## Description

If `config_from_object(..., silent=True)` fails on an already configured app, `self._conf` has already been cleared, but `configured` is still True. Calling `add_defaults()` then raises an AttributeError.

This PR only clears self._conf after the configuration loads successfully.

```python
def add_defaults(self, fun):
    """Add default configuration from dict ``d``.

    If the argument is a callable function then it will be regarded
    as a promise, and it won't be loaded until the configuration is
    actually needed.

    This method can be compared to:

    .. code-block:: pycon

        >>> celery.conf.update(d)

    with a difference that 1) no copy will be made and 2) the dict will
    not be transferred when the worker spawns child processes, so
    it's important that the same configuration happens at import time
    when pickle restores the object on the other side.
    """
    if not callable(fun):
        d, fun = fun, lambda: d
    if self.configured:
>           return self._conf.add_defaults(fun())
               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
E           AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'add_defaults'
```

title: Redact SAS tokens and lowercase account keys in AzureBlockBlobBackend.as_uri
body:
*Note*: Before submitting this pull request, please review our [contributing
guidelines](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/contributing.html).

## Description

While reading `AzureBlockBlobBackend.as_uri()` I noticed it only masks a connection string part that starts with the exact text `AccountKey=`. The Azure SDK accepts two other forms that carry a secret, and both came out in clear.

The first is a SAS connection string (`BlobEndpoint=...;SharedAccessSignature=sv=...&sig=...`), which `BlobServiceClient.from_connection_string()` accepts as is. The second is the same key in a different case: the SDK upper-cases keys before reading them (`parse_connection_str` in azure-storage-blob 12.30.1), so `accountkey=...` authenticates fine but is not matched by `startswith('AccountKey=')`.

I checked this against azure-storage-blob 12.30.1 with a fake token. On main:

```
>>> AzureBlockBlobBackend(app=app, url="azureblockblob://BlobEndpoint=https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/;SharedAccessSignature=sv=2022-11-02&sig=SECRETSIG%3D").as_uri()
'azureblockblob://BlobEndpoint=https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/;SharedAccessSignature=sv=2022-11-02&sig=SECRETSIG%3D'
>>> AzureBlockBlobBackend(app=app, url="azureblockblob://AccountName=acct;accountkey=c2VjcmV0a2V5").as_uri()
'azureblockblob://AccountName=acct;accountkey=c2VjcmV0a2V5'
```

`as_uri()` is what the worker banner prints on its `results:` line (`celery/apps/worker.py`), so the token ends up in startup logs.

The fix compares each key case-insensitively against `AccountKey` and `SharedAccessSignature` and keeps the key as the user wrote it, so the existing `AccountKey=**` output is unchanged. `include_password=True` still returns the full string.

I added two tests next to the existing `as_uri` ones. Both fail on main with an assertion error and pass with the change, and the whole `t/unit/backends/test_azureblockblob.py` passes (22 tests). flake8 is clean on both files.

body:
## Description

Fixes #10367.

`countdown`, `expires`, `time_limit` and `soft_time_limit` are documented as a number of seconds, which makes longer durations awkward to write and easy to misread:

```python
@shared_task(
    soft_time_limit=60 * 60 * 2,       # 2 hours
    time_limit=60 * 60 * 2 + 60,       # 2 hours + 1 minute
    expires=60 * 60 * 4,               # 4 hours
)
def task(): ...
```

Passing a `timedelta` instead currently fails, in two different ways:

* **`countdown` / `expires`** raise `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'datetime.timedelta' and 'int'`, from the seconds range check — far from the call site that caused it.
* **`time_limit` / `soft_time_limit`** are accepted silently and placed in the message headers as `timedelta` objects, then fail later when the message is serialized:

  ```
  timelimit header -> [datetime.timedelta(seconds=30), datetime.timedelta(seconds=10)]
  TypeError: Object of type timedelta is not JSON serializable
  ```

After this change:

```python
@shared_task(
    soft_time_limit=timedelta(hours=2),
    time_limit=timedelta(hours=2, minutes=1),
    expires=timedelta(hours=4),
)
def task(): ...
```

## Implementation

Adds `celery.utils.time.maybe_seconds()`, the inverse of the existing `maybe_timedelta()`, and uses it to normalise these four arguments in:

* `Celery.send_task()`
* `AMQP.as_task_v1()` and `AMQP.as_task_v2()`

Normalising in `send_task()` matters as well as in `amqp.py`: the native delayed-delivery routing and the expiration check both do arithmetic and comparisons on these values before the message is built, so converting only at message-creation time would leave those paths broken.

A `timedelta` and the equivalent number of seconds now produce identical task messages. Numbers, `None` and `datetime` values are unaffected, so this is backwards compatible.

Docstrings for `apply_async()` and `retry()` and the *ETA and Countdown* / *Expiration* sections of the calling guide are updated to mention the accepted types.

## Verification

New tests, all passing:

* `t/unit/utils/test_time.py` — `maybe_seconds()` over timedeltas, numbers and `None`
* `t/unit/app/test_amqp.py` — timedelta `countdown`/`expires` for `as_task_v2`; an equivalence test asserting a timedelta and the equivalent seconds produce identical messages for both protocols; a JSON-serialisability test for `timelimit`
* `t/unit/app/test_app.py` — `send_task()` normalises all four arguments

Checklist from `CONTRIBUTING.rst`:

* `pytest t/unit` — same 3 pre-existing failures as `main`, +14 passing tests, no new errors (the remaining errors are a pre-existing teardown cascade from a leaked thread in `t/unit/contrib/test_rdb.py`; running the affected modules without it gives 789 passed, 0 errors)
* `pre-commit run --files <changed>` — passed, including mypy and isort
* `bandit -b bandit.json celery/` — 0 issues
* `sphinx-build -b apicheck` / `-b configcheck` — no new warnings

title: Fix Redis result compression with decode_responses enabled
body:
## Description

A regression of #10504.

When `result_compression` is enabled and `decode_responses=True`, Redis stores results successfully, but `AsyncResult.get()` fails with UnicodeDecodeError because the Redis library tries to decode the compressed bytes as UTF-8 before Celery can decompress them.

  This PR disables compression for Redis backends with response decoding enabled

title: Fix argument forwarding through nested chains in eager execution
body:
## Description

Fixes #6200.

`chain(chain(identity.s(), identity.s())).apply(args=(1,))` loses the argument when cloning the inner chain, so its first task raises `TypeError`. The same failure affects `task_always_eager`.

Forward invocation arguments through the cloned signature's `apply()` method. This preserves keyword overrides, immutable signatures and result-parent links, and keeps a task keyword named `tasks` separate from the chain's serialized task list. Add ten unit regressions and enable the existing #6200 and #6176 integration regressions. Both strict expected-failure markers are obsolete after the argument-forwarding fix.

Validation on Python 3.13.5:

- New cases: 9 fail on the base revision; all 10 pass with the fix.
- Related task/canvas suite: 1,018 passed, 1 skipped, 2 existing xfails.
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: passed.
- An isolated in-process worker using the memory transport/backend verifies worker execution, direct `apply`, and `task_always_eager`. A separate 27-case probe covers deeper nesting, groups/chords, immutable tasks and failure propagation.

API/configuration documentation checks have the same failures on the base revision in this lightweight environment. Bandit cannot parse the existing `bandit.json`; its 47 findings match the base revision. The external-broker integration suite and full Python-version matrix were not run locally.

Prepared and tested with OpenAI Codex.

title: Retain fallback context managers until exit
body:
## Description

`FallbackContext` calls `__exit__()` on the value returned by `__enter__()`. That value may be a resource such as a path string, so it is not necessarily the object responsible for cleanup.

On CPython 3.12.13, this example deletes the temporary directory before the `with` body runs and raises `AttributeError` when exiting the block:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from celery.utils.objects import FallbackContext

with FallbackContext(None, TemporaryDirectory) as directory:
    assert Path(directory).is_dir()
```

This change keeps the context manager for cleanup and returns its `__enter__()` result to the caller. The manager is saved only after entry succeeds, so a failed entry does not keep it alive. Tests cover the manager and returned resource being different objects, failed entry, `None` return values, exception handling, and provided resources.

## Validation

- `test_objects.py`: 5 failed and 3 passed on main at `5ea4a4919aec6be425bf7103a18d011ffea1c5f1`; all 8 pass with the fix.
- `pytest -p celery.contrib.pytest t/unit/utils t/unit/app t/unit/test_generics.py -q --timeout=30`: 1,268 passed, 14 skipped, 1 xfailed, and 6 subtests passed.
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: passed, including mypy.
- Actual temporary-directory creation, file write/read and cleanup passed with the fix. Connection and producer acquisition with a memory broker also passed on both base and fixed source, including message round trips and cleanup after exceptions.

These checks used CPython 3.12.13 on macOS. The full upstream test matrix was not run locally.

title: Preserve explicitly supplied empty timer schedules
body:
## Description

`Timer` silently discards an explicitly supplied empty `Schedule`: the constructor uses `schedule or self.Schedule(...)`, and a schedule with no queued entries evaluates to false. This loses the supplied instance's configuration and any custom schedule behavior.

For example, on main:

```python
from celery.utils.timer2 import Schedule, Timer

schedule = Schedule(max_interval=7)
timer = Timer(schedule=schedule)
assert timer.schedule is schedule  # fails
```

Use the default schedule only when `schedule is None`. Add regression coverage for empty and populated schedules, plus default construction with `on_error` and `max_interval`.

## Validation

- The empty-schedule regression fails against main at `5ea4a4919aec6be425bf7103a18d011ffea1c5f1`; all 12 timer tests pass with the fix.
- `pytest -p celery.contrib.pytest t/unit/utils t/unit/worker t/unit/concurrency -q --timeout=30`: 1,320 passed, 4 skipped, 1 xfailed (46 subtests passed).
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: passed, including mypy.
- Started a solo worker with an empty custom schedule, a memory broker/backend, and a countdown task. The task completes on both base and fixed source, but only the fixed source retains and invokes the custom schedule. Worker and timer shutdown completed in both runs.

Local validation used CPython 3.12.13 on macOS with Kombu 5.6.2. The full upstream test matrix was not run locally.

title: fix(app.utils): handle multi-server URLs in sanitize_url and bugreport (#8014)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #8014

Fixes an issue where `celery report`, `app.bugreport()`, or inspecting configuration crashed with `ValueError: Port could not be cast to integer value` when `result_backend` was configured with multiple server hosts (e.g. `cache+memcached://172.19.26.240:11211;172.19.26.242:11211/`).

### Root Cause
`kombu.utils.url.maybe_sanitize_url` uses standard `urllib.parse.urlparse`, which expects a single host:port and fails to parse semicolon-separated (`;`) or comma-separated (`,`) multi-server cluster URIs, raising `ValueError` on the port casting.

### Solution
1. Added `sanitize_url(url, mask)` helper in `celery/app/utils.py` that handles single-server as well as multi-server URIs (split on `;` or `,`), sanitizing credentials on each node individually while preserving URL paths and query strings.
2. Gracefully falls back to returning the URL if parsing fails on unexpected malformed input, preventing `bugreport()` or CLI commands from crashing.
3. Updated `filter_hidden_settings()` and `bugreport()` to use `sanitize_url()`.
4. Exported `sanitize_url` in `celery.app.utils.__all__`.

### Test Coverage
Added comprehensive unit tests in `t/unit/app/test_utils.py`:
- Multi-server semicolon cluster URLs with and without credentials.
- Multi-server cluster URLs with paths and query parameters.
- Comma-separated cluster URLs with credentials.
- Fallback handling on malformed URLs.
- End-to-end `app.bugreport()` and `filter_hidden_settings()` tests with multi-server configurations.
- All 21 tests pass and Flake8 linter reports 0 errors.

cc @auvipy

title: fix(backends.database): store task children with database backend (#8336)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #8336

Resolves the issue where `AsyncResult.children` was not populated or retained when using the database result backend (`celery.backends.database:DatabaseBackend`).

### Background & Context
A previous attempt to store children (#8338) was reverted in #8475 because:
1. It used `sa.Column(PickleType)` directly in the model, forcing Python pickle regardless of `result_serializer`.
2. Existing database installations without the `children` column crashed on queries (`OperationalError: no such column: celery_taskmeta.children`).

### Solution
1. **Model Storage:** Added `children = sa.Column(sa.LargeBinary, nullable=True)` to `Task` in `celery/backends/database/models.py`.
2. **Serializer Compatibility:** Children are serialized using `self.encode(children)` on store and `self.decode(meta['children'])` on retrieval, respecting `result_serializer` (JSON, pickle, etc.).
3. **Graceful Auto-Migration:** Added `_migrate_missing_columns` helper in `SessionManager.prepare_models()` that checks existing schema and automatically executes `ALTER TABLE celery_taskmeta ADD COLUMN children BLOB/BYTEA` if the column is missing, gracefully catching existing setups and permission constraints.
4. **Child Result Reconstruction:** Reconstructs `[self.app.AsyncResult(cid) for cid in children]` when `children` is fetched.

### Test Coverage
Added comprehensive unit tests in `t/unit/backends/test_database.py`:
- `test_store_result_with_children`: Validates storing and retrieving children with both JSON and Pickle serializers.
- `test_async_result_children`: End-to-end test verifying `AsyncResult.children` returns list of `AsyncResult` objects.
- `test_migrate_missing_columns`: Verifies database auto-migration adds `children` column to legacy tables without data loss.
- All 86 database backend tests pass and Flake8 linter reports 0 errors.

cc @auvipy

title: fix(backends.database): store stamping metadata with extended results (#8887)
body:
Fixes #8887

## Description

When tasks are stamped (via `signature.stamp()` or `group.stamp()`) and `result_extended = True`, the database result backend (`celery.backends.database`) dropped all stamping metadata (`stamped_headers` and individual stamp values) upon storing. This caused a `KeyError: 'stamp'` when attempting to retrieve stamps via `_get_task_meta()`.

While document/cache backends (like Redis) serialize the entire dictionary and preserve arbitrary keys, the database backend maps attributes directly to columns in `TaskExtended`. Because `TaskExtended` lacked a `stamps` column, the stamping data was filtered out and lost.

### Changes Made
1. **Model (`celery/backends/database/models.py`)**:
   - Added `stamps = sa.Column(sa.LargeBinary, nullable=True)` to `TaskExtended`.
   - Included `stamps` in `TaskExtended.to_dict()`.
2. **Backend Logic (`celery/backends/database/__init__.py`)**:
   - In `_update_result`: If `stamped_headers` are present in `meta`, packaged the stamp headers and their values into a dict, serialized with `self.encode()`, and assigned to `task.stamps`.
   - In `_get_task_meta_for`: Deserialized `data['stamps']` using `self.decode()`, restoring `data['stamped_headers']`, individual stamp keys (`data[header] = stamp_val`), and `data['stamps']`.
3. **Tests (`t/unit/backends/test_database.py`)**:
   - Added `test_store_result_with_stamps` covering both `pickle` and `json` serializers in `test_DatabaseBackend_result_extended`.

### Testing & Verification
- `pytest t/unit/backends/test_database.py -k "test_store_result_with_stamps"`: **2 passed**
- Full Database Backend test suite (`pytest t/unit/backends/test_database.py`): **83 passed**
- Full Stamping test suite (`pytest t/unit/tasks/test_stamping.py`): **439 passed**
- Code style: Flake8 passed with 0 errors/warnings.

title: Include _keys in ConfigurationView.swap_with()
body:
## Description
`ConfigurationView.swap_with()` copies the mappings, prefix, and key_t, but leaves `_keys` unchanged. When the two views use different converters, a key that works on the source view can fail after the swap.

This PR copies `_keys` too.

title: Honor zero timeouts in the result drainer
body:
## Description

`Drainer.drain_events_until()` treats `timeout=0` as unlimited waiting. Since #10487, ResultSet.join() passes 0 after exhausting its timeout, which can cause it to wait indefinitely.
https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/918a740497a4ce883f37eb1a3e7c2a80dfcc8b7a/celery/result.py#L813-L815

This PR changes the timeout check to treat only `None` as unlimited. It also checks readiness first so already-ready results finish without waiting or raising a timeout.

title: Deny access to private attributes and dunders via registered()
body:
## Description

The `Inspect.registered()` method ([docs](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/latest/reference/celery.app.control.html#celery.app.control.Inspect.registered)) allows specifying, via `taskinfoitems`, the Task attributes to include in the response.

A possibly undesired side effect is that private attributes and dunders can also be accessed this way. For instance, requesting `__dict__` dumps all of a task's instance attributes, which — in the case of a custom `Task` subclass — could include sensitive values.

## Remediation

This PR filters out names beginning with `_` in the worker-side `registered` control handler (`celery/worker/control.py`). Public attributes remain accessible, so the documented `registered('serializer', 'max_retries')` usage is unaffected; this is the least invasive change that keeps the command out of object internals without breaking ergonomics. Unit tests included.

title: Warn when two callables collide under one task name (#10576)
body:
Closes #10576.

## What this does

A task's registered name is `f"{fun.__module__}.{fun.__name__}"`, so two distinct callables that share `__name__` inside one module collapse into a single registered task. The caller of the second one gets `SUCCESS` and the **first** function's result, and neither registration path says anything.

Task names are the wire format — they appear in messages, `task_routes`, beat schedules and monitoring — so **this changes no names**. It only makes the collapse audible, next to the `DuplicateNodenameWarning` that already covers the same class of mistake for node names:

- `DuplicateTaskNameWarning`, in the `CeleryWarning` tree, mirroring `DuplicateNodenameWarning` and `W_DUPNODE`.
- **Both** registration paths report, and each states its own outcome: the decorator path keeps the **first** callable, `register_task` replaces with the **last**. (That disagreement is the second half of the issue; this makes it visible rather than choosing a winner — happy to unify if you would rather, but that is a behaviour change and seemed yours to make.)
- The colliding callables are named with `celery.utils.imports.qualname()` — the helper that lives 94 lines above `gen_task_name` in the same module, and already prefers `__qualname__`. `Backend.prepare_exception` makes the same choice for exception types on the wire.
- One warning per name per app.

## Why identity, not the name

Detection compares the **function object**, not the name. Two closures from one factory share `__name__`, `__qualname__` **and** `__code__`, so no name-based test separates them; a module imported twice hands back the same function object. Object identity is the only thing that tells a re-registration apart from a real collision — the same distinction `DBOS.register_class` makes with `is not cls`.

## Tests

Six tests in `t/unit/app/test_app.py`, in the shape of `test_control.py::test_flatten_reply`:

- closures sharing `__name__`/`__qualname__`/`__code__`
- two classes with same-named methods
- the `register_task` path
- **negative control**: distinct explicit `name=`
- **negative control** (the near miss): identical factory shape, only `__name__` differs
- **negative control**: the *same* function registered twice, i.e. the re-import shape

`t/unit/app` + `t/unit/tasks`: 1699 passed, 0 failed. `flake8` and `isort` clean with your `setup.cfg`.

## Two things you should know before reviewing

**1. Your suite trips this 113 times, and they are real collisions.** Inside `t/unit/tasks/test_trace.py`, `TraceCase.setup_method` registers `add`, and 100+ tests then define their own local `add` in the same module. Celery keeps the first, so the "fresh" task each test believes it created is the fixture's task. I verified the consequence rather than assuming it: mutations such as `add.acks_late = True` land on `self.add` (`mutation visible on self.add -> True`). The tests pass, but the isolation is not there. I have **not** touched your suite — the fix could be explicit `name=`, or nothing at all, and that call is yours. If the output volume is the blocker, say so and I will adjust.

**2. No CI breakage, and one number in the issue thread was mine.** I first ran the full unit suite with `-W error::celery.exceptions.DuplicateTaskNameWarning` and saw 30 failures. That flag was **mine**, not yours: there is no `filterwarnings` in `setup.cfg`/`pyproject.toml` and no `-W error` in the workflows, so the warning does not fail your build.

## Scope

Python only. I did not change which callable survives, add a setting, or touch name generation. Reachability is a `__name__` collision within one module — closures from a factory, same-named methods on two classes, or two same-named functions.

If any of this was raised before, point me at the existing PR and I will close this in favour of it.

title: Respect map order in ConfigurationView lookups
body:
## Description

`ConfigurationView.__getitem__()` currently searches all maps for each key before trying the next key form. This means a prefixed key or alias in a later map can win over a value in an earlier map.

This changes the lookup to try all key forms within each map before moving to the next one, so earlier maps take precedence.

title: Keep the execv flag from leaking between tests
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #10583. Not a bug report: the full unit suite passes on `main` (3911 passed), and it passes with this change too. What this removes is an order dependency that #10583 introduced between two parts of the suite.

#10583 made `Celery.task()` read `FORKED_BY_MULTIPROCESSING` at call time rather than at import time. The reason was real: a pool child started with `spawn` imports `celery.app.base` while unpickling the app, before `process_initializer()` can announce that the child is a fresh interpreter, so the import-time constant is always empty there.

The side effect is that `@app.task` now depends on the variable's value at the moment it is called, and parts of the suite set it mid-process. `components.Pool.create()` reaches `prefork.TaskPool.on_start()`, which sets the variable and does not unset it, so from `t/unit/worker/test_worker.py::test_WorkController::test_Pool_create` onwards every `@app.task` returns a `current_app`-bound proxy:

```
$ pytest t/unit/worker t/unit/app/test_beat.py -q
7 failed, 726 passed          # RuntimeError: Test depends on current_app
$ pytest                      # the whole of t/unit
3911 passed
```

The full run is fine because later tests happen to clear the state again, so CI is unaffected. It shows up when running a subset, which is what I do while working on a change.

## Change

- `celery/app/base.py`: read the variable at import time again, so `@app.task` does not change behaviour part-way through a process.
- `celery/concurrency/prefork.py`: have `process_initializer()` set `celery.app.base.USING_EXECV` directly when the start method is not `fork`. That is what the spawned child actually needs, and it says so more directly than re-reading the environment. The variable is still set, for whatever the child starts later.
- `t/unit/conftest.py`: a `restore_execv_state()` context manager that puts both back.
- `t/unit/worker/test_worker.py`, `t/unit/concurrency/test_prefork.py`: use it in the three places that mark this process as a pool child.

## Testing

- `pytest` (the whole of `t/unit`): 3911 passed, 39 skipped, 3 xfailed, 27673 subtests — identical to `main`.
- `pytest t/unit/worker t/unit/app/test_beat.py`: 733 passed, where `main` gives 7 failed.
- `pytest t/unit/concurrency t/unit/app t/unit/fixups`: 818 passed, same as `main`.
- The behaviour #10583 fixed still works: macOS with billiard 4.3.0rc1 (spawn by default) and a redis broker runs 30/30 tasks, with the flag set in the children.
- The new assertion on `USING_EXECV` in `test_process_initializer_spawned_child` fails without the `prefork.py` change.

title: Document interaction between rate_limit and countdown/eta
body:
Fixes #5810

Turns out rate_limit isn't actually ignored for countdown/eta tasks - I went looking for the reported behavior and couldn't reproduce it on main. When a task has both an ETA and a rate limit, the strategy routes it through `limit_post_eta` (strategy.py): the timer waits for the ETA first, then the request goes into the task's token bucket, so the rate limit still applies. That path has been there since 2017 (#4251), two years before this issue.

Quick check I ran: 6 tasks with `rate_limit="2/s"` and `countdown=1` keep the same ~0.5s spacing as tasks without a countdown, just shifted by exactly the countdown. So the two options compose, one after the other.

What the issue got right is the docs. Nothing in the user guide explains how these two options interact, which is easy to trip over. So this adds two things:

- a note under `Task.rate_limit` saying the ETA comes first and the rate limit is applied after it
- a paragraph in the ETA and Countdown section of the calling guide pointing at the option

Docs build has the same warning count as main, the cross-reference resolves in the built HTML, and `test_strategy.py` + `test_consumer.py` pass (186 tests).

title: Fix linked signature option isolation during deepcopy
body:
## Description

Fixes #10593

Cloning a signature with linked callbacks currently shares those callbacks' execution options with the original template. For example, stamping two clones with different workflow IDs gives both callbacks the second ID; freezing one callback can also make the other clone reuse its task ID.

Deep-copy execution options in `Signature.__deepcopy__()` and memoize the copied dictionary before descending. This isolates nested callback options and keeps repeated references within the copied graph. Task arguments retain their existing behavior, including lazy iterators, and explicitly configured task IDs are preserved.

Regression coverage includes `link`, `link_error`, the `chord` option, serialized-dictionary controls, stamping and freeze isolation, nested/shared/circular links, lazy arguments, and explicit task IDs. No runtime dependencies are added.

## Validation

- On the original implementation, the affected test file reports 9 failed and 9 passed.
- With the fix, `t/unit/test_canvas.py`, `t/unit/tasks/test_canvas.py`, and `t/unit/tasks/test_stamping.py` report 672 passed, 2 xfailed, and 27,627 subtests passed.
- A separate real worker reproduction with the solo pool and memory broker/backend changes `(workflow, callback stamp)` from `[('first', 'second'), ('second', 'second')]` to `[('first', 'first'), ('second', 'second')]`, leaving the template callback options empty.
- Flake8, isort, and `git diff --check` pass for the modified files.

Validated locally on CPython 3.12.10 / Windows 11 against main at `3e40f4332479ccd83527908dc9249c54531380de`. The full tox matrix, external-broker integrations, all-repository pre-commit, documentation builds, and Bandit have not been run locally.

AI assistance: Codex assisted with investigation, patch preparation, and regression tests. The results above were obtained by running the code locally.
